    "front": "Consider a finite-duration sequence <i>{x(n)}</i> of length <i>N = 4</i>, where <i>x(n) = {1, 1, 1, 1}</i>. Compute the DFT <i>X(k)</i> for <i>k = 0, 1, 2, 3</i> using the direct definition (Equation 8.4.1). Show all steps.",
    "back": "<b>Step-by-Step DFT Computation:</b><br><br>Given <i>x(n) = {1, 1, 1, 1}</i> and <i>N = 4</i>, the twiddle factor is <i>W_4 = e^{-j2π/4} = e^{-jπ/2} = -j</i>.<br><br>The DFT is defined as:<br><br>\\[ X(k) = \\sum_{n=0}^{3} x(n) W_4^{kn} \\]<br><br><br>1. For <i>k = 0</i>:<br><br>   \\[ X(0) = \\sum_{n=0}^{3} x(n) W_4^{0} = 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 4 \\]<br><br><br>2. For <i>k = 1</i>:<br><br>   \\[ X(1) = \\sum_{n=0}^{3} x(n) W_4^{n} = 1 + W_4^{1} + W_4^{2} + W_4^{3} \\]<br><br>   Substituting <i>W_4 = -j</i>:<br><br>   \\[ X(1) = 1 + (-j) + (-j)^2 + (-j)^3 = 1 - j - 1 + j = 0 \\]<br><br><br>3. For <i>k = 2</i>:<br><br>   \\[ X(2) = \\sum_{n=0}^{3} x(n) W_4^{2n} = 1 + W_4^{2} + W_4^{4} + W_4^{6} \\]<br><br>   Since <i>W_4^{4} = 1</i> and <i>W_4^{6} = W_4^{2}</i>:<br><br>   \\[ X(2) = 1 + (-1) + 1 + (-1) = 0 \\]<br><br><br>4. For <i>k = 3</i>:<br><br>   \\[ X(3) = \\sum_{n=0}^{3} x(n) W_4^{3n} = 1 + W_4^{3} + W_4^{6} + W_4^{9} \\]<br><br>   Simplifying exponents:<br><br>   \\[ X(3) = 1 + (-j)^3 + (-1) + (-j)^1 = 1 + j - 1 - j = 0 \\]<br><br><br><b>Final DFT:</b><br><br>\\[ X(k) = \\{4, 0, 0, 0\\} \\]<br><br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>This example illustrates the direct computation of the DFT for a simple, constant sequence. The result shows that the DFT of a DC signal (all ones) is non-zero only at <i>k = 0</i>, corresponding to zero frequency. This aligns with the intuition that a constant signal has no frequency components other than DC. {
  "front": "Compare the method of separating variables to other techniques for solving partial differential equations (PDEs). What are its advantages and limitations?",
  "back": "<b>Advantages of Separating Variables:</b><br><ul><li><b>Simplification:</b> Reduces a PDE into ODEs, which are easier to solve analytically.</li><li><b>Applicability:</b> Effective for linear PDEs with homogeneous boundary conditions (e.g., wave, heat, and Laplace equations).</li><li><b>Physical Insight:</b> Solutions often reveal natural modes of vibration or diffusion, aiding interpretation.</li></ul><br><b>Limitations:</b><br><ul><li><b>Restrictive Assumptions:</b> Requires the PDE to be separable and boundary conditions to be homogeneous.</li><li><b>Complexity:</b> May lead to infinite series solutions (e.g., Fourier series), which can be cumbersome to evaluate.</li><li><b>Nonlinear PDEs:</b> Fails for nonlinear PDEs, where other methods (e.g., numerical or perturbation techniques) are needed.</li></ul><br><b>Alternatives:</b><br><ul><li><b>Numerical Methods:</b> Finite difference or finite element methods for complex geometries or nonlinearities.</li><li><b>Transform Methods:</b> Laplace or Fourier transforms for non-homogeneous problems.</li></ul><hr><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br>Separating variables is a cornerstone of analytical PDE solutions in engineering, but its utility depends on the problem’s structure. For example, it excels in modeling idealized systems (e.g., uniform strings) but may struggle with irregular boundaries or nonlinear materials, where numerical methods become indispensable."
}
```

{
  "front": "What is the physical interpretation of the separation constant <i>k</i> in the context of the vibrating string problem?",
  "back": "The separation constant <i>k</i> determines the spatial and temporal behavior of the string’s vibrational modes:<br><br>- For <i>k &lt; 0</i>, the solutions to the ODEs for <i>F(x)</i> and <i>G(t)</i> are sinusoidal, corresponding to standing waves (natural modes of vibration).<br>- The value of <i>k</i> is directly related to the wavelength and frequency of these modes. Specifically, <i>k = -(\\frac{n\\pi}{L})^{2}</i> for <i>n = 1, 2, 3, ...</i>, where <i>n</i> is the mode number.<br>- The boundary conditions <i>u(0,t) = 0</i> and <i>u(L,t) = 0</i> quantize <i>k</i>, leading to discrete vibrational frequencies.<hr><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br>The separation constant <i>k</i> bridges the gap between the mathematical solution and physical reality. It explains why a string can only vibrate at specific frequencies (harmonics), which is why musical instruments produce distinct pitches. This quantization is a hallmark of wave phenomena in bounded systems."
}
```

  "front": "Compare and contrast the one-dimensional wave equation and the one-dimensional heat equation in terms of their mathematical form, physical interpretation, and the nature of their solutions.",
  "back": "Here is a comparison of the one-dimensional wave equation and the one-dimensional heat equation:<br><br><br><br><table border='1'><br><tr><br><th>Feature</th><br><th>One-Dimensional Wave Equation</th><br><th>One-Dimensional Heat Equation</th><br></tr><br><tr><br><td><b>Mathematical Form</b></td><br><td>\\( \\frac{\\partial^2 u}{\\partial t^2} = c^2 \\frac{\\partial^2 u}{\\partial x^2} \\)</td><br><td>\\( \\frac{\\partial u}{\\partial t} = c^2 \\frac{\\partial^2 u}{\\partial x^2} \\)</td><br></tr><br><tr><br><td><b>Order of Time Derivative</b></td><br><td>Second-order (\\( \\frac{\\partial^2 u}{\\partial t^2} \\))</td><br><td>First-order (\\( \\frac{\\partial u}{\\partial t} \\))</td><br></tr><br><tr><br><td><b>Physical Interpretation</b></td><br><td>Models the propagation of waves (e.g., vibrations of a string, sound waves) in a medium. The solution represents the displacement of the medium as a function of space and time.</td><br><td>Models the distribution of heat (or temperature) in a one-dimensional rod over time. The solution represents the temperature at each point in the rod as a function of time.</td><br></tr><br><tr><br><td><b>Nature of Solutions</b></td><br><td>Solutions are <b>wave-like</b> and exhibit oscillatory behavior. They preserve the shape of initial disturbances and propagate them at speed <i>c</i>. Energy is conserved in ideal systems.</td><br><td>Solutions are <b>diffusive</b> and exhibit smoothing behavior. Initial disturbances spread out and decay over time, leading to a uniform temperature distribution in the long term. Energy is not conserved but dissipates.</td><br></tr><br><tr><br><td><b>Typical Initial Conditions</b></td><br><td>Requires two initial conditions: the initial displacement <i>u(x, 0)</i> and the initial velocity \\( \\frac{\\partial u}{\\partial t}(x, 0) \\).</td><br><td>Requires one initial condition: the initial temperature distribution <i>u(x, 0)</i>.</td><br></tr><br><tr><br><td><b>Boundary Conditions</b></td><br><td>Often involves fixed or free ends (e.g., <i>u(0, t) = 0</i> for a fixed end).</td><br><td>Often involves fixed temperatures or insulated boundaries (e.g., <i>u(0, t) = T_0</i> for a fixed temperature).</td><br></tr><br></table><br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>The wave and heat equations exemplify two fundamental classes of PDEs: hyperbolic and parabolic, respectively. The wave equation describes systems where information propagates as waves, while the heat equation describes systems where information diffuses. This distinction is critical in fields like acoustics, thermodynamics, and signal processing, where the behavior of the system depends on whether it is wave-dominated or diffusion-dominated."
}

{
  "front": "What is the physical significance of the constant <i>c</i> in the wave equation and the heat equation, and how does it influence the behavior of their solutions?",
  "back": "The constant <i>c</i> in the wave equation and the heat equation represents a <b>material or medium-specific parameter</b> that governs the rate at which information propagates or diffuses. Its physical significance and influence on the solutions differ for each equation:<br><br><br><br><h3>Wave Equation (\\( \\frac{\\partial^2 u}{\\partial t^2} = c^2 \\frac{\\partial^2 u}{\\partial x^2} \\)):</h3><br>- <b>Physical Significance</b>: In the wave equation, <i>c</i> represents the <b>wave propagation speed</b> in the medium. For example:<br><br>  - In a vibrating string, <i>c</i> is given by \\( c = \\sqrt{\\frac{T}{\\rho}} \\), where <i>T</i> is the tension in the string and <i>\\rho</i> is the linear mass density.<br><br>  - In acoustics, <i>c</i> is the speed of sound in the medium.<br><br>- <b>Influence on Solutions</b>: The value of <i>c</i> determines how quickly waves travel through the medium. A larger <i>c</i> means waves propagate faster, while a smaller <i>c</i> means slower propagation. The shape of the wave is preserved, but its speed and wavelength are directly affected by <i>c</i>.<br><br><br><br><h3>Heat Equation (\\( \\frac{\\partial u}{\\partial t} = c^2 \\frac{\\partial^2 u}{\\partial x^2} \\)):</h3><br>- <b>Physical Significance</b>: In the heat equation, <i>c^2</i> (often denoted as <i>\\alpha</i>) represents the <b>thermal diffusivity</b> of the material. It is given by \\( c^2 = \\frac{k}{\\rho C_p} \\), where:<br><br>  - <i>k</i> is the thermal conductivity of the material.<br><br>  - <i>\\rho</i> is the mass density.<br><br>  - <i>C_p</i> is the specific heat capacity.<br><br>- <b>Influence on Solutions</b>: The value of <i>c^2</i> determines how quickly heat diffuses through the material. A larger <i>c^2</i> means faster heat diffusion, leading to more rapid temperature equalization. A smaller <i>c^2</i> means slower diffusion, resulting in more gradual temperature changes.<br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>The constant <i>c</i> (or <i>c^2</i>) is a critical parameter that links the mathematical form of the PDE to the physical properties of the system it models. In the wave equation, <i>c</i> governs the dynamics of wave propagation, while in the heat equation, <i>c^2</i> controls the rate of thermal diffusion. Understanding the role of <i>c</i> is essential for designing systems in engineering and physics, such as optimizing materials for heat conduction or predicting wave behavior in different media."
}
```

The coefficients <i>B<sub>n</sub></i> are given by the Fourier sine series of <i>f(x)</i>. From Example 4 in Sec. 11.3, we have:<br><br>\\[ B_{n} = \\frac{8k}{n^{2} \\pi^{2}} \\sin \\frac{n \\pi}{2} \\]<br><br>   - For even <i>n</i>, <i>B<sub>n</sub> = 0</i>.<br><br>   - For odd <i>n = 2m + 1</i>, <i>B<sub>n</sub> = (-1)<sup>m</sup> \\frac{8k}{(2m+1)^{2} \\pi^{2}}</i>.<br><br><br>3. Substitute <i>B<sub>n</sub></i> into the general solution:<br><br>\\[ u(x,t) = \\frac{8k}{\\pi^{2}} \\sum_{m=0}^{\\infty} \\frac{(-1)^{m}}{(2m+1)^{2}} \\sin \\frac{(2m+1) \\pi x}{L} \\cos \\frac{(2m+1) \\pi c t}{L} \\]<br><br>   Simplifying the first few terms:<br><br>\\[ u(x,t) = \\frac{8k}{\\pi^{2}} \\left[ \\frac{1}{1^{2}} \\sin \\frac{\\pi x}{L} \\cos \\frac{\\pi c t}{L} - \\frac{1}{3^{2}} \\sin \\frac{3 \\pi x}{L} \\cos \\frac{3 \\pi c t}{L} + - \\dots \\right] \\]<br><br><br><br><b>Physical Interpretation:</b><br><br>The solution represents the superposition of standing waves (normal modes) on the string. The triangular initial displacement excites multiple odd harmonics, with the amplitude of each harmonic decreasing as <i>1/n<sup>2</sup></i>. The fundamental mode (<i>n=1</i>) dominates the motion, while higher harmonics contribute finer details to the shape of the string over time.<br><br><br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>This example illustrates how a non-smooth initial condition (triangular displacement) can be decomposed into a series of smooth sine waves. The rapid decay of the coefficients <i>B<sub>n</sub></i> ensures the series converges quickly, making the first few terms a good approximation of the solution. This problem is a classic demonstration of how Fourier series can model complex initial conditions in physical systems."
}

### Avant:
```json
{
  "front": "Consider a vibrating string of length <i>L = 2 m</i> with wave speed <i>c = 100 m/s</i>. Determine the first three eigenfunctions <i>F<sub>n</sub>(x)</i> and their corresponding eigenvalues <i>λ<sub>n</sub></i>. Also, compute the frequency of the fundamental mode (<i>n = 1</i>).",
  "back": "<b>Eigenfunctions:</b><br>The eigenfunctions are given by:<br>\\[ F_{n}(x) = \\sin\\left(\\frac{n \\pi}{L} x\\right) = \\sin\\left(\\frac{n \\pi}{2} x\\right). \\]<br>For <i>n = 1, 2, 3</i>:<br>\\[ F_{1}(x) = \\sin\\left(\\frac{\\pi}{2} x\\right), \\]<br>\\[ F_{2}(x) = \\sin\\left(\\pi x\\right), \\]<br>\\[ F_{3}(x) = \\sin\\left(\\frac{3 \\pi}{2} x\\right). \\]<br><br><b>Eigenvalues:</b><br>The eigenvalues are:<br>\\[ \\lambda_{n} = \\frac{c n \\pi}{L} = \\frac{100 n \\pi}{2} = 50 n \\pi. \\]<br>For <i>n = 1, 2, 3</i>:<br>\\[ \\lambda_{1} = 50 \\pi \\approx 157.08 \\, \\text{rad/s}, \\]<br>\\[ \\lambda_{2} = 100 \\pi \\approx 314.16 \\, \\text{rad/s}, \\]<br>\\[ \\lambda_{3} = 150 \\pi \\approx 471.24 \\, \\text{rad/s}. \\]<br><br><b>Frequency of the Fundamental Mode:</b><br>The frequency <i>f<sub>1</sub></i> is:<br>\\[ f_{1} = \\frac{\\lambda_{1}}{2 \\pi} = \\frac{50 \\pi}{2 \\pi} = 25 \\, \\text{Hz}. \\]<br><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br>This example illustrates how the eigenfunctions and eigenvalues translate into physical properties of the string. The fundamental mode (<i>n = 1</i>) corresponds to the lowest frequency of vibration, which is the pitch we perceive. Higher modes (<i>n > 1</i>) correspond to overtones, which contribute to the timbre of the sound. The wave speed <i>c</i> and string length <i>L</i> directly influence the frequencies, as seen in the formula <i>λ<sub>n</sub> = cnπ/L</i>."
}
```

{
  "front": "For the second normal mode (<i>n = 2</i>) of a vibrating string of length <i>L</i>, sketch the shape of the string at <i>t = 0</i>, <i>t = π/(2λ<sub>2</sub>)</i>, and <i>t = π/λ<sub>2</sub></i>. Describe the motion of the string over one period.",
  "back": "<b>Eigenfunction and Temporal Solution:</b><br>The second normal mode is given by:<br>\\[ u_{2}(x, t) = \\left(B_{2} \\cos(\\lambda_{2} t) + B_{2}^{\\mathrm{e}} \\sin(\\lambda_{2} t)\\right) \\sin\\left(\\frac{2 \\pi}{L} x\\right), \\]<br>where <i>λ<sub>2</sub> = 2cπ/L</i>. For simplicity, assume <i>B<sub>2</sub><sup>e</sup> = 0</i> and <i>B<sub>2</sub> = 1</i>, so:<br>\\[ u_{2}(x, t) = \\cos(\\lambda_{2} t) \\sin\\left(\\frac{2 \\pi}{L} x\\right). \\]<br><br><b>Shapes at Specific Times:</b><br><br>- <b><i>t = 0</i>:</b><br>\\[ u_{2}(x, 0) = \\sin\\left(\\frac{2 \\pi}{L} x\\right). \\]<br>The string has a full sine wave shape with one node at <i>x = L/2</i>. The left half (<i>0 <x < L/2</i>) is above the equilibrium, and the right half (<i>L/2 <x < L</i>) is below.<br><br>- <b><i>t = π/(2λ<sub>2</sub>)</i>:</b><br>\\[ u_{2}\\left(x, \\frac{\\pi}{2 \\lambda_{2}}\\right) = \\cos\\left(\\frac{\\pi}{2}\\right) \\sin\\left(\\frac{2 \\pi}{L} x\\right) = 0. \\]<br>The string is momentarily at equilibrium (flat) everywhere.<br><br>- <b><i>t = π/λ<sub>2</sub></i>:</b><br>\\[ u_{2}\\left(x, \\frac{\\pi}{\\lambda_{2}}\\right) = \\cos(\\pi) \\sin\\left(\\frac{2 \\pi}{L} x\\right) = -\\sin\\left(\\frac{2 \\pi}{L} x\\right). \\]<br>The string has the same shape as at <i>t = 0</i>, but inverted (left half below equilibrium, right half above).<br><br><b>Motion Over One Period:</b><br>The string oscillates between the shapes at <i>t = 0</i> and <i>t = π/λ<sub>2</sub></i>, passing through equilibrium at <i>t = π/(2λ<sub>2</sub>)</i>. The two halves of the string move in opposite directions: when the left half moves down, the right half moves up, and vice versa. The node at <i>x = L/2</i> remains stationary throughout.<br><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br>This example demonstrates the temporal evolution of a normal mode. The second mode's behavior—with its single node and out-of-phase segments—is characteristic of standing waves. The periodicity of the motion (<i>T = 2π/λ<sub>2</sub></i>) shows how the string returns to its initial configuration after one full cycle. This is a key concept in understanding how musical instruments produce sustained tones."
}

  "front": "How is the one-dimensional wave equation derived for a vibrating elastic string, and what physical principles are involved in its derivation?",
  "back": "The one-dimensional wave equation for a vibrating elastic string is derived using the following physical principles and steps:<br><br><br>1. <b>Assumptions</b>:<br><br>   - The string is perfectly elastic, homogeneous, and flexible.<br><br>   - The string undergoes small transverse vibrations, meaning the displacement \\( u(x,t) \\) is small compared to the length of the string.<br><br>   - The tension \\( T \\) in the string is constant and much larger than the weight of the string.<br><br>   - No external forces (e.g., gravity or damping) act on the string.<br><br><br>2. <b>Newton's Second Law</b>: Apply Newton's second law to a small segment of the string. The net force acting on the segment in the vertical direction is due to the difference in tension at the two ends of the segment.<br><br>   - The vertical component of the tension at position \\( x \\) is \\( T \\sin(\\theta) \\), where \\( \\theta \\) is the angle the string makes with the horizontal.<br><br>   - For small displacements, \\( \\sin(\\theta) \\approx \\tan(\\theta) = \\frac{\\partial u}{\\partial x} \\).<br><br>   - The net vertical force on the segment is \\( T \\left( \\frac{\\partial u}{\\partial x} \\bigg|_{x+\\Delta x} - \\frac{\\partial u}{\\partial x} \\bigg|_{x} \\right) \\).<br><br><br>3. <b>Equation of Motion</b>:<br><br>   - The mass of the segment is \\( \\rho \\Delta x \\), where \\( \\rho \\) is the linear mass density of the string.<br><br>   - The acceleration of the segment is \\( \\frac{\\partial^2 u}{\\partial t^2} \\).<br><br>   - Applying Newton's second law: \\( \\rho \\Delta x \\frac{\\partial^2 u}{\\partial t^2} = T \\left( \\frac{\\partial u}{\\partial x} \\bigg|_{x+\\Delta x} - \\frac{\\partial u}{\\partial x} \\bigg|_{x} \\right) \\).<br><br><br>4. <b>Taking the Limit</b>:<br><br>   - Divide both sides by \\( \\Delta x \\) and take the limit as \\( \\Delta x \\to 0 \\).<br><br>   - This yields the one-dimensional wave equation: <br>   \\[ \\frac{\\partial^2 u}{\\partial t^2} = c^2 \\frac{\\partial^2 u}{\\partial x^2}, \\]<br>   where \\( c = \\sqrt{\\frac{T}{\\rho}} \\) is the wave speed.<br><br><br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>The derivation of the wave equation illustrates how fundamental physical laws (e.g., Newton's second law) can be combined with mathematical approximations (e.g., small-angle approximation) to model real-world systems. This equation is not just a mathematical abstraction; it directly describes how waves propagate through a medium, such as the vibration of a musical instrument string or the transmission of sound. Understanding its derivation helps bridge the gap between physical intuition and mathematical formalism."
}

  "back": "<b>Solution:</b><br><br>1. Rewrite the PDE in polar coordinates. Recall the transformations:<br><br>\\[x = r \\cos \\theta, \\quad y = r \\sin \\theta.\\]<br><br>2. Express the partial derivatives \\(z_x\\) and \\(z_y\\) in terms of \\(z_r\\) and \\(z_\\theta\\) using the chain rule:<br><br>\\[z_x = z_r \\frac{\\partial r}{\\partial x} + z_\\theta \\frac{\\partial \\theta}{\\partial x} = z_r \\cos \\theta - z_\\theta \\frac{\\sin \\theta}{r},\\]<br><br>\\[z_y = z_r \\frac{\\partial r}{\\partial y} + z_\\theta \\frac{\\partial \\theta}{\\partial y} = z_r \\sin \\theta + z_\\theta \\frac{\\cos \\theta}{r}.\\]<br><br>3. Substitute into the PDE \\(y z_x = x z_y\\):<br><br>\\[r \\sin \\theta \\left(z_r \\cos \\theta - z_\\theta \\frac{\\sin \\theta}{r}\\right) = r \\cos \\theta \\left(z_r \\sin \\theta + z_\\theta \\frac{\\cos \\theta}{r}\\right).\\]<br><br>4. Simplify the equation:<br><br>\\[z_r r \\sin \\theta \\cos \\theta - z_\\theta \\sin^2 \\theta = z_r r \\sin \\theta \\cos \\theta + z_\\theta \\cos^2 \\theta.\\]<br><br>5. Cancel terms and rearrange:<br><br>\\[-z_\\theta (\\sin^2 \\theta + \\cos^2 \\theta) = 0 \\implies z_\\theta = 0.\\]<br><br>6. Since \\(z_\\theta = 0\\), \\(z\\) does not depend on \\(\\theta\\). Thus, \\(z = z(r)\\), meaning \\(z\\) is a function of \\(r = \\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\\) only. This describes a surface of revolution about the \\(z\\)-axis.<br><br><br><b>Example:</b><br><br>A simple example is the paraboloid of revolution:<br><br>\\[z = x^2 + y^2 = r^2.\\]<br><br>Here, \\(z\\) depends only on \\(r\\), satisfying the condition for a surface of revolution.<br><br><br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>Surfaces of revolution are generated by rotating a curve around an axis. The PDE \\(y z_x = x z_y\\) captures this symmetry by enforcing that \\(z\\) does not vary with the angular coordinate \\(\\theta\\). This problem illustrates how coordinate transformations can simplify PDEs and reveal underlying geometric properties. Such techniques are widely used in physics and engineering to model symmetric systems (e.g., cylindrical or spherical symmetry)."
}

{
  "front": "What would happen to the wave equation if the string's mass per unit length \\((\\rho)\\) were not constant (non-homogeneous string)? How would the derivation change?",
  "back": "<b>Effect of Non-Constant \\(\\rho\\):</b><br><br>If the string's mass per unit length \\(\\rho\\) is not constant (i.e., \\(\\rho = \\rho(x)\\)), the wave equation would become:<br><br>\\[\\frac{\\partial^{2} u}{\\partial t^{2}} = \\frac{T}{\\rho(x)} \\frac{\\partial^{2} u}{\\partial x^{2}}.\\]<br><br>This is a <b>variable-coefficient PDE</b>, which is significantly harder to solve than the constant-coefficient case.<br><br><br><b>Changes in Derivation:</b><br><br>1. <b>Mass of the Portion:</b> The mass of the small portion of the string would no longer be \\(\\rho \\Delta x\\), but \\(\\int_{x}^{x + \\Delta x} \\rho(\\xi) d\\xi\\). For small \\(\\Delta x\\), this can be approximated as \\(\\rho(x) \\Delta x\\), but \\(\\rho(x)\\) cannot be factored out of the force balance.<br><br>2. <b>Force Balance:</b> The vertical force balance (Newton's second law) would become:<br><br>   \\[T_{2} \\sin \\beta - T_{1} \\sin \\alpha = \\left(\\int_{x}^{x + \\Delta x} \\rho(\\xi) d\\xi\\right) \\frac{\\partial^{2} u}{\\partial t^{2}}.\\]<br><br>3. <b>Limit Process:</b> Dividing by \\(\\Delta x\\) and taking the limit as \\(\\Delta x \\rightarrow 0\\) would yield:<br><br>   \\[\\frac{\\partial^{2} u}{\\partial t^{2}} = \\frac{T}{\\rho(x)} \\frac{\\partial^{2} u}{\\partial x^{2}},\\]<br><br>   where \\(\\rho(x)\\) remains inside the equation.<br><br><br><b>Consequences:</b><br><br>- The wave speed \\(c = \\sqrt{T/\\rho(x)}\\) would vary with \\(x\\), leading to <b>non-uniform wave propagation</b>.<br><br>- Solutions would no longer be simple sinusoidal waves; they might reflect or refract at points where \\(\\rho(x)\\) changes.<br><br>- Analytical solutions would be difficult to obtain, and numerical methods (e.g., finite differences) would often be required.<br><br><br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>Non-homogeneous strings are common in real-world applications (e.g., strings with varying thickness or density). The variable-coefficient wave equation models such systems but sacrifices the simplicity of the constant-coefficient case. This problem highlights how assumptions (e.g., homogeneity) simplify models while limiting their applicability. Engineers often start with idealized models and later relax assumptions to study more complex behaviors."
}

  "front": "Why is the wave equation classified as a <i>hyperbolic</i> PDE, and what are the implications for its solutions?",
  "back": "<b>Classification as Hyperbolic:</b><br><br>The wave equation:<br><br>\\[\\frac{\\partial^{2} u}{\\partial t^{2}} = c^{2} \\frac{\\partial^{2} u}{\\partial x^{2}}\\]<br><br>is classified as a <b>hyperbolic PDE</b> because its discriminant (for the general second-order PDE \\(A u_{tt} + B u_{tx} + C u_{xx} + \\dots = 0\\)) satisfies \\(B^2 - 4 A C > 0\\). Here, \\(A = 1\\), \\(B = 0\\), and \\(C = -c^2\\), so:<br><br>\\[B^2 - 4 A C = 0 - 4(1)(-c^2) = 4 c^2 > 0.\\]<br><br><br><b>Implications for Solutions:</b><br><br>1. <b>Wave Propagation:</b> Hyperbolic PDEs describe <b>wave-like phenomena</b>, where disturbances propagate at finite speeds (here, \\(c\\)) without dissipating. Solutions are typically traveling waves or superpositions of waves.<br><br>2. <b>Characteristic Curves:</b> Hyperbolic PDEs have real characteristic curves (here, \\(x \\pm c t = \\text{const.}\\)), along which information propagates. This leads to solutions of the form:<br><br>   \\[u(x, t) = f(x - c t) + g(x + c t),\\]<br><br>   where \\(f\\) and \\(g\\) are arbitrary functions representing waves traveling in the \\(+x\\) and \\(-x\\) directions, respectively.<br><br>3. <b>Finite Speed of Propagation:</b> Initial disturbances affect the solution only within a"
}

{
  "front": "How does the method of deriving the wave equation for a vibrating string compare to the method used for modeling a vibrating membrane (e.g., a drumhead)?",
  "back": "<b>Comparison of Derivation Methods:</b><br><br>1. <b>Dimensionality:</b><br><br>   - <b>String:</b> The wave equation is one-dimensional (\\(u(x, t)\\)), derived by analyzing forces on a small segment of the string (length \\(\\Delta x\\)).<br><br>   - <b>Membrane:</b> The wave equation is two-dimensional (\\(u(x, y, t)\\)), derived by analyzing forces on a small patch of the membrane (area \\(\\Delta x \\Delta y\\)).<br><br>2. <b>Tension and Forces:</b><br><br>   - <b>String:</b> Tension \\(T\\) is tangential to the string, and the vertical force balance involves the difference in slopes at the endpoints of a segment.<br><br>   - <b>Membrane:</b> Tension \\(T\\) acts uniformly in all directions (isotropic), and the force balance involves the Laplacian \\(\\nabla^2 u = u_{xx} + u_{yy}\\), representing the curvature of the membrane.<br><br>3. <b>Resulting PDE:</b><br><br>   - <b>String:</b> \\(\\frac{\\partial^{2} u}{\\partial t^{2}} = c^{2} \\frac{\\partial^{2} u}{\\partial x^{2}}\\), where \\(c^2 = T / \\rho\\).<br><br>   - <b>Membrane:</b> \\(\\frac{\\partial^{2} u}{\\partial t^{2}} = c^{2} \\nabla^2 u = c^{2} \\left(\\frac{\\partial^{2} u}{\\partial x^{2}} + \\frac{\\partial^{2} u}{\\partial y^{2}}\\right)\\), where \\(c^2 = T / \\rho\\) (with \\(\\rho\\) now mass per unit area).<br><br>4. <b>Assumptions:</b><br><br>   - Both derivations assume small deflections, no bending resistance, and negligible external forces (e.g., gravity).<br><br>   - The membrane derivation additionally assumes uniform tension in all directions.<br><br>5. <b>Physical Interpretation:</b><br><br>   - <b>String:</b> Solutions are transverse waves traveling along a line (e.g., sinusoidal waves).<br><br>   - <b>Membrane:</b> Solutions are two-dimensional waves (e.g., circular or rectangular modes), leading to more complex patterns (e.g., nodal lines in drumheads).<br><br><br><b>Key Similarities:</b><br><br>- Both derivations use Newton's second law (\\(F = m a\\)) to relate forces to acceleration.<br><br>- Both result in hyperbolic PDEs with wave speed \\(c = \\sqrt{T / \\rho}\\).<br><br>- Both require boundary conditions (e.g., fixed edges) to solve uniquely.<br><br><br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>The method for the string is a foundational example of modeling one-dimensional wave phenomena, while the membrane extends these ideas to two dimensions. The transition from 1D to 2D introduces mathematical complexity (e.g., the Laplacian) but retains the core physical principles. This comparison highlights how dimensionality and geometry influence the form of PDEs in engineering and physics."
}
```

{
  "front": "What role do the images in Fig. 286 play in understanding the derivation of the wave equation, and how would the derivation change if the string were not depicted in a vertical plane?",
  "back": "<b>Role of Fig. 286:</b><br><br>The images in Fig. 286 serve several critical purposes in the derivation:<br><br>1. <b>Visualizing the Deflected String:</b> The figure shows the string's shape at a fixed time \\(t\\), with deflection \\(u(x, t)\\) and slope \\(\\partial u / \\partial x\\). This helps connect the abstract function \\(u(x, t)\\) to the physical system.<br><br>2. <b>Illustrating Tension Components:</b> The figure depicts the tension \\(T_{1}\\) and \\(T_{2}\\) at points \\(P\\) and \\(Q\\), along with their horizontal and vertical components. This clarifies how the force balance is applied to a small portion of the string.<br><br>3. <b>Highlighting Small-Angle Approximations:</b> The figure emphasizes that the angles \\(\\alpha\\) and \\(\\beta\\) are small, justifying the approximations \\(\\sin \\theta \\approx \\tan \\theta\\) and \\(\\cos \\theta \\approx 1\\).<br><br><br><b>Effect of Non-Vertical Orientation:</b><br><br>If the string were not depicted in a vertical plane (e.g., vibrating in 3D space), the derivation would change as follows:<br><br>1. <b>Deflection Function:</b> The deflection \\(u(x, t)\\) would become a vector \\(\\mathbf{u}(x, t) = (u_1(x, t), u_2(x, t))\\), representing displacements in two transverse directions (e.g., \\(y\\) and \\(z\\)).<br><br>2. <b>Tension Components:</b> The tension would still be tangential, but its components would now lie in 3D space. The force balance would require vector calculus (e.g., dot products to resolve components).<br><br>3. <b>Resulting PDE:</b> The wave equation would generalize to a system of two coupled PDEs (one for each transverse direction):<br><br>   \\[\\frac{\\partial^{2} u_1}{\\partial t^{2}} = c^{2} \\frac{\\partial^{2} u_1}{\\partial x^{2}}, \\quad \\frac{\\partial^{2} u_2}{\\partial t^{2}} = c^{2} \\frac{\\partial^{2} u_2}{\\partial x^{2}}.\\]<br><br>4. <b>Polarization:</b> The string could exhibit <b>polarization</b> (e.g., circular or elliptical motion), where the two transverse components are coupled. This is not possible in the 2D (vertical plane) case.<br><br><br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>Fig. 286 simplifies the derivation by restricting the problem to 2D, which is sufficient for many applications (e.g., musical instruments). However, real-world strings can vibrate in 3D, leading to richer dynamics (e.g., torsional waves or coupled transverse modes). The 2D assumption is a common simplification in introductory PDE courses, analogous to modeling a pendulum in a plane rather than 3D space."
}
```

{
  "front": "For a simply supported beam of length \\( L \\) (Fig. 293A), derive the normal mode solutions \\( u_{n}(x,t) = F_{n}(x)G_{n}(t) \\) of the vibrating beam PDE, given zero initial velocity and the boundary conditions:<br><br>- \\( u(0, t) = 0 \\) (displacement zero at left end)<br><br>- \\( u(L, t) = 0 \\) (displacement zero at right end)<br><br>- \\( u_{xx}(0, t) = 0 \\) (zero moment at left end)<br><br>- \\( u_{xx}(L, t) = 0 \\) (zero moment at right end).",
  "back": "<b>Step 1: Apply Boundary Conditions to \\( F(x) \\):</b><br><br>General spatial solution: \\( F(x) = A \\cos \\beta x + B \\sin \\beta x + C \\cosh \\beta x + D \\sinh \\beta x \\).<br><br>1. \\( F(0) = 0 \\): \\( A + C = 0 \\implies C = -A \\)<br><br>2. \\( F''(0) = 0 \\): \\( -A \\beta^{2} + C \\beta^{2} = 0 \\implies C = A \\).<br><br>   Combining with \\( C = -A \\), we get \\( A = C = 0 \\).<br><br>3. \\( F(L) = 0 \\): \\( B \\sin \\beta L + D \\sinh \\beta L = 0 \\).<br><br>4. \\( F''(L) = 0 \\): \\( -B \\beta^{2} \\sin \\beta L + D \\beta^{2} \\sinh \\beta L = 0 \\).<br><br>   For non-trivial solutions, \\( \\sin \\beta L = 0 \\) (since \\( \\sinh \\beta L \\neq 0 \\) for \\( \\beta L \\neq 0 \\)).<br><br>   Thus, \\( \\beta L = n \\pi \\) for \\( n = 1, 2, 3, \\dots \\)<br><br>   Eigenvalues: \\( \\beta_{n} = \\frac{n \\pi}{L} \\)<br><br>   Spatial modes: \\( F_{n}(x) = B_{n} \\sin \\left( \\frac{n \\pi x}{L} \\right) \\)<br><br><br><b>Step 2: Temporal Solution with Zero Initial Velocity:</b><br><br>\\( G_{n}(t) = a_{n} \\cos (c \\beta_{n}^{2} t) + b_{n} \\sin (c \\beta_{n}^{2} t) \\).<br><br>Zero initial velocity: \\( \\dot{G}_{n}(0) = 0 \\implies b_{n} = 0 \\).<br><br>Thus, \\( G_{n}(t) = a_{n} \\cos (c \\beta_{n}^{2} t) \\).<br><br><br><b>Final Normal Modes:</b><br><br>\\[ u_{n}(x,t) = F_{n}(x) G_{n}(t) = A_{n} \\sin \\left( \\frac{n \\pi x}{L} \\right) \\cos \\left( c \\left( \\frac{n \\pi}{L} \\right)^{2} t \\right) \\]<br><br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>The simply supported boundary conditions enforce zero displacement and zero bending moment at both ends, leading to sinusoidal mode shapes. The eigenvalues \\( \\beta_{n} \\) determine the natural frequencies, which scale quadratically with \\( n \\), unlike the linear scaling in strings. This reflects the beam’s stiffness-dominated dynamics, where higher modes require disproportionately more energy to excite."
}
```

{
  "front": "Solve the vibrating beam PDE for a simply supported beam with initial displacement \\( u(x,0) = f(x) = x(L - x) \\) and zero initial velocity. Express the solution as a series of normal modes.",
  "back": "<b>Step 1: Normal Mode Expansion:</b><br><br>The general solution is a superposition of normal modes:<br><br>\\[ u(x,t) = \\sum_{n=1}^{\\infty} A_{n} \\sin \\left( \\frac{n \\pi x}{L} \\right) \\cos \\left( c \\left( \\frac{n \\pi}{L} \\right)^{2} t \\right) \\]<br><br><br><b>Step 2: Determine Coefficients \\( A_{n} \\):</b><br><br>At \\( t = 0 \\), \\( u(x,0) = f(x) = \\sum_{n=1}^{\\infty} A_{n} \\sin \\left( \\frac{n \\pi x}{L} \\right) \\).<br><br>Fourier sine series coefficients:<br><br>\\[ A_{n} = \\frac{2}{L} \\int_{0}^{L} f(x) \\sin \\left( \\frac{n \\pi x}{L} \\right) dx = \\frac{2}{L} \\int_{0}^{L} x(L - x) \\sin \\left( \\frac{n \\pi x}{L} \\right) dx \\]<br><br>Integrate by parts:<br><br>\\[ A_{n} = \\frac{4 L^{2}}{n^{3} \\pi^{3}} (1 - (-1)^{n}) \\]<br><br>Thus, \\( A_{n} = 0 \\) for even \\( n \\), and \\( A_{n} = \\frac{8 L^{2}}{n^{3} \\pi^{3}} \\) for odd \\( n \\).<br><br><br><b>Final Solution:</b><br><br>\\[ u(x,t) = \\sum_{n=1,3,5,\\dots}^{\\infty} \\frac{8 L^{2}}{n^{3} \\pi^{3}} \\sin \\left( \\frac{n \\pi x}{L} \\right) \\cos \\left( c \\left( \\frac{n \\pi}{L} \\right)^{2} t \\right) \\]<br><br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>This solution demonstrates how initial conditions decompose into beam modes. The \\( n^{-3} \\) decay of coefficients reflects the smoothness of \\( f(x) \\); higher modes contribute less to the response. The series converges rapidly, making the first few terms sufficient for practical approximations. This method is widely used in structural analysis to predict dynamic responses to initial disturbances."
}

Verify by substitution that the function <i>u(x, t) = x² + t²</i> is a solution to the wave equation <i>u_{tt} = c² u_{xx}</i>. What value of <i>c</i> makes this true?
```

### Back:
```
<b>Verification:</b><br><br>1. Compute the first and second partial derivatives of <i>u(x, t) = x² + t²</i>:<br><br>   - <i>u_t = 2t</i>, <i>u_{tt} = 2</i><br><br>   - <i>u_x = 2x</i>, <i>u_{xx} = 2</i><br><br>2. Substitute into the wave equation:<br><br>   \[ u_{tt} = c² u_{xx} \implies 2 = c² \cdot 2 \]<br>3. Solve for <i>c</i>:<br><br>   \[ c² = 1 \implies c = \pm 1 \]<br><br><br><br><b>Conclusion:</b><br><br>The function <i>u(x, t) = x² + t²</i> satisfies the wave equation for <i>c = ±1</i>.<br><br><br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>This example illustrates how substitution can confirm whether a function is a solution to a PDE. The wave equation models phenomena like vibrations in strings or membranes, where <i>c</i> represents the wave propagation speed. Here, the solution <i>u(x, t) = x² + t²</i> is unusual because it grows quadratically, unlike typical oscillatory solutions. This highlights that PDEs can admit diverse solutions depending on initial and boundary conditions. Understanding such verifications is key to ensuring the validity of mathematical models in physics and engineering.
```

```

### Back:
```
<b>Verification:</b><br><br>1. Compute the first and second partial derivatives of <i>u(x, t) = sin(at) sin(bx)</i>:<br><br>   - <i>u_t = a cos(at) sin(bx)</i>, <i>u_{tt} = -a² sin(at) sin(bx)</i><br><br>   - <i>u_x = b sin(at) cos(bx)</i>, <i>u_{xx} = -b² sin(at) sin(bx)</i><br><br>2. Substitute into the wave equation:<br><br>   \[ u_{tt} = c² u_{xx} \implies -a² sin(at) sin(bx) = c² (-b² sin(at) sin(bx)) \]<br>3. Simplify and solve for the relationship between <i>a</i>, <i>b</i>, and <i>c</i>:<br><br>   \[ -a² = -b²c² \implies a² = b²c² \implies a = \pm bc \]<br><br><br><br><b>Conclusion:</b><br><br>The function <i>u(x, t) = sin(at) sin(bx)</i> satisfies the wave equation if <i>a = ±bc</i>.<br><br><br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>This solution represents a standing wave with distinct spatial and temporal frequencies. The relationship <i>a = ±bc</i> ensures that the wave speed <i>c</i> is consistent with the frequencies of oscillation in space and time. Such solutions are essential for understanding resonance and mode shapes in mechanical and acoustic systems.
```

The temperature distribution reaches a steady state where <i>∂u/∂t = 0</i> and <i>∂²u/∂x² = 0</i>, implying <i>u(x,∞) = 0</i> everywhere.</li></ul><br><hr><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br>This problem illustrates the classic 'cooling rod' scenario, where the heat equation is solved with Dirichlet boundary conditions (fixed temperature at the ends). The solution typically involves separation of variables and Fourier series, with the temperature decaying exponentially over time.   "back": "The solution is given by the Fourier cosine series (12):<br><br>\\[ u(x, t) = \\sum_{n=0}^{\\infty} A_n \\cos\\left(\\frac{n \\pi x}{L}\\right) e^{-\\left(\\frac{c n \\pi}{L}\\right)^2 t}. \\]<br><br>The coefficients \\( A_n \\) are computed using (13):<br>\\[ A_0 = \\frac{1}{L} \\left[ \\int_0^{L/2} x \\, dx + \\int_{L/2}^L (L - x) \\, dx \\right] = \\frac{L}{4}. \\]<br><br>For \\( n \\geq 1 \\):<br>\\[ A_n = \\frac{2}{L} \\left[ \\int_0^{L/2} x \\cos\\left(\\frac{n \\pi x}{L}\\right) \\, dx + \\int_{L/2}^L (L - x) \\cos\\left(\\frac{n \\pi x}{L}\\right) \\, dx \\right]. \\]<br><br>Evaluating the integrals:<br>\\[ A_n = \\frac{2L}{n^2 \\pi^2} \\left( 2 \\cos\\left(\\frac{n \\pi}{2}\\right) - \\cos(n \\pi) - 1 \\right). \\]<br><br>The solution simplifies to:<br>\\[ u(x, t) = \\frac{L}{4} - \\frac{8L}{\\pi^2} \\left\\{ \\frac{1}{2^2} \\cos\\left(\\frac{2 \\pi x}{L}\\right) e^{-\\left(\\frac{2 c \\pi}{L}\\right)^2 t} + \\frac{1}{6^2} \\cos\\left(\\frac{6 \\pi x}{L}\\right) e^{-\\left(\\frac{6 c \\pi}{L}\\right)^2 t} + \\cdots \\right\\}. \\]<br><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br>This example illustrates how the Fourier cosine series captures the initial triangular temperature distribution.   "back": "The solution is given by the Fourier cosine series (12):<br><br>\\[ u(x, t) = \\sum_{n=0}^{\\infty} A_n \\cos\\left(\\frac{n \\pi x}{L}\\right) e^{-\\left(\\frac{c n \\pi}{L}\\right)^2 t}. \\]<br><br>The coefficients \\( A_n \\) are computed using (13):<br>\\[ A_0 = \\frac{1}{L} \\left[ \\int_0^{L/2} x \\, dx + \\int_{L/2}^L (L - x) \\, dx \\right] = \\frac{L}{4}. \\]<br><br>For \\( n \\geq 1 \\):<br>\\[ A_n = \\frac{2}{L} \\left[ \\int_0^{L/2} x \\cos\\left(\\frac{n \\pi x}{L}\\right) \\, dx + \\int_{L/2}^L (L - x) \\cos\\left(\\frac{n \\pi x}{L}\\right) \\, dx \\right]. \\]<br><br>Evaluating the integrals:<br>\\[ A_n = \\frac{2L}{n^2 \\pi^2} \\left( 2 \\cos\\left(\\frac{n \\pi}{2}\\right) - \\cos(n \\pi) - 1 \\right). \\]<br><br>The solution simplifies to:<br>\\[ u(x, t) = \\frac{L}{4} - \\frac{8L}{\\pi^2} \\left\\{ \\frac{1}{2^2} \\cos\\left(\\frac{2 \\pi x}{L}\\right) e^{-\\left(\\frac{2 c \\pi}{L}\\right)^2 t} + \\frac{1}{6^2} \\cos\\left(\\frac{6 \\pi x}{L}\\right) e^{-\\left(\\frac{6 c \\pi}{L}\\right)^2 t} + \\cdots \\right\\}. \\]<br><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br>This example illustrates how the Fourier cosine series captures the initial triangular temperature distribution. The higher-order terms decay exponentially, reflecting the physical intuition that temperature gradients smooth out over time in an insulated system.<br><br>![img-19.jpeg](img-19.jpeg)<br>Caption: Triangular initial temperature distribution in the bar"
}

{
  "front": "What would happen to the reconstructed signal if the anti-aliasing filter in a sampling system had a non-zero transition band? Explain the consequences for the sampled signal and the reconstructed waveform.",
  "back": "An anti-aliasing filter is used before sampling to remove frequency components above the Nyquist frequency <i>f_N = f_s/2</i> (where <i>f_s</i> is the sampling rate). If the filter has a non-zero transition band (i.e., it does not perfectly attenuate frequencies above <i>f_N</i>), the following consequences arise:<br><br><br><br>1. <b>Aliasing:</b><br><br>   - Frequencies in the transition band (e.g., <i>f_N \\lt f \\lt f_s</i>) are not fully attenuated and will alias into the baseband <i>[0, f_N]</i> during sampling.<br><br>   - For example, a frequency <i>f = f_s - f_0</i> (where <i>f_0 \\lt f_N</i>) will appear as <i>f_0</i> in the sampled signal, corrupting the original spectrum.<br><br><br>2. <b>Distortion in Reconstructed Signal:</b><br><br>   - The reconstructed signal will contain spurious frequency components that were not present in the original signal. This manifests as:<br><br>     - <b>High-Frequency Noise:</b> Unwanted tones or hissing sounds.<br><br>     - <b>Phase Distortion:</b> The aliased components may interfere constructively or destructively with legitimate frequencies, altering the waveform's shape.<br><br>     - <b>Loss of Fidelity:</b> The reconstructed signal will no longer be a perfect replica of the original, especially for signals with rich harmonic content (e.g., music or speech).<br><br><br>3. <b>Practical Implications:</b><br><br>   - In audio systems, aliasing introduces artifacts that degrade sound quality.<br><br>   - In digital communication, aliasing can cause intersymbol interference, increasing bit error rates.<br><br>   - In imaging systems, aliasing manifests as moiré patterns or jagged edges.<br><br><br>4. <b>Mitigation Strategies:</b><br><br>   - Use a filter with a steeper roll-off (e.g., higher-order Butterworth or Chebyshev filters) to minimize the transition band.<br><br>   - Oversample the signal (i.e., increase <i>f_s</i>) to push the transition band further from the Nyquist frequency, making it easier to filter.<br><br>   - Apply digital post-processing to remove aliased components, though this is less effective than proper anti-aliasing.<br><br><br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>The anti-aliasing filter is critical in the sampling theorem, which guarantees perfect reconstruction of a band-limited signal. A non-zero transition band violates the theorem's assumptions, leading to irreversible distortion. This highlights the trade-off between filter complexity (steepness) and sampling rate in real-world systems. The Nyquist rate (<i>f_s = 2B</i>) is a theoretical minimum; practical systems often sample at 2.5–4 times the highest frequency to accommodate filter imperfections."
}

For <i>g(x) = 0</i>, this reduces to the superposition of two traveling waves.<br><br>2. <b>Wave Propagation:</b><n - The right-traveling wave <i>f(x - ct)</i> moves in the positive <i>x</i>-direction with speed <i>c</i>, preserving its shape.<br><br>   - The left-traveling wave <i>f(x + ct)</i> moves in the negative <i>x</i>-direction with speed <i>c</i>, also preserving its shape.<br><br>3. <b>Superposition Principle:</b> At any time <i>t</i>, the total deflection <i>u(x, t)</i> is the sum of these two waves. This explains phenomena like:<br><br>   - <b>Reflection:</b> When a wave reaches a fixed boundary (e.g., <i>x = 0</i> or <i>x = L</i>), it reflects and travels in the opposite direction, changing sign (for fixed ends).<br><br>   - <b>Interference:</b> The two waves interfere constructively or destructively, creating the observed standing wave patterns.<br><br>4. <b>Connection to Standing Waves:</b> The superposition of left- and right-traveling waves of the same frequency produces standing waves, which are the basis of the separation of variables solution. For example, <i>\\sin(kx - \\omega t) + \\sin(kx + \\omega t) = 2 \\sin(kx) \\cos(\\omega t)</i>.<br><br><br><b>Visualization in Fig. 291:</b><br><br>- The left part of the figure shows the two traveling waves (dashed lines) at various <i>t</i>.<br><br>- The right part shows their superposition, illustrating how the initial deflection splits into two waves moving in opposite directions and reflecting off the boundaries.<br><br><br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>This figure bridges D'Alembert's solution (traveling waves) and the separation of variables solution (standing waves). It provides an intuitive understanding of how energy propagates in a bounded system, reflecting off boundaries and interfering to create the observed vibrational modes. This duality is fundamental in wave physics, from acoustics to electromagnetism."
}

{
  "front": "Consider a metal bar of length \\( L = \\pi \\) meters, with thermal diffusivity \\( c^2 = 1 \\). The bar is perfectly insulated laterally, and its ends are kept at zero temperature. The initial temperature distribution is given by \\( f(x) = \\sin(x) \\).<br><br><br>Solve the one-dimensional heat equation for this bar and provide the temperature distribution \\( u(x, t) \\) as a function of \\( x \\) and \\( t \\).",
  "back": "We solve the one-dimensional heat equation:<br><br>\\[ \\frac{\\partial u}{\\partial t} = c^2 \\frac{\\partial^2 u}{\\partial x^2}, \\quad c^2 = 1, \\]<br><br>with boundary conditions \\( u(0, t) = 0 \\) and \\( u(\\pi, t) = 0 \\), and initial condition \\( u(x, 0) = \\sin(x) \\).<br><br><br><br><b>Step 1: Separation of Variables.</b><br><br>Assume \\( u(x, t) = F(x)G(t) \\). Substituting into the heat equation and separating variables gives:<br><br>\\[ \\frac{\\dot{G}}{G} = \\frac{F''}{F} = -p^2. \\]<br><br>This yields two ODEs:<br><br>\\[ F'' + p^2 F = 0, \\quad \\dot{G} + p^2 G = 0. \\]<br><br><br><br><b>Step 2: Solve the Spatial ODE.</b><br><br>The general solution to \\( F'' + p^2 F = 0 \\) is:<br><br>\\[ F(x) = A \\cos(px) + B \\sin(px). \\]<br><br>Applying the boundary conditions:<br><br>- \\( F(0) = 0 \\implies A = 0 \\).<br><br>- \\( F(\\pi) = 0 \\implies B \\sin(p\\pi) = 0 \\). For non-trivial solutions, \\( \\sin(p\\pi) = 0 \\implies p = n \\), where \\( n = 1, 2, \\dots \\).<br><br>Thus, the spatial eigenfunctions are:<br><br>\\[ F_n(x) = \\sin(nx). \\]<br><br><br><br><b>Step 3: Solve the Temporal ODE.</b><br><br>For \\( p = n \\), the temporal ODE becomes:<br><br>\\[ \\dot{G} + n^2 G = 0. \\]<br><br>The general solution is:<br><br>\\[ G_n(t) = B_n e^{-n^2 t}. \\]<br><br><br><br><b>Step 4: Construct the General Solution.</b><br><br>The eigenfunctions are:<br><br>\\[ u_n(x, t) = B_n \\sin(nx) e^{-n^2 t}. \\]<br><br>The general solution is a superposition of these eigenfunctions:<br><br>\\[ u(x, t) = \\sum_{n=1}^{\\infty} B_n \\sin(nx) e^{-n^2 t}. \\]<br><br><br><br><b>Step 5: Apply the Initial Condition.</b><br><br>At \\( t = 0 \\), \\( u(x, 0) = \\sin(x) \\). Thus:<br><br>\\[ \\sin(x) = \\sum_{n=1}^{\\infty} B_n \\sin(nx). \\]<br><br>This is the Fourier sine series of \\( \\sin(x) \\). Comparing terms, we see that \\( B_1 = 1 \\) and \\( B_n = 0 \\) for \\( n \\geq 2 \\).<br><br><br><br><b>Final Solution:</b><br><br>\\[ u(x, t) = \\sin(x) e^{-t}. \\]<br><br><br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>This example illustrates how the initial condition can align perfectly with one of the eigenfunctions, simplifying the solution to a single term. The exponential decay reflects the physical dissipation of heat over time. The solution demonstrates the power of Fourier series in solving PDEs with homogeneous boundary conditions, as it allows the initial condition to be matched exactly by a superposition of eigenfunctions."
}
```

The thermal diffusivity <i>c²</i> is calculated as:<br><br>\\[ c^2 = \\frac{K}{\\sigma \\rho} = \\frac{0.95}{0.092 \\cdot 8.92} = 1.158 \\, \\text{cm}^2/\\text{sec}. \\]<br><br>The eigenvalue <i>λ₁²</i> is:<br><br>\\[ \\lambda_1^2 = \\left( \\frac{c \\pi}{L} \\right)^2 = \\frac{1.158 \\cdot \\pi^2}{80^2} = 0.001785 \\, \\text{sec}^{-1}. \\]<br><br>Thus, the solution is:<br><br>\\[ u(x,t) = 100 \\sin \\frac{\\pi x}{80} e^{-0.001785 t}. \\]<br><br>2. <b>Time to reach 50°C:</b><br><br>The maximum temperature occurs at the midpoint of the bar (<i>x = 40 cm</i>). Set <i>u(40,t) = 50</i>:<br><br>\\[ 100 e^{-0.001785 t} = 50 \\implies e^{-0.001785 t} = 0.5. \\]<br><br>Taking the natural logarithm of both sides:<br><br>\\[ -0.001785 t = \\ln(0.5) \\implies t = \\frac{\\ln(0.5)}{-0.001785} = 388 \\, \\text{sec} \\approx 6.5 \\, \\text{min}. \\]<br><br><br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>This example illustrates how a single Fourier mode (here, the first sine term) dominates the solution when the initial condition matches that mode. The exponential decay reflects the physical process of heat loss through the ends of the bar. The time constant <i>1/λ₁²</i> governs how quickly the temperature equilibrates: larger bars or materials with lower thermal diffusivity would take longer to cool. This problem is a direct application of the general solution derived for the heat equation."

### Avant:
```json
{
  "front": "A laterally insulated bar of length <i>L</i> has ends kept at 0°C and an initial temperature distribution given by:<br><br>\\[ f(x) = \\begin{cases}\n    x & \\text{if } 0 \\lt x \\lt L/2, \\\\\n    L - x & \\text{if } L/2 \\lt x \\lt L.\n\\end{cases} \\]<br><br><br>1. Derive the Fourier sine series coefficients <i>Bₙ</i> for this initial condition.<br><br>2. Write the complete solution <i>u(x,t)</i> for the temperature distribution.<br><br>3. Explain why only odd <i>n</i> terms appear in the solution and why their amplitudes decrease as <i>1/n²</i>.",
  "back": "<b>Solution:</b><br><br>1. <b>Fourier sine coefficients:</b><br><br>The coefficients <i>Bₙ</i> are given by:<br><br>\\[ B_n = \\frac{2}{L} \\left( \\int_0^{L/2} x \\sin \\frac{n \\pi x}{L} \\, dx + \\int_{L/2}^L (L - x) \\sin \\frac{n \\pi x}{L} \\, dx \\right). \\]<br><br>Integration by parts yields:<br><br>- For even <i>n</i>: <i>Bₙ = 0</i>.<br><br>- For odd <i>n</i>: <i>Bₙ = (4L)/(n² π²)</i> if <i>n = 1, 5, 9, ...</i>, and <i>Bₙ = -(4L)/(n² π²)</i> if <i>n = 3, 7, 11, ...</i>.<br><br><br>2. <b>Temperature distribution:</b><br><br>The solution is:<br><br>\\[ u(x,t) = \\frac{4L}{\\pi^2} \\left[ \\sin \\frac{\\pi x}{L} e^{-\\left( \\frac{c \\pi}{L} \\right)^2 t} - \\frac{1}{9} \\sin \\frac{3\\pi x}{L} e^{-\\left( \\frac{3c \\pi}{L} \\right)^2 t} + \\frac{1}{25} \\sin \\frac{5\\pi x}{L} e^{-\\left( \\frac{5c \\pi}{L} \\right)^2 t} - \\cdots \\right]. \\]<br><br>3. <b>Explanation of terms:</b><br><br>- <b>Odd <i>n</i> only:</b> The initial condition <i>f(x)</i> is symmetric about <i>x = L/2</i> and matches the symmetry of <i>sin(nπx/L)</i> only for odd <i>n</i>. Even <i>n</i> terms would introduce asymmetry, which is absent in <i>f(x)</i>.<br><br>- <b>Amplitude decay as <i>1/n²</i>:</b> The initial condition <i>f(x)</i> is piecewise linear and continuous, but its derivative is discontinuous at <i>x = L/2</i>. The Fourier coefficients of such functions decay as <i>1/n²</i>, reflecting the smoothness of <i>f(x)</i>. Faster decay (e.g., <i>1/n⁴</i>) would occur for smoother functions (e.g., with continuous second derivatives).<br><br><br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>This example demonstrates how the shape of the initial temperature distribution determines the Fourier coefficients. The triangular wave <i>f(x)</i> is a classic case where only odd harmonics appear, and their amplitudes decrease quadratically with <i>n</i>. This reflects the trade-off between spatial resolution (higher <i>n</i>) and temporal persistence (slower decay). The solution also shows how the heat equation acts as a low-pass filter, smoothing out sharp features over time."
}
```

{
  "front": "Compare the temporal evolution of the temperature distribution in a bar for two initial conditions: (1) a single sine mode <i>sin(πx/L)</i>, and (2) a triangular wave (as in Example 3). What key differences arise, and why?",
  "back": "<b>Comparison of temporal evolution:</b><br><br>1. <b>Single sine mode (<i>sin(πx/L)</i>):</b><br><br>   - The solution is a single term: <i>u(x,t) = B₁ sin(πx/L) e^{-λ₁² t}</i>.<br><br>   - The shape of the temperature distribution remains <b>unchanged</b> over time; only the amplitude decays exponentially.<br><br>   - The decay rate is slow (<i>λ₁² = (cπ/L)²</i>), so the temperature persists for a long time.<br><br>   - The solution is smooth and simple, with no spatial variation in the decay rate.<br><br><br>2. <b>Triangular wave (Example 3):</b><br><br>   - The solution is a sum of odd sine modes: <i>u(x,t) = Σ Bₙ sin(nπx/L) e^{-λₙ² t}</i>, where <i>n = 1, 3, 5, ...</i>.<br><br>   - The shape of the temperature distribution <b>changes over time</b> because higher modes decay faster than lower modes.<br><br>   - Initially, the distribution has sharp corners (at <i>x = L/2</i>), but these smooth out quickly as the higher modes (<i>n ≥ 3</i>) decay.<br><br>   - The decay rate is non-uniform: the lowest mode (<i>n = 1</i>) dominates at later times, while higher modes disappear rapidly.<br><br><br><b>Key differences and reasons:</b><br><br>- <b>Shape preservation:</b> A single sine mode preserves its shape because it is an eigenfunction of the heat equation. A triangular wave, however, is a superposition of modes, each decaying at its own rate, leading to shape evolution.<br><br>- <b>Decay rate:</b> The triangular wave's higher modes decay much faster (<i>λₙ² ∝ n²</i>), causing rapid smoothing of sharp features. The single mode decays slowly because it lacks high-frequency components.<br><br>- <b>Physical interpretation:</b> The triangular wave's initial sharp corners represent steep temperature gradients, which drive rapid heat flux and faster decay. The single mode has no such gradients, so heat loss is slower.<br><br><br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>This comparison illustrates how the initial condition's spatial complexity determines the solution's temporal behavior. Single-mode initial conditions are idealized cases that rarely occur in practice, but they are useful for understanding the fundamental behavior of the heat equation. Real-world initial conditions (e.g., triangular waves) are superpositions of modes, and their evolution reflects the interplay between spatial resolution and temporal decay. This is why the heat equation is often described as a low-pass filter: it attenuates high-frequency components over time."
}
```

The trade-offs between <i>L</i>, <i>T</i>, and <i>\rho</i> are fundamental in instrument design, balancing playability, sound quality, and structural integrity.',<br>            'tags': 'EM3_Chapter12 Vibrating_String Instrument_Design Catégorie::Elaborative_Interrogation'<br>        },<br>        {<br>            'type': 'Basique',<br>            'subdeck': '05_Exercices_et_Exemples',<br>            'front': 'For a string of length <i>L = \pi</i> and <i>c^2 = 1</i>, with zero initial displacement and initial velocity <i>u_t(x, 0) = 0.01x</i> for <i>0 \leq x \leq \frac{1}{2}\pi</i> and <i>u_t(x, 0) = 0.01(\pi - x)</i> for <i>\frac{1}{2}\pi \leq x \leq \pi</i>, derive the deflection <i>u(x, t)</i> and explain the physical meaning of the solution.',<br>            'back': 'Given the initial conditions:<br><br>- <i>u(x, 0) = 0</i> (zero initial displacement),<br><br>- <i>u_t(x, 0) = g(x)</i>, where <i>g(x) = 0.01x</i> for <i>0 \leq x \leq \frac{1}{2}\pi</i> and <i>g(x) = 0.01(\pi - x)</i> for <i>\frac{1}{2}\pi \leq x \leq \pi</i>.<br><br><br><br>The general solution for the wave equation is:<br><br>\[u(x, t) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} B_n \sin(n t) \sin(n x),\]<br><br><br><br>where <i>B_n</i> are the Fourier sine coefficients of <i>g(x)</i> scaled by <i>1/(n c)</i> (here, <i>c = 1</i>):<br><br>\[B_n = \frac{2}{n \pi} \int_{0}^{\pi} g(x) \sin(n x) dx.\]<br><br><br><br>Split the integral into two parts:<br><br>\[B_n = \frac{2}{n \pi} \left( \int_{0}^{\pi/2} 0.01x \sin(n x) dx + \int_{\pi/2}^{\pi} 0.01(\pi - x) \sin(n x) dx \right).\]<br><br><br><br>Integrating by parts yields:<br><br>\[B_n = \frac{0.02}{n \pi} \left( \frac{\sin(\frac{n \pi}{2})}{n^2} - \frac{\pi \cos(\frac{n \pi}{2})}{2n} + \frac{\pi \cos(n \pi)}{n} - \frac{\sin(\frac{n \pi}{2})}{n^2} \right) = \frac{0.02}{n^2} \left( \frac{\cos(n \pi) - \cos(\frac{n \pi}{2})}{n \pi} \right).\]<br><br><br><br>Simplifying using trigonometric identities:<br><br>\[B_n = \begin{cases}
\frac{0.08}{n^3 \pi} & \text{if } n \text{ is odd}, \\
0 & \text{if } n \text{ is even}.
\end{cases}\]<br><br><br><br>Thus, the solution is:<br><br>\[u(x, t) = \sum_{n=1,3,5,\ldots}^{\infty} \frac{0.08}{n^3 \pi} \sin(n t) \sin(n x).\]<br><br><br><br><b>Physical Meaning:</b><br><br>The initial velocity profile <i>g(x)</i> is a triangular pulse centered at <i>x = \pi/2</i>. The solution shows that this pulse decomposes into a series of odd harmonics, with the fundamental mode (<i>n = 1</i>) dominating. The string's motion is a superposition of standing waves, each oscillating at its natural frequency. The rapid decay of <i>B_n</i> with <i>n</i> ensures that higher harmonics contribute less to the overall motion, resulting in a smooth, localized deflection propagating along the string.<br><br><br><br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>This example illustrates how initial velocity conditions (e.g., striking a string) excite vibrational modes. The triangular velocity profile is a simplified model of a plucked or hammered string. The dominance of the fundamental mode explains why the perceived pitch of a struck string (e.g., piano) is clear and distinct, even though multiple harmonics are present.',<br>            'tags': 'EM3_Chapter12 Wave_Equation Initial_Velocity'<br>        },<br>        {<br>            'type': 'Basique',<br>            'subdeck': '04_Synthèse_et_Relations',<br>            'front': 'What is the physical significance of the Fourier coefficients <i>A_n</i> and <i>B_n</i> in the solution to the wave equation for a vibrating string, and how do they relate to the initial conditions?',<br>            'back':

**Ancien Back :**


**Nouveau Front :**
What is the physical significance of the Fourier coefficients \(A_n\) and \(B_n\) in the solution to the wave equation for a vibrating string, and how do they relate to the initial conditions?

**Nouveau Back :**
<b>Physical Significance of \(A_n\) and \(B_n\):</b><br><br>The Fourier coefficients \(A_n\) and \(B_n\) in the solution to the wave equation:<br><br>\[u(x, t) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \left( A_n \cos(n c t) + B_n \sin(n c t) \right) \sin\left(\frac{n \pi x}{L}\right)\]<br><br>represent the amplitudes of the <i>n</i>-th normal mode (or harmonic) of the vibrating string. Their physical significance is as follows:<br><br><ul><li><b>\(A_n\):</b> Determines the contribution of the <i>n</i>-th mode to the <b>initial displacement</b> of the string. A larger \(A_n\) means the <i>n</i>-th harmonic has a stronger presence in the initial shape of the string.</li><br><br><li><b>\(B_n\):</b> Determines the contribution of the <i>n</i>-th mode to the <b>initial velocity</b> of the string. A larger \(B_n\) means the <i>n</i>-th harmonic is more strongly excited by the initial motion of the string.</li></ul><br><br><b>Relation to Initial Conditions:</b><br><br>The coefficients \(A_n\) and \(B_n\) are directly derived from the initial conditions of the string:<br><br><ol><li><b>Initial Displacement \(u(x, 0) = f(x)\):</b><br>\[A_n = \frac{2}{L} \int_{0}^{L} f(x) \sin\left(\frac{n \pi x}{L}\right) dx.\]<br>This integral projects the initial shape \(f(x)\) onto the <i>n</i>-th normal mode, quantifying how much of that mode is present in the initial displacement.</li><br><br><li><b>Initial Velocity \(u_t(x, 0) = g(x)\):</b><br>\[B_n = \frac{2}{n c \pi} \int_{0}^{L} g(x) \sin\left(\frac{n \pi x}{L}\right) dx.\]<br>This integral projects the initial velocity profile \(g(x)\) onto the <i>n</i>-th normal mode, scaled by the mode's frequency \(n c / (2L)\).</li></ol><br><br><b>Key Insights:</b><br><br><ul><li>The Fourier coefficients decompose the initial conditions into a sum of standing waves (normal modes). Each mode oscillates at its own natural frequency, and the coefficients determine how much each mode contributes to the overall motion.</li><br><li>The decay rate of \(A_n\) and \(B_n\) with increasing \(n\) reflects the smoothness of the initial conditions. For example, a discontinuous initial displacement (e.g., a plucked string) will have coefficients that decay slowly, leading to a richer harmonic content.</li><br><li>In musical instruments, the relative magnitudes of \(A_n\) and \(B_n\) explain the timbre of the sound. A violin and a piano playing the same note will have different harmonic content due to differences in their initial conditions (plucking vs. striking).</li></ul><br><br><hr><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br>Les coefficients de Fourier \(A_n\) et \(B_n\) agissent comme une "empreinte digitale" des conditions initiales de la corde. Imaginez une corde de guitare pincée : sa forme initiale (déplacement) et la manière dont elle est relâchée (vitesse) déterminent quelles harmoniques seront excitées et avec quelle intensité. C'est pourquoi une corde pincée près du chevalet sonne plus "métallique" (plus d'harmoniques élevées) qu'une corde pincée près du manche. Ces coefficients permettent de prédire mathématiquement ce comportement, reliant la physique des ondes à la musique.

Let:<br>\\[ f_1(z) = \\phi(z) + i \\psi(z), \\quad f_2(z) = \\phi(z) - i \\psi(z) \\]<br><br>Then:<br>\\[ u(x, y) = 2 \\phi(y + 2i x) = 2 \\phi(y - 2i x) \\]<br><br>Alternatively, express the solution in terms of real functions:<br>\\[ u(x, y) = F(y + 2x) + G(y - 2x) \\]<br><br>where <i>F</i> and <i>G</i> are arbitrary twice-differentiable functions.<br><br><hr><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br>This example demonstrates how the method of characteristics transforms a hyperbolic PDE into its normal form, simplifying the solution process. The general solution represents two waves traveling in opposite directions, analogous to d'Alembert's solution for the wave equation. The use of complex characteristics is a mathematical tool to handle the transformation, but the final solution is real-valued."
}

  "back": "<b>Given:</b><br><ul><li>Length of string, <i>L = 1</i></li><li>Wave speed, <i>c = 1</i></li><li>Initial velocity, <i>u_t(x, 0) = 0</i></li><li>Initial deflection, <i>f(x) = k sin(πx)</i></li></ul><br><b>Step 1: Apply d'Alembert's Solution</b><br>For zero initial velocity, d'Alembert's solution is:<br>\\[ u(x, t) = \\frac{1}{2} [f(x + ct) + f(x - ct)] \\]<br><br>Substitute <i>f(x) = k sin(πx)</i> and <i>c = 1</i>:<br>\\[ u(x, t) = \\frac{k}{2} [\\sin(\\pi(x + t)) + \\sin(\\pi(x - t))] \\]<br><br><b>Step 2: Simplify Using Trigonometric Identity</b><br>Using the identity <i>sin(a) + sin(b) = 2 sin((a+b)/2) cos((a-b)/2)</i>:<br>\\[ u(x, t) = k \\sin(\\pi x) \\cos(\\pi t) \\]<br><br><b>Step 3: Interpret the Solution</b><br>The solution represents a <b>standing wave</b> with:<br><ul><li>Amplitude <i>k sin(πx)</i>, which varies sinusoidally along the string.</li><li>Temporal oscillation <i>cos(πt)</i>, which describes the vibration over time.</li></ul><br>The string vibrates in its fundamental mode, with nodes at <i>x = 0</i> and <i>x = 1</i> (fixed ends) and an antinode at <i>x = 0.5</i>.<br><br><b>Sketch:</b><br>The deflection <i>u(x, t)</i> at different times <i>t</i> will show a sinusoidal shape oscillating between <i>-k sin(πx)</i> and <i>k sin(πx)</i>. At <i>t = 0</i>, the string is at its maximum deflection. At <i>t = 0.5</i>, the string passes through its equilibrium position. At <i>t = 1</i>, the string reaches its maximum deflection in the opposite direction.<br><br><hr><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br>This example illustrates how d'Alembert's solution simplifies the analysis of vibrating strings. The standing wave pattern arises from the superposition of two traveling waves moving in opposite directions. The fundamental mode is the simplest vibration pattern, but higher modes (e.g., <i>sin(2πx)</i>) would produce more complex patterns with additional nodes and antinodes."
}

The discriminant is:<br>\\[ D = AC - B^2 = 1 \\cdot 1 - 1^2 = 0 \\]<br><br>Thus, the PDE is <b>parabolic</b>.<br><br><b>Step 2: Solve the Characteristic Equation</b><br>The characteristic equation is:<br>\\[ A y'^2 - 2B y' + C = y'^2 - 2 y' + 1 = 0 \\implies (y' - 1)^2 = 0 \\implies y' = 1 \\]<br><br>The solution is:<br>\\[ y - x = \\text{const} \\]<br><br>Define a new variable:<br>\\[ v = y - x \\]<br><br>For parabolic PDEs, we need a second independent variable. Choose:<br>\\[ w = x \\]<br><br><b>Step 3: Transform the PDE</b><br>Express the derivatives in terms of <i>v</i> and <i>w</i>:<br>\\[ u_x = u_v v_x + u_w w_x = -u_v + u_w \\]<br>\\[ u_y = u_v v_y + u_w w_y = u_v \\]<br>\\[ u_{xx} = (-u_{vv} + u_{wv})(-1) + (-u_{vw} + u_{ww}) = u_{vv} - 2 u_{vw} + u_{ww} \\]<br>\\[ u_{xy} = (-u_{vv} + u_{wv}) \\cdot 1 + (-u_{vw} + u_{ww}) \\cdot 0 = -u_{vv} + u_{vw} \\]<br>\\[ u_{yy} = u_{vv} \\cdot 1 + u_{vw} \\cdot 0 = u_{vv} \\]<br><br>Substitute into the original PDE:<br>\\[ u_{xx} + 2 u_{xy} + u_{yy} = (u_{vv} - 2 u_{vw} + u_{ww}) + 2(-u_{vv} + u_{vw}) + u_{vv} = u_{ww} = 0 \\]<br><br><b>Step 4: Solve the Transformed PDE</b><br>The normal form is:<br>\\[ u_{ww} = 0 \\]<br><br>The general solution is:<br>\\[ u(w, v) = w F(v) + G(v) = x F(y - x) + G(y - x) \\]<br><br>where <i>F</i> and <i>G</i> are arbitrary twice-differentiable functions.<br><br><hr><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br>This example demonstrates how the method of characteristics simplifies a parabolic PDE to its normal form. The solution represents a wave or disturbance that propagates along the characteristic <i>y - x = const</i>. The arbitrary functions <i>F</i> and <i>G</i> are determined by initial or boundary conditions, reflecting the diffusive nature of parabolic PDEs."

Choose:<br>\\[ w = x \\]<br><br>Express the derivatives in terms of <i>v</i> and <i>w</i>:<br>\\[ u_x = u_v v_x + u_w w_x = -u_v + u_w \\]<br>\\[ u_y = u_v v_y + u_w w_y = u_v \\]<br>\\[ u_{xx} = (-u_{vv} + u_{wv})(-1) + (-u_{vw} + u_{ww}) = u_{vv} - 2 u_{vw} + u_{ww} \\]<br>\\[ u_{xy} = (-u_{vv} + u_{wv}) \\cdot 1 + (-u_{vw} + u_{ww}) \\cdot 0 = -u_{vv} + u_{vw} \\]<br>\\[ u_{yy} = u_{vv} \\cdot 1 + u_{vw} \\cdot 0 = u_{vv} \\]<br><br>Substitute into the original PDE:<br>\\[ u_{xx} + 2 u_{xy} + u_{yy} = (u_{vv} - 2 u_{vw} + u_{ww}) + 2(-u_{vv} + u_{vw}) + u_{vv} = u_{ww} = 0 \\]<br><br>The normal form is:<br>\\[ u_{ww} = 0 \\]<br><br>The general solution is:<br>\\[ u(w, v) = w F(v) + G(v) = x F(y - x) + G(y - x) \\]<br><br>where <i>F</i> and <i>G</i> are arbitrary twice-differentiable functions.<br><br><hr><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br>This example demonstrates how the method of characteristics simplifies a parabolic PDE to its normal form. The solution represents a wave or disturbance that propagates along the characteristic <i>y - x = const</i>. The arbitrary functions <i>F</i> and <i>G</i> are determined by initial or boundary conditions, reflecting the diffusive nature of parabolic PDEs."

This transforms the PDE into an ODE:<br><br>\\[ \\frac{\\partial \\hat{u}_s}{\\partial t} + c^2 w^2 \\hat{u}_s = 0. \\]<br><br>3. Solve the ODE to obtain:<br><br>\\[ \\hat{u}_s(w,t) = C(w) e^{-c^2 w^2 t}. \\]<br><br>4. Apply the initial condition \\( \\hat{u}_s(w,0) = \\hat{f}_s(w) \\) to find \\( C(w) = \\hat{f}_s(w) \\).<br><br>5. Take the inverse Fourier sine transform and substitute \\( \\hat{f}_s(w) \\):<br><br>\\[ u(x,t) = \\frac{2}{\\pi} \\int_0^{\\infty} \\int_0^{\\infty} f(p) \\sin wp \\, e^{-c^2 w^2 t} \\sin wx \\, dp \\, dw. \\tag{20} \\]<br><br><br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>The Fourier sine transform is used here because the bar is semi-infinite and the boundary condition \\( u(0,t) = 0 \\) is homogeneous. This transform naturally incorporates the boundary condition into the solution, avoiding the need for additional constraints. The solution shows how heat diffuses from the initial distribution while respecting the fixed temperature at \\( x = 0 \\). This approach is particularly useful for problems with Dirichlet boundary conditions on semi-infinite domains."
}

Substitute back to obtain:<br><br>\\[ u(x,t) = \\frac{2}{\\pi} \\int_0^{\\infty} \\frac{1 - \\cos w}{w} e^{-c^2 w^2 t} \\sin wx \\, dw. \\]<br><br><br><b>Behavior:</b><br><br>- As \\( t \\to 0 \\): The term \\( e^{-c^2 w^2 t} \\to 1 \\), so the solution approaches the initial condition:<br><br>  \\[ u(x,0) = \\frac{2}{\\pi} \\int_0^{\\infty} \\frac{1 - \\cos w}{w} \\sin wx \\, dw = f(x). \\]<br><br>  This integral evaluates to 1 for \\( 0 \\leq x \\leq 1 \\) and 0 otherwise, matching the initial condition.<br><br>- As \\( t \\to \\infty \\): The exponential term \\( e^{-c^2 w^2 t} \\) decays rapidly for \\( w \\neq 0 \\), causing the integral to approach 0. Thus, \\( u(x,t) \\to 0 \\) for all \\( x \\), reflecting the dissipation of heat over time.<br><br><br><hr><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>This example illustrates how the initial temperature distribution diffuses over time while respecting the boundary condition \\( u(0,t) = 0 \\). The integral representation shows that the solution is a superposition of sine waves with frequencies \\( w \\), each decaying at a rate determined by \\( e^{-c^2 w^2 t} \\). The behavior as \\( t \\to 0 \\) and \\( t \\to \\infty \\) aligns with physical intuition: the initial condition is recovered instantaneously, and heat eventually dissipates to zero everywhere."

The Fourier transform is ideal for infinite domains where boundary conditions are irrelevant, while the Fourier sine transform is tailored for semi-infinite domains with \\( u(0,t) = 0 \\). The sine transform’s use of sine functions inherently satisfies the boundary condition, simplifying the solution process.   "back": "<b>Step-by-Step Resolution Using Fourier Transform:</b><br><br><br><br>1. Start with the heat equation:<br>\\[ \\frac{\\partial u}{\\partial t} = c^2 \\frac{\\partial^2 u}{\\partial x^2}. \\]<br><br>2. Take the Fourier transform of both sides with respect to <i>x</i>. Let <i>\\hat{u}(w, t) = \\mathcal{F}(u(x, t))</i>. Using the property of the Fourier transform for derivatives:<br>\\[ \\mathcal{F}(u_t) = \\frac{\\partial \\hat{u}}{\\partial t}, \\quad \\mathcal{F}(u_{xx}) = -w^2 \\hat{u}. \\]<br><br>3. The heat equation transforms into an ordinary differential equation (ODE) in <i>t</i>:<br>\\[ \\frac{\\partial \\hat{u}}{\\partial t} = -c^2 w^2 \\hat{u}. \\]<br><br>4. Solve the ODE by separating variables:<br>\\[ \\frac{d\\hat{u}}{\\hat{u}} = -c^2 w^2 dt \\implies \\hat{u}(w, t) = C(w) e^{-c^2 w^2 t}, \\]<br>where <i>C(w)</i> is determined by the initial condition.<br><br>5. Apply the initial condition <i>u(x, 0) = f(x)</i>. The Fourier transform of <i>f(x)</i> is:<br>\\[ \\hat{f}(w) = \\mathcal{F}(f(x)) = \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2\\pi}} \\int_{-\\infty}^{\\infty} f(v) e^{-iwv} dv. \\]<br>For the given <i>f(x)</i>:<br>\\[ \\hat{f}(w) = \\frac{U_0}{\\sqrt{2\\pi}} \\int_{-1}^{1} e^{-iwv} dv = \\frac{U_0}{\\sqrt{2\\pi}} \\left[ \\frac{e^{-iwv}}{-iw} \\right]_{-1}^{1} = \\frac{U_0}{w\\sqrt{2\\pi}} (e^{iw} - e^{-iw}) = \\frac{U_0}{w\\sqrt{2\\pi}} \\cdot 2i \\sin(w) = \\sqrt{\\frac{2}{\\pi}} \\frac{U_0 \\sin(w)}{w}. \\]<br><br>6. Substitute <i>C(w) = \\hat{f}(w)</i> into the solution for <i>\\hat{u}</i>:<br>\\[ \\hat{u}(w, t) = \\sqrt{\\frac{2}{\\pi}} \\frac{U_0 \\sin(w)}{w} e^{-c^2 w^2 t}. \\]<br><br>7. Use the inverse Fourier transform to obtain <i>u(x, t)</i>:<br>\\[ u(x, t) = \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2\\pi}} \\int_{-\\infty}^{\\infty} \\hat{u}(w, t) e^{iwx} dw = \\frac{U_0}{\\pi} \\int_{-\\infty}^{\\infty} \\frac{\\sin(w)}{w} e^{-c^2 w^2 t} e^{iwx} dw. \\]<br><br>8. Simplify the integral using the Euler formula and symmetry. The imaginary part cancels out, leaving:<br>\\[ u(x, t) = \\frac{U_0}{\\pi} \\int_{-\\infty}^{\\infty} \\frac{\\sin(w)}{w} e^{-c^2 w^2 t} \\cos(wx) dw. \\]<br><br>9. Recognize that this integral can be expressed in terms of the error function, yielding the same result as the Fourier integral method:<br>\\[ u(x, t) = \\frac{U_0}{2} \\left[ \\text{erf}\\left(\\frac{x + 1}{2c\\sqrt{t}}\\right) - \\text{erf}\\left(\\frac{x - 1}{2c\\sqrt{t}}\\right) \\right]. \\]<br><br><br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>This example demonstrates the equivalence of Fourier integral and Fourier transform methods for solving the heat equation. The Fourier transform simplifies the PDE into an ODE, making it easier to solve analytically. This approach is particularly powerful for problems defined over infinite domains, where boundary conditions are replaced by integrability conditions. The method is widely used in physics and engineering to solve linear PDEs with constant coefficients."
}

The imaginary part cancels out, leaving:<br>\\[ u(x, t) = \\frac{U_0}{\\pi} \\int_{-\\infty}^{\\infty} \\frac{\\sin(w)}{w} e^{-c^2 w^2 t} \\cos(wx) dw. \\]<br><br>9. Recognize that this integral can be expressed in terms of the error function, yielding the same result as the Fourier integral method:<br>\\[ u(x, t) = \\frac{U_0}{2} \\left[ \\text{erf}\\left(\\frac{x + 1}{2c\\sqrt{t}}\\right) - \\text{erf}\\left(\\frac{x - 1}{2c\\sqrt{t}}\\right) \\right]. \\]<br><br><hr><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>This example demonstrates the equivalence of Fourier integral and Fourier transform methods for solving the heat equation. The Fourier transform simplifies the PDE into an ODE, making it easier to solve analytically. This approach is particularly powerful for problems defined over infinite domains, where boundary conditions are replaced by integrability conditions. The Gaussian kernel describes how heat diffuses over time, smoothing out the initial temperature profile. {
  "front": "Why does the solution to the heat equation for an infinite bar involve a Gaussian kernel, and what physical interpretation does this have?",
  "back": "<b>Explanation of the Gaussian Kernel in the Heat Equation:</b><br><br><br><br>The solution to the heat equation for an infinite bar is given by:<br>\\[ u(x, t) = \\frac{1}{2c\\sqrt{\\pi t}} \\int_{-\\infty}^{\\infty} f(v) \\exp \\left\\{ -\\frac{(x - v)^2}{4c^2 t} \\right\\} dv. \\]<br><br>The term <i>\\exp \\left\\{ -\\frac{(x - v)^2}{4c^2 t} \\right\\}</i> is a Gaussian kernel, which arises due to the following reasons:<br><br>1. <b>Diffusion Process:</b> The heat equation models the diffusion of heat, where the temperature at any point <i>x</i> and time <i>t</i> depends on the initial temperature distribution <i>f(v)</i>. The Gaussian kernel describes how the influence of the initial temperature at point <i>v</i> spreads out over time.<br><br>2. <b>Fundamental Solution:</b> The Gaussian kernel is the fundamental solution (or Green's function) of the heat equation. It represents the temperature distribution at time <i>t</i> due to an initial point source of heat (a Dirac delta function) at <i>v = 0</i>. The width of the Gaussian increases with time, reflecting the spread of heat.<br><br>3. <b>Central Limit Theorem Analogy:</b> The diffusion of heat can be thought of as the result of many small, random molecular collisions. The Gaussian shape emerges from the central limit theorem, which states that the sum of many independent random variables tends toward a Gaussian distribution.<br><br>4. <b>Physical Interpretation:</b><br>   - The term <i>4c^2 t</i> in the denominator of the exponent determines the width of the Gaussian. As <i>t</i> increases, the Gaussian becomes wider and shorter, indicating that heat spreads out and the temperature gradient decreases.<br>   - The prefactor <i>1/(2c√(πt))</i> ensures that the total heat (integral of <i>u(x, t)</i> over all <i>x</i>) is conserved over time, as required by the physics of the problem.<br><br>5. <b>Mathematical Properties:</b><br>   - The Gaussian kernel is symmetric, reflecting the isotropic nature of diffusion in an infinite bar.<br>   - It decays rapidly to zero as <i>|x - v|</i> increases, meaning that the influence of distant points diminishes quickly.<br><br><br><br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>The Gaussian kernel is a hallmark of diffusion processes, not just in heat transfer but also in other fields like probability (Brownian motion) and signal processing (Gaussian filters). Its appearance in the solution to the heat equation underscores the deep connection between physics and mathematics, where the same mathematical structures describe seemingly disparate phenomena. Understanding this kernel is crucial for grasping how initial conditions evolve over time in diffusive systems."
}
```

The arguments of the error function in the solution, <i>(x ± 1)/(2c√t)</i>, reflect how the initial step edges at <i>x = ±1</i> diffuse over time. This function is also used in signal processing, quantum mechanics, and finance, making it a versatile and essential concept in engineering and physics."

  "back": "<b>Definition of the Fourier Transform:</b><br><br><br><br>The Fourier transform is an integral transform that decomposes a function into its constituent frequencies. For a function <i>f(x)</i>, the Fourier transform <i>\\hat{f}(w)</i> is defined as:<br>\\[ \\hat{f}(w) = \\mathcal{F}(f(x)) = \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2\\pi}} \\int_{-\\infty}^{\\infty} f(x) e^{-iwx} dx. \\]<br><br>The inverse Fourier transform reconstructs the original function from its transform:<br>\\[ f(x) = \\mathcal{F}^{-1}(\\hat{f}(w)) = \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2\\pi}} \\int_{-\\infty}^{\\infty} \\hat{f}(w) e^{iwx} dw. \\]<br><br><b>Application to the Heat Equation:</b><br><br><br><br>The heat equation for an infinite bar is:<br>\\[ \\frac{\\partial u}{\\partial t} = c^2 \\frac{\\partial^2 u}{\\partial x^2}. \\]<br><br>To solve it using the Fourier transform:<br><br>1. Take the Fourier transform of both sides with respect to <i>x</i>. Using the property <i>\\mathcal{F}(u_{xx}) = -w^2 \\hat{u}</i>, the PDE transforms into an ODE:<br>\\[ \\frac{\\partial \\hat{u}}{\\partial t} = -c^2 w^2 \\hat{u}. \\]<br><br>2. Solve the ODE for <i>\\hat{u}(w, t)</i>:<br>\\[ \\hat{u}(w, t) = \\hat{f}(w) e^{-c^2 w^2 t}, \\]<br>where <i>\\hat{f}(w)</i> is the Fourier transform of the initial condition <i>u(x, 0) = f(x)</i>.<br><br>3. Apply the inverse Fourier transform to obtain <i>u(x, t)</i>:<br>\\[ u(x, t) = \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2\\pi}} \\int_{-\\infty}^{\\infty} \\hat{f}(w) e^{-c^2 w^2 t} e^{iwx} dw. \\]<br><br>4. Substitute <i>\\hat{f}(w)</i> and simplify using the convolution theorem or direct integration to recover the solution in terms of the initial condition <i>f(x)</i>.<br><br><b>Advantages of the Fourier Transform Method:</b><br>- Reduces a PDE to an ODE, which is easier to solve.<br>- Naturally handles problems defined over infinite domains.<br>- Provides insight into the frequency-domain behavior of the solution.<br><br><br><br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>The Fourier transform is a cornerstone of mathematical physics and engineering, enabling the analysis of linear systems in the frequency domain. Its application to the heat equation demonstrates how integral transforms can simplify complex PDEs into more manageable forms. This method is not only limited to heat transfer but is also widely used in signal processing, quantum mechanics, and control theory, making it a versatile tool for engineers and scientists."
}
