v)^2}{4c^2 t} \\right\\} dv. \\]<br><br>3. <b>Applicability:</b> Both methods are well-suited for problems defined over infinite domains, where boundary conditions are replaced by integrability conditions.<br><br>4. <b>Physical Interpretation:</b> Both approaches highlight the diffusive nature of the heat equation, where the Gaussian kernel describes how heat spreads over time.<br><br><b>Differences:</b><br><br><table border='1'><tr><th>Feature</th><th>Fourier Integral Method</th><th>Fourier Transform Method</th></tr><tr><td><b>Mathematical Tool</b></td><td>Directly uses Fourier integrals to represent <i>f(x)</i>.</td><td>Uses the Fourier transform to convert the PDE into an ODE.</td></tr><tr><td><b>Derivation Steps</b></td><td>Assumes a solution of the form <i>u(x, t) = ∫ A(w) e^{iwx} e^{-c^2 w^2 t} dw</i> and determines <i>A(w)</i> from the initial condition.</td><td>Takes the Fourier transform of the PDE, solves the resulting ODE, and then applies the inverse transform.</td></tr><tr><td><b>Complexity</b></td><td>Involves direct integration and interchange of integral orders.</td><td>Requires knowledge of Fourier transform properties and inversion.</td></tr><tr><td><b>Intermediate Results</b></td><td>Yields the solution as a double integral, which is then simplified.</td><td>Yields an intermediate ODE in the frequency domain, which is solved before inversion.</td></tr><tr><td><b>Conceptual Focus</b></td><td>Emphasizes the integral representation of the solution.</td><td>Emphasizes the transformation of the PDE into a simpler form.</td></tr></table><br><b>When to Use Each Method:</b><br>- The <b>Fourier integral method</b> is often more intuitive for problems where the initial condition is already expressed as an integral (e.g., piecewise constant functions).<br>- The <b>Fourier transform method</b> is more systematic and general, especially for problems where the initial condition is not easily expressed as a simple integral. It is also more adaptable to other types of PDEs (e.g., wave equation, Laplace equation).<br><br><hr><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>Both methods are powerful tools for solving the heat equation, but they offer different perspectives. The Fourier integral method is closely tied to the physical interpretation of diffusion, while the Fourier transform method provides a more algebraic approach. Understanding both methods deepens one's grasp of how integral transforms can be used to solve PDEs, a skill that is invaluable in advanced engineering and physics courses."

Instead, it is represented by a Dirac delta function, <i>\\hat{f}(w) = \\sqrt{2\\pi} \\delta(w)</i>, which is a generalized function.<br><br>2. <b>Breakdown of the Solution:</b><br>   - The solution to the heat equation derived via Fourier methods assumes that <i>\\hat{f}(w)</i> exists and is well-behaved. If <i>f(x)</i> is not absolutely integrable, the solution may not converge or may require reinterpretation using generalized functions.<br>   - For <i>f(x) = 1</i>, the formal solution would be:<br>     \\[ u(x, t) = \\frac{1}{2c\\sqrt{\\pi t}} \\int_{-\\infty}^{\\infty} \\exp \\left\\{ -\\frac{(x - v)^2}{4c^2 t} \\right\\} dv = 1, \\]<br>     which suggests that the temperature remains constant everywhere. However, this result is physically unrealistic for an infinite bar, as it implies infinite heat content.<br><br>3. <b>Physical Interpretation:</b><br>   - A non-integrable initial condition like <i>f(x) = 1</i> implies that the total heat content of the bar is infinite. This violates the conservation of energy and leads to a solution that does not decay over time, which is inconsistent with the diffusive nature of the heat equation.<br>   - In reality, such initial conditions are idealizations and do not occur in physical systems. They are often used as limiting cases or require regularization (e.g., considering a finite domain or a localized initial condition).<br><br>4. <b>Mathematical Workarounds:</b><br>   - For non-integrable initial conditions, one can use the theory of distributions (generalized functions) to interpret the solution. For example, the Dirac delta function allows the Fourier transform of a constant to be defined in a distributional sense.<br>   - Alternatively, one can consider the problem on a finite domain with appropriate boundary conditions, which ensures integrability.<br><br><br><br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>This question highlights the importance of mathematical assumptions in solving PDEs. The absolute integrability of the initial condition is not just a technical requirement but a reflection of physical realism. Understanding these limitations is crucial for applying mathematical methods to real-world problems, where idealized conditions often break down. This concept is also relevant in signal processing, where non-integrable signals (e.g., DC signals) require special handling."
}

{
  "front": "What is the physical significance of the parameter <i>c</i> in the heat equation <i>u_t = c^2 u_{xx}</i>, and how does it influence the temperature distribution?",
  "back": "<b>Physical Significance of <i>c</i> in the Heat Equation:</b><br><br><br><br>The heat equation is given by:<br>\\[ \\frac{\\partial u}{\\partial t} = c^2 \\frac{\\partial^2 u}{\\partial x^2}. \\]<br><br>The parameter <i>c</i> is the <b>thermal diffusivity</b> of the material, defined as:<br>\\[ c^2 = \\frac{k}{\\rho C_p}, \\]<br>where:<br>- <i>k</i> is the thermal conductivity (ability of the material to conduct heat).<br>- <i>ρ</i> is the density of the material.<br>- <i>C_p</i> is the specific heat capacity (amount of heat required to raise the temperature of a unit mass by one degree).<br><br><b>Influence on Temperature Distribution:</b><br><br>1. <b>Rate of Diffusion:</b><br>   - A larger <i>c</i> means the material diffuses heat more quickly. This results in faster spreading of the temperature profile and a more rapid approach to thermal equilibrium.<br>   - A smaller <i>c</i> means the material diffuses heat more slowly, leading to a more gradual change in temperature over time.<br><br>2. <b>Width of the Gaussian Kernel:</b><br>   - In the solution to the heat equation, the Gaussian kernel is:<br>     \\[ \\exp \\left\\{ -\\frac{(x - v)^2}{4c^2 t} \\right\\}. \\]<br>   - The term <i>4c^2 t</i> in the denominator determines the width of the Gaussian. For a given time <i>t</i>, a larger <i>c</i> results in a wider Gaussian, indicating that heat has spread further from the initial source.<br><br>3. <b>Time Evolution:</b><br>   - The time scale of the diffusion process is inversely proportional to <i>c^2</i>. For example, the time it takes for the temperature to reach a certain distribution scales as <i>1/c^2</i>. Thus, materials with higher thermal diffusivity reach equilibrium faster.<br><br>4. <b>Material Properties:</b><br>   - Metals typically have high thermal diffusivity due to their high thermal conductivity and low specific heat capacity, leading to rapid heat diffusion.<br>   - Insulators have low thermal diffusivity, resulting in slow heat diffusion.<br><br><br><br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>The thermal diffusivity <i>c</i> is a fundamental property that characterizes how quickly a material responds to changes in temperature. It plays a critical role in applications such as heat exchangers, insulation design, and thermal management in electronics. Understanding its influence on the heat equation solution is essential for predicting temperature distributions in engineering systems."
}
```

  "front": "What is the general form of the solutions to the Helmholtz equation for a rectangular membrane, and how are the boundary conditions applied to derive the specific eigenfunctions?",
  "back": "<b>General Solutions:</b><br><br>The Helmholtz equation for a rectangular membrane is given by:<br>\\[ \\nabla^2 F + k^2 F = 0 \\]<br>with solutions of the form:<br>\\[ H(x) = A \\cos kx + B \\sin kx \\quad \\text{and} \\quad Q(y) = C \\cos py + D \\sin py \\]<br>where <i>A, B, C, D</i> are constants.<br><br><br><br><b>Applying Boundary Conditions:</b><br><br>The boundary conditions require that the solution <i>F = HQ</i> vanishes on the edges of the membrane, i.e., at <i>x = 0, x = a, y = 0, y = b</i>. This leads to:<br>\\[ H(0) = 0, \\quad H(a) = 0, \\quad Q(0) = 0, \\quad Q(b) = 0. \\]<br>From <i>H(0) = A = 0</i>, we get <i>A = 0</i>. Then, <i>H(a) = B \\sin ka = 0</i>. Since <i>B ≠ 0</i> (otherwise <i>H(x) ≡ 0</i>), we must have <i>\\sin ka = 0</i>, which implies:<br>\\[ ka = m\\pi \\quad \\Rightarrow \\quad k = \\frac{m\\pi}{a}, \\quad m = 1, 2, \\dots \\]<br>Similarly, for <i>Q(y)</i>, we find <i>C = 0</i> and:<br>\\[ p = \\frac{n\\pi}{b}, \\quad n = 1, 2, \\dots \\]<br>Thus, the eigenfunctions are:<br>\\[ F_{mn}(x, y) = \\sin \\frac{m\\pi x}{a} \\sin \\frac{n\\pi y}{b}, \\quad m, n = 1, 2, \\dots \\]<br><br><br><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>The Helmholtz equation arises in the separation of variables for the wave equation governing the vibration of a rectangular membrane. The boundary conditions ensure that the membrane is fixed along its edges, leading to standing wave solutions. The eigenfunctions <i>F<sub>mn</sub></i> represent the spatial modes of vibration, while the eigenvalues <i>λ<sub>mn</sub></i> determine the frequencies of these modes. This framework is foundational in understanding how membranes and other two-dimensional systems vibrate, with applications in acoustics, structural engineering, and physics."
}
```

{
  "front": "What are <b>eigenfunctions</b> and <b>eigenvalues</b> in the context of a vibrating rectangular membrane, and how do they relate to the wave equation?",
  "back": "<b>Eigenfunctions:</b><br><br>Eigenfunctions, denoted <i>F<sub>mn</sub>(x, y)</i>, are the spatial solutions to the Helmholtz equation that satisfy the boundary conditions of the membrane. For a rectangular membrane, they are given by:<br>\\[ F_{mn}(x, y) = \\sin \\frac{m\\pi x}{a} \\sin \\frac{n\\pi y}{b}, \\quad m, n = 1, 2, \\dots \\]<br>These functions describe the spatial patterns (modes) of vibration of the membrane.<br><br><br><br><b>Eigenvalues:</b><br><br>Eigenvalues, denoted <i>λ<sub>mn</sub></i>, are the corresponding constants that determine the natural frequencies of the membrane's vibration. They are derived from the Helmholtz equation and are given by:<br>\\[ \\lambda_{mn} = c \\pi \\sqrt{\\frac{m^2}{a^2} + \\frac{n^2}{b^2}}. \\]<br>The frequency of the mode <i>u<sub>mn</sub></i> is <i>λ<sub>mn</sub> / 2π</i>.<br><br><br><br><b>Relation to the Wave Equation:</b><br><br>The wave equation for the membrane is:<br>\\[ \\frac{\\partial^2 u}{\\partial t^2} = c^2 \\nabla^2 u. \\]<br>Using separation of variables, <i>u(x, y, t) = F(x, y)G(t)</i>, we obtain the Helmholtz equation for <i>F</i> and an ordinary differential equation (ODE) for <i>G</i>. The eigenfunctions <i>F<sub>mn</sub></i> solve the Helmholtz equation, while the eigenvalues <i>λ<sub>mn</sub></i> appear in the ODE for <i>G(t)</i>:<br>\\[ G_{mn}(t) = B_{mn} \\cos \\lambda_{mn} t + B_{mn}^* \\sin \\lambda_{mn} t. \\]<br>Thus, the full solution to the wave equation is:<br>\\[ u_{mn}(x, y, t) = F_{mn}(x, y) G_{mn}(t). \\]<br><br><br><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>Eigenfunctions and eigenvalues are fundamental to solving partial differential equations (PDEs) like the wave equation using separation of variables. They provide a way to decompose complex vibrations into simpler, independent modes, each with its own frequency. This decomposition is analogous to breaking down a musical chord into individual notes and is essential for analyzing systems in physics, engineering, and applied mathematics."
}
```

  "front": "What are <b>nodal lines</b> in the context of a vibrating membrane, and how do they arise from the eigenfunctions?",
  "back": "<b>Definition of Nodal Lines:</b><br><br>Nodal lines are curves on the surface of a vibrating membrane where the displacement <i>u(x, y, t)</i> is always zero, regardless of time. These lines represent points on the membrane that remain stationary during vibration.<br><br><br><br><b>Arising from Eigenfunctions:</b><br><br>For a rectangular membrane, the eigenfunctions are:<br>\\[ F_{mn}(x, y) = \\sin \\frac{m\\pi x}{a} \\sin \\frac{n\\pi y}{b}. \\]<br>The nodal lines occur where <i>F<sub>mn</sub>(x, y) = 0</i>. This happens when either:<br>- <i>\\sin \\frac{m\\pi x}{a} = 0</i>, which implies <i>x = \\frac{ka}{m}</i> for <i>k = 0, 1, \\dots, m</i>, or<br>- <i>\\sin \\frac{n\\pi y}{b} = 0</i>, which implies <i>y = \\frac{lb}{n}</i> for <i>l = 0, 1, \\dots, n</i>.<br><br>Thus, the nodal lines form a grid of horizontal and vertical lines on the membrane.<br><br><br><br><b>Example:</b><br><br>For the eigenfunction <i>F<sub>12</sub>(x, y) = \\sin \\pi x \\sin 2\\pi y</i>, the nodal lines are:<br>- <i>\\sin \\pi x = 0</i> at <i>x = 0</i> and <i>x = 1</i> (the boundaries), and<br>- <i>\\sin 2\\pi y = 0</i> at <i>y = 0, y = 1/2, y = 1</i>.<br><br>The line <i>y = 1/2</i> is an internal nodal line where the membrane does not move.<br><br><br><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>Nodal lines are a visual manifestation of the standing wave patterns formed by the superposition of waves traveling in opposite directions. They are critical in understanding the behavior of vibrating systems, as they reveal the spatial structure of the modes. In engineering, nodal lines help predict stress concentrations in structures or design musical instruments with specific acoustic properties. Their study bridges the gap between abstract mathematical solutions and tangible physical phenomena."
}
```

For example, <i>λ<sub>12</sub> = λ<sub>21</sub> = cπ√5</i>. This occurs because the expression <i>m² + n²</i> is symmetric in <i>m</i> and <i>n</i>. Additionally, some integers can be expressed as the sum of two squares in multiple ways (e.g., <i>65 = 1² + 8² = 4² + 7²</i>), leading to more than two eigenfunctions sharing the same eigenvalue.<br><br><br><br><b>Physical Implication:</b><br><br>This phenomenon, known as <i>degeneracy</i>, implies that multiple vibrational modes can oscillate at the same frequency. For instance, <i>F<sub>12</sub></i> and <i>F<sub>21</sub></i> have nodal lines at <i>y = 1/2</i> and <i>x = 1/2</i>, respectively. When these modes are combined, the resulting vibration can exhibit complex nodal line patterns that depend on the relative amplitudes of the modes.<br><br><br><br><b>Example:</b><br><br>For <i>λ<sub>18</sub> = λ<sub>81</sub> = λ<sub>47</sub> = λ<sub>74</sub> = cπ√65</i>, four distinct eigenfunctions correspond to the same eigenvalue. This degeneracy arises because 65 can be written as the sum of two squares in multiple ways, reflecting the symmetry of the square membrane.<br><br><br><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>Degeneracy is a consequence of symmetries in the system and is common in physical systems with high degrees of symmetry, such as square or circular membranes. It allows for richer vibrational behavior, as multiple modes can be excited simultaneously at the same frequency. This has practical implications in fields like acoustics, where degeneracy can influence the timbre of a sound, or in structural engineering, where it can affect the stability of a vibrating system."
}

{
  "front": "How does the separation of variables method applied to the wave equation for a rectangular membrane lead to the determination of its vibrational modes?",
  "back": "<b>Step-by-Step Application of Separation of Variables:</b><br><br>1. <b>Wave Equation:</b><br>   The wave equation for the membrane is:<br>   \\[ \\frac{\\partial^2 u}{\\partial t^2} = c^2 \\nabla^2 u. \\]<br><br>2. <b>Assume Separable Solution:</b><br>   We assume a solution of the form <i>u(x, y, t) = F(x, y)G(t)</i>. Substituting into the wave equation gives:<br>   \\[ F(x, y) G''(t) = c^2 G(t) \\nabla^2 F(x, y). \\]<br>   Dividing both sides by <i>c²FG</i> yields:<br>   \\[ \\frac{G''(t)}{c^2 G(t)} = \\frac{\\nabla^2 F(x, y)}{F(x, y)} = -\\lambda, \\]<br>   where <i>λ</i> is a separation constant.<br><br><br><br>3. <b>Spatial Equation (Helmholtz Equation):</b><br>   The spatial part leads to the Helmholtz equation:<br>   \\[ \\nabla^2 F + \\lambda F = 0. \\]<br>   For a rectangular membrane, we further separate <i>F(x, y) = H(x)Q(y)</i>, yielding:<br>   \\[ H''(x) + k^2 H(x) = 0 \\quad \\text{and} \\quad Q''(y) + p^2 Q(y) = 0, \\]<br>   where <i>k² + p² = λ</i>. The solutions are:<br>   \\[ H(x) = A \\cos kx + B \\sin kx \\quad \\text{and} \\quad Q(y) = C \\cos py + D \\sin py. \\]<br><br>4. <b>Apply Boundary Conditions:</b><br>   The boundary conditions <i>u = 0</i> on the edges of the membrane imply <i>F = 0</i> at <i>x = 0, x = a, y = 0, y = b</i>. This leads to:<br>   \\[ H(0) = H(a) = 0 \\quad \\Rightarrow \\quad A = 0, \\quad k = \\frac{m\\pi}{a}, \\]<br>   \\[ Q(0) = Q(b) = 0 \\quad \\Rightarrow \\quad C = 0, \\quad p = \\frac{n\\pi}{b}. \\]<br>   Thus, the eigenfunctions are:<br>   \\[ F_{mn}(x, y) = \\sin \\frac{m\\pi x}{a} \\sin \\frac{n\\pi y}{b}. \\]<br><br>5. <b>Temporal Equation:</b><br>   The temporal part becomes:<br>   \\[ G''(t) + c^2 \\lambda G(t) = 0, \\]<br>   where <i>λ = k² + p² = π²(m²/a² + n²/b²)</i>. The solution is:<br>   \\[ G_{mn}(t) = B_{mn} \\cos \\lambda_{mn} t + B_{mn}^* \\sin \\lambda_{mn} t. \\]<br><br>6. <b>Full Solution:</b><br>   The vibrational modes of the membrane are given by:<br>   \\[ u_{mn}(x, y, t) = F_{mn}(x, y) G_{mn}(t) = \\left(B_{mn} \\cos \\lambda_{mn} t + B_{mn}^* \\sin \\lambda_{mn} t\\right) \\sin \\frac{m\\pi x}{a} \\sin \\frac{n\\pi y}{b}. \\]<br><br><br><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>The separation of variables method is a powerful tool for solving PDEs by reducing them to simpler ODEs. In this case, it decomposes the complex vibration of the membrane into independent spatial and temporal components. The spatial eigenfunctions <i>F<sub>mn</sub></i> describe the standing wave patterns, while the temporal solutions <i>G<sub>mn</sub></i> describe the harmonic motion of each mode. This approach is widely used in physics and engineering to analyze systems governed by wave equations, such as strings, membranes, and electromagnetic fields."
}
```

  "back": "<b>Effect of Changing Boundary Conditions:</b><br><br>If the boundary conditions of the membrane were changed from <i>fixed edges</i> (Dirichlet conditions, <i>u = 0</i>) to <i>free edges</i> (Neumann conditions, <i>∂u/∂n = 0</i>), the following changes would occur:<br><br>1. <b>Eigenfunctions:</b><br>   For free edges, the spatial solutions <i>H(x)</i> and <i>Q(y)</i> would satisfy:<br>   \\[ H'(0) = H'(a) = 0 \\quad \\text{and} \\quad Q'(0) = Q'(b) = 0. \\]<br>   The general solutions remain:<br>   \\[ H(x) = A \\cos kx + B \\sin kx \\quad \\text{and} \\quad Q(y) = C \\cos py + D \\sin py. \\]<br>   However, applying the Neumann conditions leads to:<br>   \\[ H'(x) = -A k \\sin kx + B k \\cos kx. \\]<br>   Thus, <i>H'(0) = Bk = 0</i> implies <i>B = 0</i>, and <i>H'(a) = -A k \\sin ka = 0</i> implies <i>ka = mπ</i>. Therefore:<br>   \\[ H_m(x) = \\cos \\frac{m\\pi x}{a}, \\quad m = 0, 1, 2, \\dots \\]<br>   Similarly, <i>Q_n(y) = \\cos \\frac{n\\pi y}{b}</i>. The eigenfunctions become:<br>   \\[ F_{mn}(x, y) = \\cos \\frac{m\\pi x}{a} \\cos \\frac{n\\pi y}{b}. \\]<br><br>2. <b>Eigenvalues:</b><br>   The eigenvalues are still given by:<br>   \\[ \\lambda_{mn} = c \\pi \\sqrt{\\frac{m^2}{a^2} + \\frac{n^2}{b^2}}, \\]<br>   but now <i>m, n = 0, 1, 2, \\dots</i>. The case <i>m = n = 0</i> corresponds to a rigid-body mode (no vibration), which is not physically meaningful for a free membrane.<br><br><br><br>3. <b>Nodal Lines:</b><br>   The nodal lines for free-edge conditions would differ significantly from those of a fixed membrane. For example, the mode <i>F<sub>11</sub></i> would have no internal nodal lines, as the cosine functions do not vanish inside the domain. This contrasts with the fixed-edge case, where <i>F<sub>11</sub></i> has nodal lines at the boundaries.<br><br><br><br>4. <b>Physical Implications:</b><br>   - The fundamental frequency (lowest non-zero eigenvalue) would be lower for a free-edge membrane compared to a fixed-edge membrane of the same dimensions, as the constraints are less restrictive.<br>   - The vibrational patterns would be less localized, with more uniform displacement across the membrane.<br>   - Degeneracy could still occur in square membranes, but the eigenfunctions and nodal lines would differ.<br><br><br><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>Boundary conditions play a critical role in determining the vibrational behavior of a system. Fixed edges impose strict constraints, leading to standing waves with nodes at the boundaries. Free edges, on the other hand, allow the membrane to move more freely, resulting in different eigenfunctions and nodal patterns. This distinction is essential in engineering applications, such as designing drumheads or analyzing the vibration of plates in mechanical structures, where boundary conditions can significantly influence performance and stability."
}

{
  "front": "How does the geometry of a membrane (e.g., rectangular vs. square) influence its vibrational modes and degeneracy?",
  "back": "<b>Influence of Geometry on Vibrational Modes:</b><br><br>1. <b>Rectangular Membrane (<i>a ≠ b</i>):</b><br>   - The eigenvalues are given by:<br>     \\[ \\lambda_{mn} = c \\pi \\sqrt{\\frac{m^2}{a^2} + \\frac{n^2}{b^2}}. \\]<br>   - For <i>a ≠ b</i>, <i>λ<sub>mn</sub> ≠ λ<sub>nm</sub></i> unless <i>m = n</i>. Thus, each pair <i>(m, n)</i> typically corresponds to a unique eigenvalue, and degeneracy is rare.<br>   - The eigenfunctions are:<br>     \\[ F_{mn}(x, y) = \\sin \\frac{m\\pi x}{a} \\sin \\frac{n\\pi y}{b}, \\]<br>     and their nodal lines form a grid aligned with the membrane's edges.<br><br><br><br>2. <b>Square Membrane (<i>a = b</i>):</b><br>   - The eigenvalues simplify to:<br>     \\[ \\lambda_{mn} = c \\pi \\sqrt{m^2 + n^2}. \\]<br>   - Degeneracy occurs when <i>m ≠ n</i>, as <i>λ<sub>mn</sub> = λ<sub>nm</sub></i>. For example, <i>λ<sub>12</sub> = λ<sub>21</sub> = cπ√5</i>.<br>   - The eigenfunctions <i>F<sub>mn</sub></i> and <i>F<sub>nm</sub></i> have different nodal line patterns, leading to richer vibrational behavior.<br>   - Degeneracy can also occur for higher modes if <i>m² + n²</i> can be expressed as the sum of two squares in multiple ways (e.g., <i>65 = 1² + 8² = 4² + 7²</i>).<br><br><br><br><b>Physical Implications:</b><br><br>- In rectangular membranes, the lack of degeneracy means that each vibrational mode has a unique frequency, simplifying the analysis but limiting the complexity of the vibrational patterns.<br>- In square membranes, degeneracy allows for multiple modes to vibrate at the same frequency, enabling more intricate nodal line patterns. This can lead to phenomena such as mode mixing, where the superposition of degenerate modes produces complex vibrations.<br><br><br><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>The geometry of a membrane directly influences its vibrational properties by determining the symmetry and degeneracy of its modes. Rectangular membranes, with their lower symmetry, typically exhibit non-degenerate modes, while square membranes, with higher symmetry, often exhibit degeneracy. This geometric dependence is crucial in applications such as musical instrument design, where the shape of a drumhead affects its sound, or in structural engineering, where the geometry of a plate influences its vibrational response to external forces."
}

The eigenvalues determine the frequencies of these modes, while the eigenfunctions describe their spatial patterns. By computing the first few eigenvalues and eigenfunctions, we gain insight into the fundamental vibrational behavior of the membrane, which is essential for applications in acoustics and structural dynamics."
}

  "back": "The zeros of the Bessel function \\( J_0 \\) determine the nodal lines and normal modes as follows:<br><br>- The \\( m \\)-th normal mode corresponds to the eigenfunction \\( u_m(r,t) = (A_m \\cos(\\lambda_m t) + B_m \\sin(\\lambda_m t)) J_0(k_m r) \\), where \\( k_m = \\frac{\\alpha_m}{R} \\).<br><br>- The function \\( J_0(k_m r) \\) has \\( m-1 \\) zeros between \\( r = 0 \\) and \\( r = R \\), each corresponding to a circular nodal line where the membrane does not move.<br><br>- For example:<br><br>  - \\( m = 1 \\): No nodal lines (entire membrane moves in unison).<br><br>  - \\( m = 2 \\): One nodal line at \\( r = \\frac{\\alpha_1 R}{\\alpha_2} \\), dividing the membrane into a central region and an outer ring moving in opposite directions.<br><br>  - \\( m = 3 \\): Two nodal lines, creating three concentric regions with alternating motion.<br><br><br>The irregular spacing of the zeros of \\( J_0 \\) (unlike the regular spacing of sine function zeros) results in normal modes that are not harmonically related, explaining why a drum's sound differs from that of a violin.<br><br><br><img src='img-309.jpg'><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>Nodal lines are regions of zero displacement and are a direct consequence of the spatial eigenfunctions' structure. For circular membranes, the Bessel function's zeros dictate these lines, unlike the straight nodal lines in rectangular membranes (e.g., vibrating strings). This irregularity in nodal line spacing is why drums produce a more complex, non-harmonic sound compared to string instruments. Understanding nodal patterns is crucial for designing musical instruments and analyzing structural vibrations."
}

The wave speed \\( c \\) determines the temporal evolution of the modes, while the coefficients \\( B_{mn} \\) quantify the contribution of each spatial mode to the initial displacement. The nodal lines represent locations where the membrane does not move, corresponding to zeros of the sine functions. The first term dominates because its coefficient is much larger than those of higher-order terms, reflecting the smoothness of the initial displacement."
}

Adjusting the limits:<br>- When \\( s = 0 \\), \\( z = -\\frac{x}{2c\\sqrt{t}} \\).<br>- When \\( s = \\infty \\), \\( z = \\infty \\).<br><br>The integral becomes:<br>\\[ u(x,t) = \\frac{1}{2c\\sqrt{\\pi t}} \\int_{-x/(2c\\sqrt{t})}^{\\infty} e^{-z^2} (2c\\sqrt{t} dz) = \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{\\pi}} \\int_{-x/(2c\\sqrt{t})}^{\\infty} e^{-z^2} dz \\]<br><br>Using the definition of the error function and the fact that \\( \\text{erf}(\\infty) = 1 \\), we can write:<br>\\[ u(x,t) = \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{\\pi}} \\left( \\int_{-x/(2c\\sqrt{t})}^{0} e^{-z^2} dz + \\int_{0}^{\\infty} e^{-z^2} dz \\right) = \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{\\pi}} \\left( \\frac{\\sqrt{\\pi}}{2} \\text{erf}\\left(\\frac{x}{2c\\sqrt{t}}\\right) + \\frac{\\sqrt{\\pi}}{2} \\right) \\]<br><br>Simplifying:<br>\\[ u(x,t) = \\frac{1}{2} + \\frac{1}{2} \\text{erf}\\left(\\frac{x}{2c\\sqrt{t}}\\right) \\]<br><br>However, since \\( \\text{erf}(-x) = -\\text{erf}(x) \\), we can also write:<br>\\[ u(x,t) = \\frac{1}{2} - \\frac{1}{2} \\text{erf}\\left(- \\frac{x}{2c\\sqrt{t}}\\right) \\]<br><hr><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>This solution models the diffusion of heat from a step-function initial condition, representing a sudden temperature jump at \\( x = 0 \\). }

  "back": "The integral solution to the heat equation is:<br>\\[ u(x,t) = \\frac{1}{2c\\sqrt{\\pi t}} \\int_{-\\infty}^{\\infty} f(s) e^{-\\frac{(x-s)^2}{4c^2 t}} ds \\]<br><br>Substitute \\( f(s) = s \\) for \\( |s| \\lt 1 \\) and \\( 0 \\) otherwise:<br>\\[ u(x,t) = \\frac{1}{2c\\sqrt{\\pi t}} \\int_{-1}^{1} s e^{-\\frac{(x-s)^2}{4c^2 t}} ds \\]<br><br>Let \\( z = \\frac{x-s}{2c\\sqrt{t}} \\), then \\( s = x - 2c\\sqrt{t} z \\) and \\( ds = -2c\\sqrt{t} dz \\). Adjusting the limits:<br>- When \\( s = -1 \\), \\( z = \\frac{x+1}{2c\\sqrt{t}} \\).<br>- When \\( s = 1 \\), \\( z = \\frac{x-1}{2c\\sqrt{t}} \\).<br><br>The integral becomes:<br>\\[ u(x,t) = \\frac{1}{2c\\sqrt{\\pi t}} \\int_{\\frac{x+1}{2c\\sqrt{t} }}^{\\frac{x-1}{2c\\sqrt{t} }} (x - 2c\\sqrt{t} z) e^{-z^2} (-2c\\sqrt{t} dz) \\]<br>\\[ = \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{\\pi}} \\int_{\\frac{x-1}{2c\\sqrt{t} }}^{\\frac{x+1}{2c\\sqrt{t} }} (x - 2c\\sqrt{t} z) e^{-z^2} dz \\]<br><br>Split the integral:<br>\\[ u(x,t) = \\frac{x}{\\sqrt{\\pi}} \\int_{\\frac{x-1}{2c\\sqrt{t} }}^{\\frac{x+1}{2c\\sqrt{t} }} e^{-z^2} dz - \\frac{2c\\sqrt{t}}{\\sqrt{\\pi}} \\int_{\\frac{x-1}{2c\\sqrt{t} }}^{\\frac{x+1}{2c\\sqrt{t} }} z e^{-z^2} dz \\]<br><br>The first integral can be expressed in terms of the error function:<br>\\[ \\int_{\\frac{x-1}{2c\\sqrt{t} }}^{\\frac{x+1}{2c\\sqrt{t} }} e^{-z^2} dz = \\frac{\\sqrt{\\pi}}{2} \\left[ \\text{erf}\\left(\\frac{x+1}{2c\\sqrt{t}}\\right) - \\text{erf}\\left(\\frac{x-1}{2c\\sqrt{t}}\\right) \\right] \\]<br><br>The second integral can be evaluated directly:<br>\\[ \\int_{\\frac{x-1}{2c\\sqrt{t} }}^{\\frac{x+1}{2c\\sqrt{t} }} z e^{-z^2} dz = \\frac{1}{2} \\left[ e^{-\\left(\\frac{x-1}{2c\\sqrt{t}}\\right)^2} - e^{-\\left(\\frac{x+1}{2c\\sqrt{t}}\\right)^2} \\right] \\]<br><br>Thus, the solution is:<br>\\[ u(x,t) = \\frac{x}{2} \\left[ \\text{erf}\\left(\\frac{x+1}{2c\\sqrt{t}}\\right) - \\text{erf}\\left(\\frac{x-1}{2c\\sqrt{t}}\\right) \\right] - \\frac{c\\sqrt{t}}{\\sqrt{\\pi}} \\left[ e^{-\\left(\\frac{x-1}{2c\\sqrt{t}}\\right)^2} - e^{-\\left(\\frac{x+1}{2c\\sqrt{t}}\\right)^2} \\right] \\]<br><hr><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>This solution demonstrates how the heat equation evolves a linear initial temperature distribution within a finite interval. The error function terms capture the diffusion of the initial linear profile, while the exponential terms reflect the influence of the boundaries at \\( x = \\pm 1 \\). The solution highlights the interplay between the initial condition and the heat kernel, which governs the rate of diffusion. This problem is relevant in engineering applications where heat sources are localized and time-dependent."
}

{
  "front": "Consider a rectangular elastic membrane fixed along its edges, with dimensions \\( a \\) and \\( b \\). The membrane is initially displaced in the shape of a sinusoidal function \\( u(x,y,0) = A \\sin(\\frac{\\pi x}{a}) \\sin(\\frac{\\pi y}{b}) \\) and released from rest. Derive the expression for the displacement \\( u(x,y,t) \\) as a function of time.",
  "back": "To solve this problem, we use separation of variables and the method of eigenfunction expansion for the two-dimensional wave equation:<br><br>1. <b>Wave Equation</b>: The governing equation is \\( u_{tt} = c^2 (u_{xx} + u_{yy}) \\), with boundary conditions \\( u(0,y,t) = u(a,y,t) = u(x,0,t) = u(x,b,t) = 0 \\) (fixed edges) and initial conditions \\( u(x,y,0) = A \\sin(\\frac{\\pi x}{a}) \\sin(\\frac{\\pi y}{b}) \\), \\( u_t(x,y,0) = 0 \\) (released from rest).<br><br>2. <b>Separation of Variables</b>: Assume a solution of the form \\( u(x,y,t) = X(x)Y(y)T(t) \\). Substituting into the wave equation and separating variables yields:<br>\\[ \\frac{T''}{c^2 T} = \\frac{X''}{X} + \\frac{Y''}{Y} = -k^2 \\]<br>where \\( k^2 \\) is a separation constant. This leads to three ODEs:<br>\\[ X'' + \\lambda X = 0, \\quad Y'' + \\mu Y = 0, \\quad T'' + c^2 k^2 T = 0 \\]<br>where \\( k^2 = \\lambda + \\mu \\).<br><br>3. <b>Boundary Conditions</b>: Applying the boundary conditions for \\( X(x) \\) and \\( Y(y) \\) gives:<br>\\[ X(x) = \\sin(\\frac{n \\pi x}{a}), \\quad Y(y) = \\sin(\\frac{m \\pi y}{b}) \\]<br>where \\( n \\) and \\( m \\) are positive integers, and the eigenvalues are \\( \\lambda_n = (\\frac{n \\pi}{a})^2 \\), \\( \\mu_m = (\\frac{m \\pi}{b})^2 \\).<br><br>4. <b>Time-Dependent Solution</b>: The ODE for \\( T(t) \\) becomes:<br>\\[ T'' + c^2 (\\lambda_n + \\mu_m) T = 0 \\]<br>with solution \\( T(t) = C \\cos(\\omega_{nm} t) + D \\sin(\\omega_{nm} t) \\), where \\( \\omega_{nm} = c \\sqrt{\\lambda_n + \\mu_m} \\).<br><br>5. <b>Initial Conditions</b>: The initial condition \\( u_t(x,y,0) = 0 \\) implies \\( D = 0 \\). The initial displacement condition \\( u(x,y,0) = A \\sin(\\frac{\\pi x}{a}) \\sin(\\frac{\\pi y}{b}) \\) matches the mode \\( n=1, m=1 \\), so the solution is:<br>\\[ u(x,y,t) = A \\sin(\\frac{\\pi x}{a}) \\sin(\\frac{\\pi y}{b}) \\cos(\\omega_{11} t) \\]<br>where \\( \\omega_{11} = c \\sqrt{(\\frac{\\pi}{a})^2 + (\\frac{\\pi}{b})^2} \\).<hr><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br>This example illustrates how separation of variables can be extended to two-dimensional problems. The solution shows that the membrane vibrates in a single mode (the fundamental mode) because the initial displacement matches one of the eigenfunctions of the system. This is analogous to the one-dimensional case but involves two spatial variables, demonstrating the increased complexity of higher-dimensional wave problems."
}
```

  "front": "Derive the expression for the resultant vertical force acting on a small segment of a vibrating membrane, starting from the vertical components of the forces on opposite sides.",
  "back": "The vertical components of the forces along the right and left sides of the membrane segment are given by:<br>\\[ T \\Delta y \\sin \\beta \\quad \\text{and} \\quad -T \\Delta y \\sin \\alpha, \\]<br>where \\( T \\) is the tension, \\( \\Delta y \\) is the segment length, and \\( \\alpha \\) and \\( \\beta \\) are the angles of inclination at the midpoints of the left and right edges, respectively. The negative sign for the left side indicates the force is directed downward.<br><br>Since the angles are small, we approximate \\( \\sin \\theta \\approx \\tan \\theta \\). The resultant vertical force is the sum of these components:<br>\\[ T \\Delta y (\\tan \\beta - \\tan \\alpha). \\]<br><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br>This resultant force is a key step in deriving the wave equation for membranes. The approximation \\( \\sin \\theta \\approx \\tan \\theta \\) simplifies the expression by relating the angles to the spatial derivatives of the membrane's displacement, which is essential for formulating the PDE."
}

### Avant:
```json
{
  "front": "Derive the two-dimensional wave equation for a vibrating rectangular membrane, starting from Newton's second law applied to a small portion of the membrane. Include all key assumptions and intermediate steps.",
  "back": "<b>Derivation of the Two-Dimensional Wave Equation:</b><br><br><br><br>1. Consider a small rectangular portion of the membrane with dimensions \\(\\Delta x\\) and \\(\\Delta y\\). The membrane is under uniform tension \\(T\\) (force per unit length).<br><br><br><br>2. The vertical component of the tension force on the left side of the portion (at \\(x\\)) is approximately \\(T \\Delta y \\sin \\alpha \\approx T \\Delta y \\tan \\alpha = T \\Delta y u_x(x, y_2)\\), where \\(u_x\\) is the partial derivative of the displacement \\(u\\) with respect to \\(x\\).<br><br><br><br>3. The vertical component of the tension force on the right side (at \\(x + \\Delta x\\)) is \\(T \\Delta y \\sin \\beta \\approx T \\Delta y \\tan \\beta = T \\Delta y u_x(x + \\Delta x, y_1)\\). The net vertical force from these two sides is:<br><br>\\[ T \\Delta y \\left[ u_x(x + \\Delta x, y_1) - u_x(x, y_2) \\right] \\tag{1} \\]<br><br><br><br>4. Similarly, the net vertical force from the top and bottom sides (at \\(y + \\Delta y\\) and \\(y\\)) is:<br><br>\\[ T \\Delta x \\left[ u_y(x_1, y + \\Delta y) - u_y(x_2, y) \\right] \\tag{2} \\]<br><br><br><br>5. By Newton's second law, the sum of these forces equals the mass of the portion (\\(\\rho \\Delta A = \\rho \\Delta x \\Delta y\\)) times its vertical acceleration (\\(\\frac{\\partial^2 u}{\\partial t^2}\\)):<br><br>\\[ \\rho \\Delta x \\Delta y \\frac{\\partial^2 u}{\\partial t^2} = T \\Delta y \\left[ u_x(x + \\Delta x, y_1) - u_x(x, y_2) \\right] + T \\Delta x \\left[ u_y(x_1, y + \\Delta y) - u_y(x_2, y) \\right]. \\]<br><br><br><br>6. Divide both sides by \\(\\rho \\Delta x \\Delta y\\) to obtain:<br><br>\\[ \\frac{\\partial^2 u}{\\partial t^2} = \\frac{T}{\\rho} \\left[ \\frac{u_x(x + \\Delta x, y_1) - u_x(x, y_2)}{\\Delta x} + \\frac{u_y(x_1, y + \\Delta y) - u_y(x_2, y)}{\\Delta y} \\right]. \\]<br><br><br><br>7. Take the limit as \\(\\Delta x \\to 0\\) and \\(\\Delta y \\to 0\\). The terms in brackets become the second partial derivatives \\(\\frac{\\partial^2 u}{\\partial x^2}\\) and \\(\\frac{\\partial^2 u}{\\partial y^2}\\), respectively. This yields the two-dimensional wave equation:<br><br>\\[ \\frac{\\partial^2 u}{\\partial t^2} = c^2 \\left( \\frac{\\partial^2 u}{\\partial x^2} + \\frac{\\partial^2 u}{\\partial y^2} \\right), \\quad c^2 = \\frac{T}{\\rho}. \\tag{3} \\]<br><br><br><br>8. The expression in parentheses is the Laplacian \\(\\Delta^2 u\\) of \\(u\\), so the equation can also be written as:<br><br>\\[ \\frac{\\partial^2 u}{\\partial t^2} = c^2 \\Delta^2 u. \\tag{3'} \\]<br><br><br><br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>This derivation connects the physical behavior of a vibrating membrane (e.g., a drumhead) to a partial differential equation (PDE). The wave equation (3) describes how the displacement \\(u(x, y, t)\\) evolves over time due to tension and inertia. The constant \\(c = \\sqrt{T/\\rho}\\) represents the wave speed, showing how tension and mass density influence the propagation of waves. This PDE is foundational in physics and engineering for modeling wave phenomena in two dimensions, such as sound waves, electromagnetic waves, and mechanical vibrations."
}
```

{
  "front": "Solve the interior Dirichlet problem for Laplace's equation on a sphere of radius <i>R</i>, where the boundary condition is given by <i>f(φ) = cos<sup>2</sup> φ</i>. Provide the full solution, including the calculation of the coefficients <i>A<sub>n</sub></i> in the Fourier-Legendre series (17).",
  "back": "<b>Answer:</b><br><b>Step 1: Express the solution as a Fourier-Legendre series</b><br>The general solution for the interior problem is:<br>\\[u(r, \\phi) = \\sum_{n=0}^{\\infty} A_n r^n P_n(\\cos \\phi).\\tag{17}\\]<br><br><b>Step 2: Apply the boundary condition at <i>r = R</i></b><br>At <i>r = R</i>, the solution must match <i>f(φ) = cos<sup>2</sup> φ</i>:<br>\\[u(R, \\phi) = \\sum_{n=0}^{\\infty} A_n R^n P_n(\\cos \\phi) = \\cos^2 \\phi.\\]<br><br><b>Step 3: Use orthogonality of Legendre polynomials</b><br>The coefficients <i>A<sub>n</sub></i> are given by:<br>\\[A_n = \\frac{2n + 1}{2 R^n} \\int_{0}^{\\pi} f(\\phi) P_n(\\cos \\phi) \\sin \\phi \\, d\\phi.\\tag{19}\\]<br>Substitute <i>f(φ) = cos<sup>2</sup> φ</i> and <i>w = cos φ</i> (<i>dw = -sin φ dφ</i>):<br>\\[A_n = \\frac{2n + 1}{2 R^n} \\int_{-1}^{1} w^2 P_n(w) \\, dw.\\]<br><br><b>Step 4: Evaluate the integral for <i>n = 0, 1, 2</i></b><br>Recall the first few Legendre polynomials:<br>\\[P_0(w) = 1, \\quad P_1(w) = w, \\quad P_2(w) = \\frac{1}{2}(3w^2 - 1).\\]<br>Compute the integrals:<br>- For <i>n = 0</i>:<br>\\[\\int_{-1}^{1} w^2 P_0(w) \\, dw = \\int_{-1}^{1} w^2 \\, dw = \\frac{2}{3}.\\]<br>- For <i>n = 1</i>:<br>\\[\\int_{-1}^{1} w^2 P_1(w) \\, dw = \\int_{-1}^{1} w^3 \\, dw = 0.\\]<br>- For <i>n = 2</i>:<br>\\[\\int_{-1}^{1} w^2 P_2(w) \\, dw = \\int_{-1}^{1} w^2 \\cdot \\frac{1}{2}(3w^2 - 1) \\, dw = \\frac{1}{2} \\left(3 \\cdot \\frac{2}{5} - \\frac{2}{3}\\right) = \\frac{2}{15}.\\]<br>For <i>n ≥ 3</i>, the integrals vanish because <i>w<sup>2</sup></i> is orthogonal to <i>P<sub>n</sub>(w)</i> for <i>n > 2</i>.<br><br><b>Step 5: Compute <i>A<sub>n</sub></i></b><br>\\[A_0 = \\frac{1}{2 R^0} \\cdot \\frac{2}{3} = \\frac{1}{3}, \\quad A_1 = 0, \\quad A_2 = \\frac{5}{2 R^2} \\cdot \\frac{2}{15} = \\frac{1}{3 R^2}.\\]<br><br><b>Step 6: Write the final solution</b><br>\\[u(r, \\phi) = A_0 r^0 P_0(\\cos \\phi) + A_2 r^2 P_2(\\cos \\phi) = \\frac{1}{3} + \\frac{r^2}{3 R^2} (3 \\cos^2 \\phi - 1).\\]<br><br><b>Simplification:</b><br>\\[u(r, \\phi) = \\frac{1}{3} + \\frac{r^2}{R^2} \\cos^2 \\phi - \\frac{r^2}{3 R^2} = \\cos^2 \\phi + \\frac{1}{3} \\left(1 - \\frac{r^2}{R^2}\\right).\\]<br><hr><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br>This example illustrates how Fourier-Legendre series decompose a boundary condition into spherical harmonics. The orthogonality of Legendre polynomials ensures that only a finite number of terms contribute for polynomial <i>f(φ)</i>. The solution shows how the potential varies inside the sphere, transitioning from the boundary condition at <i>r = R</i> to a constant value at <i>r = 0</i> (the sphere's center)."
}
```

  "back": "<b>Solution:</b><br><br>1. <b>Boundary Condition:</b><br><br>The potential on the sphere's surface (<i>r = 1</i>) is:<br><br>\\[ f(\\phi) = \\begin{cases}\n110 & \\text{if } 0 \\leq \\phi &lt; \\pi/2 \\\\\n0 & \\text{if } \\pi/2 &lt; \\phi \\leq \\pi.\n\\end{cases} \\]<br><br><br>2. <b>Coefficients <i>A<sub>n</sub></i> for Interior Potential:</b><br><br>Using the formula for <i>A<sub>n</sub></i> (with <i>R = 1</i>):<br><br>\\[ A_n = \\frac{2n+1}{2} \\cdot 110 \\int_0^{\\pi/2} P_n(\\cos \\phi) \\sin \\phi \\, d\\phi. \\]<br>Substitute <i>w = cos φ</i> and integrate from 0 to 1:<br><br>\\[ A_n = 55(2n+1) \\sum_{m=0}^{M} (-1)^m \\frac{(2n-2m)!}{2^n m! (n-m)! (n-2m)!} \\int_0^1 w^{n-2m} \\, dw, \\]<br>where <i>M = n/2</i> for even <i>n</i> and <i>M = (n-1)/2</i> for odd <i>n</i>. The integral evaluates to <i>1/(n-2m+1)</i>.<br><br><br><br>3. <b>First Three Non-Zero Coefficients:</b><br><br>- For <i>n = 0</i>: <i>A<sub>0</sub> = 55</i>.<br><br>- For <i>n = 1</i>: <i>A<sub>1</sub> = 165/2</i>.<br><br>- For <i>n = 3</i>: <i>A<sub>3</sub> = -385/8</i> (note <i>A<sub>2</sub> = 0</i>).<br><br><br><br>4. <b>Interior Potential (<i>r ≤ 1</i>):</b><br><br>\\[ u(r, \\phi) = 55 + \\frac{165}{2} r P_1(\\cos \\phi) - \\frac{385}{8} r^3 P_3(\\cos \\phi) + \\cdots \\]<br><br><br>5. <b>Exterior Potential (<i>r ≥ 1</i>):</b><br><br>Since <i>B<sub>n</sub> = A<sub>n</sub></i> for <i>R = 1</i>:<br><br>\\[ u(r, \\phi) = \\frac{55}{r} + \\frac{165}{2r^2} P_1(\\cos \\phi) - \\frac{385}{8r^4} P_3(\\cos \\phi) + \\cdots \\]<br><br><br><br><i>Note:</i> Far from the sphere, the potential approximates that of a point charge: <i>55/r</i>.<br><br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>This problem demonstrates how boundary conditions on a sphere can be expanded into a series of Legendre polynomials. The coefficients <i>A<sub>n</sub></i> and <i>B<sub>n</sub></i> are determined by the orthogonality of these polynomials, which simplifies the integration process. The solution inside the sphere grows with <i>r<sup>n</sup></i>, while outside it decays as <i>1/r<sup>n+1</sup></i>, reflecting the physical behavior of electrostatic potentials. The vanishing of <i>A<sub>2</sub></i> is a consequence of the symmetry of the boundary condition."
}

{
  "front": "Consider a sphere of radius <i>R = 1</i> kept at a potential <i>f(φ) = cos 2φ</i> on its surface.<br><br><b>Problem:</b> Find the potential <i>u(r, φ)</i> inside the sphere. What is the potential at the North Pole, the equator, and the South Pole?",
  "back": "<b>Solution:</b><br><br>1. <b>Express <i>f(φ)</i> in Terms of Legendre Polynomials:</b><br><br>Using the identity for <i>cos 2φ</i>:<br><br>\\[ \\cos 2\\phi = 2\\cos^2 \\phi - 1 = 2w^2 - 1, \\quad w = \\cos \\phi. \\]<br>Express <i>2w<sup>2</sup> - 1</i> in terms of <i>P<sub>2</sub>(w)</i>:<br><br>\\[ 2w^2 - 1 = \\frac{4}{3} P_2(w) - \\frac{1}{3}, \\quad \\text{where } P_2(w) = \\frac{3}{2} w^2 - \\frac{1}{2}. \\]<br><br><br>2. <b>Potential Inside the Sphere:</b><br><br>The general solution for the interior potential is:<br><br>\\[ u(r, \\phi) = \\sum_{n=0}^{\\infty} A_n r^n P_n(\\cos \\phi). \\]<br>Since <i>f(φ)</i> only involves <i>P<sub>2</sub>(cos φ)</i>, all <i>A<sub>n</sub> = 0</i> except <i>A<sub>0</sub></i> and <i>A<sub>2</sub></i>. Thus:<br><br>\\[ u(r, \\phi) = A_0 + A_2 r^2 P_2(\\cos \\phi). \\]<br>From the boundary condition:<br><br>\\[ A_0 = -\\frac{1}{3}, \\quad A_2 = \\frac{4}{3}. \\]<br>So the potential is:<br><br>\\[ u(r, \\phi) = \\frac{4}{3} r^2 P_2(\\cos \\phi) - \\frac{1}{3} = \\frac{2}{3} r^2 (3 \\cos^2 \\phi - 1) - \\frac{1}{3}. \\]<br><br><br>3. <b>Potential at Key Points:</b><br><br>- <b>North Pole (φ = 0):</b> <i>cos φ = 1</i> ⇒ <i>u = (2/3)(3 - 1) - 1/3 = 1</i>.<br><br>- <b>Equator (φ = π/2):</b> <i>cos φ = 0</i> ⇒ <i>u = (2/3)(0 - 1) - 1/3 = -1</i>.<br><br>- <b>South Pole (φ = π):</b> <i>cos φ = -1</i> ⇒ <i>u = (2/3)(3 - 1) - 1/3 = 1</i>.<br><br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>This example illustrates how a boundary condition involving trigonometric functions can be decomposed into Legendre polynomials, simplifying the solution of Laplace's equation. The potential inside the sphere is a weighted sum of these polynomials, with coefficients determined by the boundary condition. The symmetry of <i>cos 2φ</i> ensures that only even-order polynomials contribute, and the potential at the poles and equator reflects the angular dependence of the boundary condition."
}
```

{
  "front": "What are the normal modes of vibration for a circular membrane, and how do they relate to the Bessel function <i>J<sub>0</sub></i>?",
  "back": "<b>Normal Modes of Vibration:</b><br><br>The normal modes of vibration for a circular membrane are the fundamental patterns of motion that satisfy the wave equation with fixed boundary conditions. For a circular membrane of radius <i>R</i>, the normal modes are given by:<br><br>\\[ W_m(r) G_m(t) = \\left(A_m \\cos \\lambda_m t + B_m \\sin \\lambda_m t\\right) J_0\\left(\\frac{\\alpha_m}{R} r\\right) \\]<br>where:<br><br>- <i>J<sub>0</sub></i> is the Bessel function of the first kind of order zero.<br><br>- <i>α<sub>m</sub></i> are the positive zeros of <i>J<sub>0</sub></i> (i.e., <i>J<sub>0</sub>(α<sub>m</sub>) = 0</i>).<br><br>- <i>λ<sub>m</sub> = c α<sub>m</sub>/R</i>, where <i>c</i> is the wave speed.<br><br>- <i>A<sub>m</sub></i> and <i>B<sub>m</sub></i> are constants determined by the initial conditions.<br><br><br><br><b>Relation to Bessel Function <i>J<sub>0</sub></i>:</b><br><br>The Bessel function <i>J<sub>0</sub></i> arises due to the radial symmetry of the circular membrane. It describes the radial dependence of the normal modes, analogous to how sine and cosine functions describe the spatial dependence in rectangular geometries. The zeros of <i>J<sub>0</sub></i> (<i>α<sub>m</sub></i>) determine the discrete frequencies <i>λ<sub>m</sub></i> at which the membrane can vibrate, corresponding to the eigenvalues of the problem.<br><br><br><br><img src='img-38.jpg'><br><br><small>Fig. 309: Normal modes of the circular membrane for vibrations independent of the angle.</small><br><br><br><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>Normal modes are the building blocks of any vibration in a continuous system. For a circular membrane, these modes are characterized by concentric nodal circles (where the membrane does not move), whose positions are determined by the zeros of the Bessel function. This is a direct consequence of solving the Helmholtz equation in polar coordinates, where separation of variables leads to Bessel's differential equation. Understanding these modes is crucial for applications such as designing drumheads, analyzing acoustic resonators, or studying the vibrations of circular plates in mechanical engineering."
}
```

  "back": "<b>Solution:</b><br><br><br>1. <b>Coefficient Verification:</b><br>   The Fourier-Legendre coefficients are given by:<br>   \\[ A_n = \\frac{2n + 1}{2} \\int_{-1}^{1} f(x) P_n(x) \\, dx \\]<br>   where \\( f(x) \\) is the boundary function and \\( P_n(x) \\) are the Legendre polynomials.<br><br>   - For \\( A_0 \\): \\( P_0(x) = 1 \\), so \\( A_0 = \\frac{1}{2} \\int_{-1}^{1} f(x) \\, dx \\).<br>   - For \\( A_1 \\): \\( P_1(x) = x \\), so \\( A_1 = \\frac{3}{2} \\int_{-1}^{1} x f(x) \\, dx \\).<br>   - For \\( A_2 \\): \\( P_2(x) = \\frac{1}{2} (3x^2 - 1) \\), so \\( A_2 = \\frac{5}{2} \\int_{-1}^{1} \\frac{1}{2} (3x^2 - 1) f(x) \\, dx \\).<br>   - For \\( A_3 \\): \\( P_3(x) = \\frac{1}{2} (5x^3 - 3x) \\), so \\( A_3 = \\frac{7}{2} \\int_{-1}^{1} \\frac{1}{2} (5x^3 - 3x) f(x) \\, dx \\).<br><br>   (The exact values depend on \\( f(x) \\), but the process is as above.)<br><br><br><br>2. <b>Computation of \\( A_4, \\dots, A_{10} \\):</b><br>   Use the same formula for higher \\( n \\):<br>   - \\( A_4 \\): \\( P_4(x) = \\frac{1}{8} (35x^4 - 30x^2 + 3) \\).<br>   - \\( A_5 \\): \\( P_5(x) = \\frac{1}{8} (63x^5 - 70x^3 + 15x) \\).<br>   - Continue similarly for \\( A_6 \\) to \\( A_{10} \\).<br><br>   (These integrals are typically computed numerically or symbolically for a given \\( f(x) \\).)<br><br><br><br>3. <b>Graphical Analysis:</b><br>   - Plot the partial sums \\( S_N(x) = \\sum_{n=0}^{N} A_n P_n(x) \\) for \\( N = 0, 1, 2, \\dots, 10 \\).<br>   - Observe how the partial sums converge to \\( f(x) \\) as \\( N \\) increases.<br>   - Note the Gibbs phenomenon near discontinuities, where overshoots persist even for large \\( N \\).<br><br>   ![partial_sums](partial_sums.jpeg)<br><br>   (Note: The image shows the boundary function and its partial sums.)<br><br><br><br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>Fourier-Legendre series are the spherical analog of Fourier series, used to represent functions on a sphere. The coefficients \\( A_n \\) quantify how much each Legendre polynomial contributes to the function. Graphical analysis of partial sums reveals the convergence properties of the series, including the Gibbs phenomenon, which is a hallmark of Fourier-like expansions near discontinuities. This is critical for solving boundary value problems in spherical domains, such as the potential around a non-uniformly charged sphere."
}

  "front": "Study the Gibbs phenomenon graphically for the Fourier-Legendre series expansion in Example 1 (Fig. 314). What causes the overshoot near discontinuities, and why does it persist even as more terms are added to the series?",
  "back": "<b>Solution:</b><br><br><br>1. <b>Graphical Observation:</b><br>   - The Gibbs phenomenon manifests as an overshoot (or undershoot) near discontinuities in the boundary function \\( f(x) \\).<br>   - As more terms are added to the partial sum \\( S_N(x) \\), the width of the overshoot narrows, but its amplitude remains approximately constant (about 8.9% of the jump height).<br><br>   ![gibbs_phenomenon](gibbs_phenomenon.jpeg)<br><br>   (Note: The image shows the overshoot near a discontinuity.)<br><br><br><br>2. <b>Cause of the Gibbs Phenomenon:</b><br>   - The Fourier-Legendre series (like Fourier series) represents a function as a sum of smooth, infinitely differentiable polynomials. Near a discontinuity, these smooth functions cannot perfectly approximate the jump.<br>   - The overshoot arises because the partial sums \\( S_N(x) \\) attempt to minimize the mean squared error over the entire interval. The error is concentrated near the discontinuity, leading to oscillations.<br><br><br><br>3. <b>Why the Overshoot Persists:</b><br>   - The amplitude of the overshoot does not decrease with \\( N \\) because the series prioritizes global error minimization over local accuracy. The oscillations become more localized but do not vanish.<br><br><br><br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>The Gibbs phenomenon is a fundamental limitation of Fourier-like expansions when approximating discontinuous functions. It highlights the trade-off between global accuracy and local behavior. In engineering applications, such as signal processing or solving boundary value problems, the Gibbs phenomenon can introduce artifacts (e.g., ringing in images or spurious oscillations in potentials). Understanding its cause helps in designing mitigation strategies, such as using Fejér sums or filtering techniques."
}
```

{
  "front": "Solve the Dirichlet problem for the electrostatic potential between two coaxial cylinders of radii \\( r_1 = 2 \\) cm and \\( r_2 = 4 \\) cm, kept at potentials \\( U_1 = 220 \\mathrm{V} \\) and \\( U_2 = 140 \\mathrm{V} \\), respectively. Sketch the equipotential lines and compare them to the spherical case.",
  "back": "<b>Solution:</b><br><br><br>1. <b>General Solution:</b><br>   For cylindrical symmetry, the potential depends only on \\( r \\) and satisfies:<br>   \\[ u(r) = c \\ln r + k \\]<br><br>2. <b>Apply Boundary Conditions:</b><br>   - At \\( r = r_1 = 2 \\) cm: \\( u(r_1) = 220 = c \\ln 2 + k \\).<br>   - At \\( r = r_2 = 4 \\) cm: \\( u(r_2) = 140 = c \\ln 4 + k \\).<br><br>3. <b>Solve for \\( c \\) and \\( k \\):</b><br>   - Subtract the two equations: \\( 220 - 140 = c (\\ln 2 - \\ln 4) \\).<br>   - Simplify: \\( 80 = c (\\ln 2 - 2 \\ln 2) = -c \\ln 2 \\).<br>   - Thus, \\( c = -\\frac{80}{\\ln 2} \\).<br>   - Substitute back to find \\( k = 220 - c \\ln 2 = 220 + 80 = 300 \\).<br><br>4. <b>Final Solution:</b><br>   \\[ u(r) = -\\frac{80}{\\ln 2} \\ln r + 300 \\]<br><br>5. <b>Equipotential Lines:</b><br>   - The equipotential lines are concentric cylinders (surfaces of constant \\( r \\)).<br>   - Sketch:<br><br>     ![cylindrical_equipotentials](cylindrical_equipotentials.jpeg)<br><br>   - Comparison with spherical case: In spherical symmetry, equipotential surfaces are concentric spheres, and the potential decays as \\( \\frac{1}{r} \\). In cylindrical symmetry, the potential decays logarithmically, reflecting the slower field decay in 2D.<br><br><br><br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>This problem illustrates the difference between cylindrical and spherical symmetry in electrostatics. The logarithmic potential in cylindrical coordinates arises from the infinite extent of the system in the \\( z \\)-direction, leading to a slower decay of the field compared to the \\( \\frac{1}{r} \\) potential in 3D. This is critical for designing cylindrical capacitors or understanding the behavior of long transmission lines, where edge effects are negligible."
}
```

  "back": "The general solution for a traveling wave on a string is given by:<br>\\[ w(x, t) = f(x - ct) + g(x + ct) \\]<br>where <i>c</i> is the wave speed, and <i>f</i> and <i>g</i> are determined by initial and boundary conditions.<br><br>For Example 1, assume the left end (<i>x</i> = 0) undergoes sinusoidal motion:<br>\\[ w(0, t) = \\sin(t) \\]<br>This implies <i>f(-ct) + g(ct) = \\sin(t)</i>. If the string is initially at rest and undisturbed, <i>g(x + ct) = 0</i>, so <i>f(-ct) = \\sin(t)</i>. Let <i>u = -ct</i>, then <i>f(u) = \\sin(-u/c)</i>. Thus, the solution is:<br>\\[ w(x, t) = \\sin\\left(t - \\frac{x}{c}\\right) \\]<br><br>If the sinusoidal motion starts at <i>t</i> = 2π, the boundary condition becomes:<br>\\[ w(0, t) = u(t - 2π) \\sin(t) \\]<br>where <i>u(t)</i> is the unit step function. The solution then becomes:<br>\\[ w(x, t) = u\\left(t - 2π - \\frac{x}{c}\\right) \\sin\\left(t - \\frac{x}{c}\\right) \\]<br>This represents a wave that begins propagating only after <i>t</i> = 2π + <i>x/c</i>.<hr><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br>This problem illustrates how boundary conditions shape the form of traveling waves. The use of the unit step function demonstrates how delayed inputs affect wave propagation, a concept critical in signal processing and control systems. The solution also highlights the role of characteristic lines (<i>x ± ct</i>) in determining how information travels through the medium."
}

  "back": "The general solution for a traveling wave on a string is given by:<br>\\[ w(x, t) = f(x - ct) + g(x + ct) \\]<br>where <i>c</i> is the wave speed, and <i>f</i> and <i>g</i> are determined by initial and boundary conditions.<br><br>For Example 1, assume the left end (<i>x</i> = 0) undergoes sinusoidal motion:<br>\\[ w(0, t) = \\sin(t) \\]<br>This implies <i>f(-ct) + g(ct) = \\sin(t)</i>. If the string is initially at rest and undisturbed, <i>g(x + ct) = 0</i>, so <i>f(-ct) = \\sin(t)</i>. Let <i>u = -ct</i>, then <i>f(u) = \\sin(-u/c)</i>. Thus, the solution is:<br>\\[ w(x, t) = \\sin\\left(t - \\frac{x}{c}\\right) \\]<br><br>If the sinusoidal motion starts at <i>t</i> = 2π, the boundary condition becomes:<br>\\[ w(0, t) = u(t - 2π) \\sin(t) \\]<br>where <i>u(t)</i> is the unit step function. The solution then becomes:<br>\\[ w(x, t) = u\\left(t - 2π - \\frac{x}{c}\\right) \\sin\\left(t - \\frac{x}{c}\\right) \\]<br>This represents a wave that begins propagating only after <i>t</i> = 2π + <i>x/c</i>.<br><br>![img-48.jpeg](img-48.jpeg)<hr><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br>This problem illustrates how boundary conditions shape the form of traveling waves. The use of the unit step function demonstrates how delayed inputs affect wave propagation, a concept critical in signal processing and control systems. The solution also highlights the role of characteristic lines (<i>x ± ct</i>) in determining how information travels through the medium."
}

{
  "front": "What are the three main steps to solve a partial differential equation (PDE) using Laplace transforms when one of the independent variables ranges over the positive axis?",
  "back": "<b>Steps to solve a PDE using Laplace transforms:</b><br><br><br>1. Take the Laplace transform with respect to one of the two variables (usually <i>t</i>). This converts the PDE into an ordinary differential equation (ODE) for the transform of the unknown function, incorporating derivatives with respect to the other variable and the given boundary/initial conditions.<br><br>2. Solve the resulting ODE to obtain the transform of the unknown function.<br><br>3. Take the inverse Laplace transform to recover the solution of the original PDE.<br><br><br><b>Note:</b> This method simplifies the problem if the coefficients of the PDE do not depend on the transformed variable (e.g., <i>t</i>).<br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>This method leverages the Laplace transform’s ability to convert differential equations into algebraic ones, simplifying the solution process. It is particularly useful for PDEs with one semi-infinite domain (e.g., <i>t ≥ 0</i>), as it reduces the problem to an ODE, which is easier to solve. The approach is analogous to solving ODEs with Laplace transforms, as seen in earlier chapters, but extended to handle partial derivatives in one variable."
}

  "front": "Consider a semi-infinite elastic string initially at rest along the <i>x</i>-axis from <i>x = 0</i> to <i>∞</i>. For <i>t > 0</i>, the left end of the string (<i>x = 0</i>) is moved according to the function:<br><br>\\[ w(0, t) = f(t) = \\left\\{\\begin{array}{c l}\n\\sin t & \\text{if } 0 \\leq t \\leq 2\\pi \\\\\n0 & \\text{otherwise}\n\\end{array}\\right. \\]<br><br>Additionally, <i>w(x, t) → 0</i> as <i>x → ∞</i> for <i>t ≥ 0</i>. <br><br>Using Laplace transforms, derive the displacement <i>w(x, t)</i> of the string.<br><br><br><br><img src='img-47.jpg'>",
  "back": "<b>Solution:</b><br><br><br>1. <b>Formulate the PDE and conditions:</b><br><br>   The wave equation for the string is:<br><br>   \\[ \\frac{\\partial^2 w}{\\partial t^2} = c^2 \\frac{\\partial^2 w}{\\partial x^2}, \\quad x > 0, \\, t > 0 \\]<br><br>   with initial conditions:<br><br>   \\[ w(x, 0) = 0, \\quad \\frac{\\partial w}{\\partial t}(x, 0) = 0 \\]<br><br>   and boundary conditions:<br><br>   \\[ w(0, t) = f(t), \\quad \\lim_{x \\to \\infty} w(x, t) = 0. \\]<br><br><br>2. <b>Take the Laplace transform with respect to <i>t</i>:</b><br><br>   Let <i>W(x, s)</i> be the Laplace transform of <i>w(x, t)</i>. The wave equation transforms to:<br><br>   \\[ s^2 W(x, s) - s w(x, 0) - \\frac{\\partial w}{\\partial t}(x, 0) = c^2 \\frac{d^2 W}{dx^2}. \\]<br><br>   Using the initial conditions, this simplifies to:<br><br>   \\[ s^2 W(x, s) = c^2 \\frac{d^2 W}{dx^2}. \\]<br><br>   The boundary condition at <i>x = 0</i> becomes:<br><br>   \\[ W(0, s) = F(s), \\]<br><br>   where <i>F(s)</i> is the Laplace transform of <i>f(t)</i>.<br><br><br>3. <b>Solve the ODE for <i>W(x, s)</i>:</b><br><br>   The ODE is:<br><br>   \\[ \\frac{d^2 W}{dx^2} - \\frac{s^2}{c^2} W = 0. \\]<br><br>   The general solution is:<br><br>   \\[ W(x, s) = A e^{\\frac{s}{c} x} + B e^{-\\frac{s}{c} x}. \\]<br><br>   To satisfy <i>W(x, s) → 0</i> as <i>x → ∞</i>, we must have <i>A = 0</i>. Thus:<br><br>   \\[ W(x, s) = B e^{-\\frac{s}{c} x}. \\]<br><br>   Using the boundary condition at <i>x = 0</i>:<br><br>   \\[ W(0, s) = B = F(s). \\]<br><br>   Therefore:<br><br>   \\[ W(x, s) = F(s) e^{-\\frac{s}{c} x}. \\]<br><br><br>4. <b>Compute <i>F(s)</i>:</b><br><br>   The Laplace transform of <i>f(t)</i> is:<br><br>   \\[ F(s) = \\mathcal{L}\\{f(t)\\} = \\int_0^{2\\pi} e^{-st} \\sin t \\, dt. \\]<br><br>   Using integration by parts or tables, this evaluates to:<br><br>   \\[ F(s) = \\frac{1 - e^{-2\\pi s}}{s^2 + 1}. \\]<br><br><br>5. <b>Take the inverse Laplace transform:</b><br><br>   We have:<br><br>   \\[ W(x, s) = \\frac{1 - e^{-2\\pi s}}{s^2 + 1} e^{-\\frac{s}{c} x}. \\]<br><br>   The inverse Laplace transform of <i>e^{-\\frac{s}{c} x} / (s^2 + 1)</i> is the delayed sine function:<br><br>   \\[ \\mathcal{L}^{-1}\\left\\{ \\frac{e^{-\\frac{s}{c} x}}{s^2 + 1} \\right\\} = u\\left(t - \\frac{x}{c}\\right) \\sin\\left(t - \\frac{x}{c}\\right), \\]<br><br>   where <i>u(t)</i> is the unit step function. Similarly, the inverse of <i>e^{-2\\pi s} e^{-\\frac{s}{c} x} / (s^2 + 1)</i> is:<br><br>   \\[ u\\left(t - 2\\pi - \\frac{x}{c}\\right) \\sin\\left(t - 2\\pi - \\frac{x}{c}\\right). \\]<br><br>   Combining these, the solution is:<br><br>   \\[ w(x, t) = u\\left(t - \\frac{x}{c}\\right) \\sin\\left(t - \\frac{x}{c}\\right) - u\\left(t - 2\\pi - \\frac{x}{c}\\right) \\sin\\left(t - 2\\pi - \\frac{x}{c}\\right). \\]<br><br><br><b>Interpretation:</b><br><br>The solution represents a wave traveling along the string with speed <i>c</i>. The first term corresponds to the initial sine wave propagating to the right, while the second term cancels it out after <i>t = 2π</i>, reflecting the boundary condition at <i>x = 0</i>.<br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>This example illustrates how Laplace transforms can simplify the solution of PDEs by reducing them to ODEs. The key insight is that the transform converts time derivatives into algebraic terms, making the problem more tractable. The semi-infinite domain ensures that only one boundary condition (at <i>x = 0</i>) is needed, and the solution propagates as a wave without reflections from the right. This method is widely used in physics and engineering for problems involving wave propagation or heat conduction in semi-infinite media."
}
```

```json
{
  "front": "Why does using Laplace transforms simplify the solution of a PDE when the coefficients of the equation do not depend on the transformed variable (e.g., <i>t</i>)?",
  "back": "<b>Explanation:</b><br><br>When the coefficients of the PDE do not depend on the transformed variable (e.g., <i>t</i>), taking the Laplace transform with respect to <i>t</i> eliminates all derivatives with respect to <i>t</i>, converting them into algebraic terms involving the Laplace variable <i>s</i>. This reduces the PDE to an ODE in the remaining variable (e.g., <i>x</i>), which is significantly easier to solve. The transformed equation incorporates the initial conditions directly, further simplifying the problem.<br><br><br>For example, consider a PDE of the form:<br><br>\\[ \\frac{\\partial^2 w}{\\partial t^2} + a(x) \\frac{\\partial w}{\\partial t} + b(x) w = c^2 \\frac{\\partial^2 w}{\\partial x^2}. \\]<br><br>Taking the Laplace transform with respect to <i>t</i> yields:<br><br>\\[ s^2 W(x, s) - s w(x, 0) - \\frac{\\partial w}{\\partial t}(x, 0) + a(x) \\left[ s W(x, s) - w(x, 0) \\right] + b(x) W(x, s) = c^2 \\frac{d^2 W}{dx^2}. \\]<br><br>This is now an ODE in <i>x</i>, with <i>s</i> acting as a parameter. The absence of <i>t</i>-dependence in the coefficients ensures that the ODE remains tractable.<br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>The simplification arises because the Laplace transform is a linear operator that converts differentiation into multiplication by <i>s</i>, effectively turning differential equations into algebraic ones. This is particularly powerful for PDEs with time as an independent variable, as it reduces the problem to an ODE in space, which can often be solved using standard techniques. The method is analogous to solving ODEs with Laplace transforms but extends the idea to handle partial derivatives in one variable."
}
```

The boundary condition acts as the <i>source</i> of the wave propagating along the string. The displacement <i>w(x, t)</i> at any point <i>x > 0</i> and time <i>t</i> is determined by the history of the boundary motion at <i>x = 0</i>.<br><br>2. The solution <i>w(x, t)</i> represents a wave traveling to the right with speed <i>c</i>. The term <i>u(t - x/c) sin(t - x/c)</i> shows that the wave is delayed by <i>x/c</i>, the time it takes for the disturbance to reach position <i>x</i>.<br><br>3. The second term in the solution, <i>-u(t - 2π - x/c) sin(t - 2π - x/c)</i>, cancels the wave after <i>t = 2π</i>, ensuring the string returns to rest once the boundary motion ceases. This reflects the finite duration of the input signal <i>f(t)</i>.<br><br><br><b>Key Insight:</b><br><br>The boundary condition <i>w(0, t)</i> is the driving force for the wave equation. Its form (e.g., sinusoidal, step function) directly shapes the resulting wave propagating through the medium. In this case, the finite-duration sine wave generates a pulse-like disturbance that travels along the string.<br><hr><b>Contexte Explicatif:</b><br><br>Boundary conditions are critical in PDEs because they define how the system interacts with its environment. For the wave equation, the boundary condition at <i>x = 0</i> determines the input signal that excites the system. The semi-infinite domain ensures that the wave propagates without reflections, making the solution easier to interpret. This setup is common in problems involving signal transmission or wave propagation in unbounded media."

  "front": "Compare the use of Laplace transforms for solving PDEs with their use for solving ODEs. What are the key similarities and differences?",
  "back": "<b>Similarities:</b><br><br>1. <b>Transform Mechanism:</b> In both cases, the Laplace transform converts differential equations into algebraic equations, simplifying the solution process.<br><br>2. <b>Initial Conditions:</b> The Laplace transform automatically incorporates initial conditions (e.g., <i>w(x, 0)</i> or <i>y(0)</i>) into the transformed equation, eliminating the need for separate handling.<br><br>3. <b>Inverse Transform:</b> The final step in both cases is taking the inverse Laplace transform to recover the solution in the original domain.<br><br>4. <b>Linearity:</b> The Laplace transform is a linear operator, so it preserves the linearity of the original differential equation.<br><br><br><b>Differences:</b><br><br><table><br><tr><th>Aspect</th><th>ODEs</th><th>PDEs</th></tr><br><tr><td><b>Equation Type</b></td><td>The original equation is an ODE (single independent variable).</td><td>The original equation is a PDE (multiple independent variables).</td></tr><br><tr><td><b>Transformed Equation</b></td><td>The Laplace transform yields an algebraic equation in <i>s</i>.</td><td>The Laplace transform (with respect to one variable, e.g., <i>t</i>) yields an ODE in the remaining variable(s) (e.g., <i>x</i>).</td></tr><br><tr><td><b>Dependence on Coefficients</b></td><td>The method works regardless of whether the coefficients depend on the independent variable.</td><td>The method simplifies the problem only if the coefficients do <i>not</i> depend on the transformed variable (e.g., <i>t</i>).</td></tr><br><tr><td><b>Boundary Conditions</b></td><td>Only initial conditions are relevant.</td><td>Both initial and boundary conditions must be incorporated into the transformed equation.</td></tr><br><tr><td><b>Complexity</b></td><td>Generally simpler, as the transformed equation is algebraic.</td><td>More complex, as the transformed equation is still a differential equation (ODE) in the remaining variable(s).</td></tr><br></table><br><br><b>Key Insight:</b><br><br>For PDEs, the Laplace transform reduces the problem to an ODE, which is still a differential equation but simpler than the original PDE. This is analogous to how the Laplace transform reduces an ODE to an algebraic equation. The choice of which variable to transform is critical in PDEs, as it determines the form of the resulting ODE.<br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>The Laplace transform is a versatile tool for solving both ODEs and PDEs, but its application to PDEs requires additional care. The method is most effective when the PDE has a semi-infinite domain in one variable (e.g., <i>t ≥ 0</i>), as this avoids complications from boundary conditions at infinity. The comparison highlights how the Laplace transform adapts to different types of differential equations while maintaining its core advantage: converting differentiation into algebraic operations."
}
```

### Avant:
```json
{
  "front": "What is the role of the unit step function <i>u(t)</i> in the solution of the semi-infinite string problem, and why is it necessary?",
  "back": "<b>Role of the Unit Step Function:</b><br><br>The unit step function <i>u(t)</i> (also called the Heaviside function) is defined as:<br><br>\\[ u(t) = \\left\\{\\begin{array}{c l}\n0 & \\text{if } t < 0 \\\\\n1 & \\text{if } t \\geq 0\n\\end{array}\\right. \\]<br><br>In the solution of the semi-infinite string problem, the unit step function serves two critical purposes:<br><br><br>1. <b>Time Delay:</b> The term <i>u(t - x/c)</i> ensures that the wave disturbance does not appear at position <i>x</i> until time <i>t = x/c</i>. This reflects the physical reality that a wave traveling at speed <i>c</i> takes time <i>x/c</i> to reach position <i>x</i> from the boundary at <i>x = 0</i>.<br><br>2. <b>Finite Duration:</b> The term <i>u(t - 2π - x/c)</i> ensures that the wave is canceled out after <i>t = 2π + x/c</i>, corresponding to the finite duration of the boundary condition <i>f(t)</i>. This prevents the wave from persisting indefinitely.<br><br><br><b>Mathematical Form of the Solution:</b><br><br>The solution is:<br><br>\\[ w(x, t) = u\\left(t - \\frac{x}{c}\\right) \\sin\\left(t - \\frac{x}{c}\\right) - u\\left(t - 2\\pi - \\frac{x}{c}\\right) \\sin\\left(t - 2\\pi - \\frac{x}{c}\\right). \\]<br><br>Without the unit step functions, the solution would imply that the wave exists for all <i>t</i>, which contradicts the boundary condition <i>f(t)</i> (which is zero for <i>t > 2π</i>).<br><br><br><b>Why It Is Necessary:</b><br><br>1. <b>Causality:</b> The unit step function enforces causality, ensuring that the wave at position <i>x</i> is only influenced by the boundary motion at <i>x = 0</i> after the wave has had time to propagate to <i>x</i>.<br><br>2. <b>Boundary Condition Matching:</b> The boundary condition <i>f(t)</i> is zero for <i>t > 2π</i>. The unit step function ensures that the solution respects this by canceling the wave after <i>t = 2π</i>.<br><br>3. <b>Physical Realism:</b> Without the unit step function, the solution would predict non-zero displacement for all <i>t</i>, even when the boundary is at rest. This would violate energy conservation and the principle of superposition.<br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>The unit step function is a mathematical tool that models the sudden onset or cessation of a signal. In wave propagation problems, it ensures that the solution adheres to physical laws, such as causality and finite signal duration. Its use in the semi-infinite string problem highlights how mathematical abstractions (like the unit step function) can capture real-world phenomena, such as the finite propagation speed of waves."
}
```

{
  "front": "Consider a semi-infinite string initially at rest. The left end of the string (<i>x = 0</i>) is moved according to the function:<br><br>\\[ w(0, t) = f(t) = \\left\\{\\begin{array}{c l}\n\\sin(\\pi t) & \\text{if } 0 \\leq t \\leq 1 \\\\\n0 & \\text{otherwise}\n\\end{array}\\right. \\]<br><br>Using Laplace transforms, derive the displacement <i>w(x, t)</i> of the string. Assume the wave speed is <i>c</i> and <i>w(x, t) → 0</i> as <i>x → ∞</i>.",
  "back": "<b>Solution:</b><br><br><br>1. <b>Formulate the PDE and conditions:</b><br><br>   The wave equation is:<br><br>   \\[ \\frac{\\partial^2 w}{\\partial t^2} = c^2 \\frac{\\partial^2 w}{\\partial x^2}, \\quad x > 0, \\, t > 0 \\]<br><br>   with initial conditions:<br><br>   \\[ w(x, 0) = 0, \\quad \\frac{\\partial w}{\\partial t}(x, 0) = 0 \\]<br><br>   and boundary conditions:<br><br>   \\[ w(0, t) = f(t), \\quad \\lim_{x \\to \\infty} w(x, t) = 0. \\]<br><br><br>2. <b>Take the Laplace transform with respect to <i>t</i>:</b><br><br>   Let <i>W(x, s)</i> be the Laplace transform of <i>w(x, t)</i>. The wave equation transforms to:<br><br>   \\[ s^2 W(x, s) = c^2 \\frac{d^2 W}{dx^2}. \\]<br><br>   The boundary condition at <i>x = 0</i> becomes:<br><br>   \\[ W(0, s) = F(s), \\]<br><br>   where <i>F(s)</i> is the Laplace transform of <i>f(t)</i>.<br><br><br>3. <b>Solve the ODE for <i>W(x, s)</i>:</b><br><br>   The ODE is:<br><br>   \\[ \\frac{d^2 W}{dx^2} - \\frac{s^2}{c^2} W = 0. \\]<br><br>   The general solution is:<br><br>   \\[ W(x, s) = A e^{\\frac{s}{c} x} + B e^{-\\frac{s}{c} x}. \\]<br><br>   To satisfy <i>W(x, s) → 0</i> as <i>x → ∞</i>, we set <i>A = 0</i>. Thus:<br><br>   \\[ W(x, s) = B e^{-\\frac{s}{c} x}. \\]<br><br>   Using the boundary condition at <i>x = 0</i>:<br><br>   \\[ W(0, s) = B = F(s). \\]<br><br>   Therefore:<br><br>   \\[ W(x, s) = F(s) e^{-\\frac{s}{c} x}. \\]<br><br><br>4. <b>Compute <i>F(s)</i>:</b><br><br>   The Laplace transform of <i>f(t)</i> is:<br><br>   \\[ F(s) = \\mathcal{L}\\{f(t)\\} = \\int_0^1 e^{-st} \\sin(\\pi t) \\, dt. \\]<br><br>   Using integration by parts or tables, this evaluates to:<br><br>   \\[ F(s) = \\frac{\\pi (1 - e^{-s})}{s^2 + \\pi^2}. \\]<br><br><br>5. <b>Take the inverse Laplace transform:</b><br><br>   We have:<br><br>   \\[ W(x, s) = \\frac{\\pi (1 - e^{-s})}{s^2 + \\pi^2} e^{-\\frac{s}{c} x}. \\]<br><br>   The inverse Laplace transform of <i>e^{-\\frac{s}{c} x} / (s^2 + π^2)</i> is the delayed sine function:<br><br>   \\[ \\mathcal{L}^{-1}\\left\\{ \\frac{e^{-\\frac{s}{c} x}}{s^2 + \\pi^2} \\right\\} = u\\left(t - \\frac{x}{c}\\right) \\sin\\left(\\pi \\left(t - \\frac{x}{c}\\right)\\right). \\]<br><br>   Similarly, the inverse of <i>e^{-s} e^{-\\frac{s}{c} x} / (s^2 + π^2)</i> is:<br><br>   \\[ u\\left(t - 1 - \\frac{x}{c}\\right) \\sin\\left(\\pi \\left(t - 1 - \\frac{x}{c}\\right)\\right). \\]<br><br>   Combining these, the solution is:<br><br>   \\[ w(x, t) = \\pi \\left[ u\\left(t - \\frac{x}{c}\\right) \\sin\\left(\\pi \\left(t - \\frac{x}{c}\\right)\\right) - u\\left(t - 1 - \\frac{x}{c}\\right) \\sin\\left(\\pi \\left(t - 1 - \\frac{x}{c}\\right)\\right) \\right]. \\]<br><br><br><b>Interpretation:</b><br><br>The solution represents a half-sine wave pulse traveling along the string with speed <i>c</i>. The first term corresponds to the initial pulse propagating to the right, while the second term cancels it out after <i>t = 1</i>, reflecting the boundary condition at <i>x = 0</i>.<br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>This problem demonstrates how the Laplace transform method can be applied to a modified boundary condition. The key steps remain the same: transform the PDE, solve the resulting ODE, and invert the transform. The unit step function ensures that the solution respects the finite duration of the input signal, while the sine function reflects the shape of the boundary motion. This approach is widely applicable to problems involving wave propagation with time-dependent boundary conditions."
}
```

Specifically:<br><br>1. The wave would persist indefinitely, as there is no finite duration for the boundary motion.<br><br>2. The solution would no longer include a cancellation term (e.g., the second unit step function in the original problem), as the boundary condition does not return to zero.<br><br>3. The amplitude of the wave at any position <i>x</i> would oscillate sinusoidally with the same frequency as <i>f(t)</i>, but with a phase delay of <i>x/c</i>.<br><br><br><b>Adaptation of the Laplace Transform Method:</b><br><br>1. <b>Laplace Transform of <i>f(t)</i>:</b><br><br>   For <i>f(t) = sin(t)</i>, the Laplace transform is:<br><br>   \\[ F(s) = \\mathcal{L}\\{sin(t)\\} = \\frac{1}{s^2 + 1}. \\]<br><br>   This is simpler than the finite-duration case, as there is no exponential term (e.g., <i>e^{-2πs}</i>).<br><br><br>2. <b>Transformed Solution:</b><br><br>   The transformed solution would be:<br><br>   \\[ W(x, s) = F(s) e^{-\\frac{s}{c} x} = \\frac{e^{-\\frac{s}{c} x}}{s^2 + 1}. \\]<br><br><br>3. <b>Inverse Laplace Transform:</b><br><br>   The inverse transform of <i>e^{-\\frac{s}{c} x} / (s^2 + 1)</i> is:<br><br>   \\[ w(x, t) = u\\left(t - \\frac{x}{c}\\right) \\sin\\left(t - \\frac{x}{c}\\right). \\]<br><br>   This represents a continuous sine wave propagating to the right with speed <i>c</i>, delayed by <i>x/c</i>.<br><br><br><b>Key Differences from the Finite-Duration Case:</b><br><br>- The solution is simpler, as there is no need to account for the cancellation of the wave after a finite time.<br><br>- The unit step function <i>u(t - x/c)</i> still appears to enforce causality, but there is no second step function to cancel the wave.<br><br>- The solution is valid for all <i>t ≥ x/c</i>, reflecting the periodic nature of the boundary condition.<br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>Periodic boundary conditions are common in problems involving steady-state oscillations, such as AC circuits or continuous wave propagation. The Laplace transform method adapts seamlessly to such cases, though the inverse transform may simplify significantly. The absence of a finite duration in the boundary condition eliminates the need for cancellation terms, resulting in a cleaner solution. This highlights the flexibility of the Laplace transform for handling both transient and steady-state problems."
}

Apply the Laplace transform to the wave equation:<br><br>   \\( \\mathcal{L}\\left\\{\\frac{\\partial^{2} w}{\\partial t^{2}} \\right\\} = s^{2} W - s w(x,0) - \\frac{\\partial w}{\\partial t}(x,0) \\).<br><br>2. Assuming initial conditions \\( w(x,0) = 0 \\) and \\( \\frac{\\partial w}{\\partial t}(x,0) = 0 \\), this reduces to \\( s^{2} W \\).<br><br>3. For example:<br>  - In a vibrating string, <i>c</i> is given by \\( c = \\sqrt{\\frac{T}{\\rho}} \\), where <i>T</i> is the tension in the string and <i>\\rho</i> is the linear mass density.<br>  - In acoustics, <i>c</i> is the speed of sound in the medium.<br>  - In electromagnetic waves, <i>c</i> is the speed of light in a vacuum or dielectric medium.<br><br>- <b>Influence on Solutions</b>: The value of <i>c</i> determines how quickly waves travel through the medium. Solutions can exhibit reflection, refraction, and interference, depending on boundary conditions.<br><br><br><br><h3>Heat Equation (\\( \\frac{\\partial u}{\\partial t} = c^2 \\frac{\\partial^2 u}{\\partial x^2} \\)):</h3><br><br>- <b>Physical Significance</b>: In the heat equation, <i>c²</i> (often denoted as <i>\\alpha</i>) represents the <b>thermal diffusivity</b> of the material. A larger <i>c²</i> means faster heat diffusion, leading to more rapid temperature equalization. A smaller <i>c²</i> means slower diffusion, resulting in more gradual temperature changes. The heat equation smooths out initial conditions over time, acting as a low-pass filter that removes high-frequency components (sharp gradients) more rapidly than low-frequency components (smooth variations).<br><br><br><br><h3>Traveling Wave Solutions:</h3><br><br>The term \\( f\\left(t - \\frac{x}{c}\\right) \\) in solutions to the wave equation represents a wave traveling in the positive \\( x \\)-direction with speed \\( c \\).
