## [MISTRAL QA] Carte Corrigée

### Avant:
```json
{
  "front": "What is the key advantage of using a graphical model to represent a joint probability distribution compared to explicitly modeling all possible dependencies between variables?",
  "back": "The key advantage of using a graphical model to represent a joint probability distribution is that it leverages conditional independence assumptions to reduce the complexity of the model. Instead of explicitly modeling all possible dependencies (which would require a fully connected graph and a computationally intractable number of parameters), a graphical model:<br><br><br>1. Uses the graph structure to encode which variables are conditionally independent given their parents. This sparsity in the graph translates to a factorized form of the joint distribution, where each node's distribution depends only on its parents.<br><br>2. Reduces the number of parameters needed to describe the joint distribution. For example, in the graph shown in Figure 8.2, the joint distribution is factorized as:<br><br>\\[ p(x_1, x_2, \\ldots, x_7) = p(x_1) p(x_2) p(x_3) p(x_4 \\mid x_1, x_2, x_3) p(x_5 \\mid x_1, x_3) p(x_6 \\mid x_4) p(x_7 \\mid x_4, x_5). \\]<br><br>This factorization avoids terms like <i>p(x<sub>7</sub> | x<sub>3</sub>)</i>, which would be required in a fully connected model.<br><br>3. Enables efficient inference and learning algorithms by exploiting the graph structure to perform computations locally (e.g., message-passing algorithms).<br><br><img src='img-2.jpg'><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>Graphical models provide a visual and mathematical framework for handling high-dimensional data. By focusing only on the most relevant dependencies, they make it feasible to model complex systems that would otherwise be intractable. This is particularly important in fields like machine learning, where datasets often involve thousands or millions of variables. The graph structure also makes it easier to interpret the relationships between variables, which is valuable for tasks like feature selection and causal inference."
}
```

## [MISTRAL QA] Carte Corrigée

### Avant:
```json
{
  "front": "Derive the decomposition of the joint probability distribution <i>p(a, b, c)</i> using the product rule of probability, and explain how this decomposition is represented graphically.",
  "back": "Using the product rule of probability, the joint distribution <i>p(a, b, c)</i> can be decomposed as follows:<br><br><br><br>1. First application of the product rule:<br><br>\\[ p(a, b, c) = p(c \\mid a, b) p(a, b) \\]<br><br><br>2. Second application of the product rule to the term <i>p(a, b)</i>:<br><br>\\[ p(a, b) = p(b \\mid a) p(a) \\]<br><br><br>3. Substituting back, we obtain the full decomposition:<br><br>\\[ p(a, b, c) = p(c \\mid a, b) p(b \\mid a) p(a) \\]<br><br><br>Graphically, this decomposition is represented by a directed graph where:<br><br>- Each variable (<i>a</i>, <i>b</i>, <i>c</i>) is a node.<br><br>- For each conditional distribution, directed links (arrows) are drawn from the parent nodes (variables on which the distribution is conditioned) to the child node.<br><br>- For <i>p(c | a, b)</i>, arrows point from <i>a</i> and <i>b</i> to <i>c</i>.<br><br>- For <i>p(b | a)</i>, an arrow points from <i>a</i> to <i>b</i>.<br><br>- For <i>p(a)</i>, there are no incoming arrows since it is unconditional.<br><br><br><img src='img-1.jpg'><br><br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>This decomposition is not just a mathematical trick; it reflects how dependencies propagate in real-world systems. For example, in medical diagnosis, a symptom (<i>c</i>) might depend on two underlying conditions (<i>a</i> and <i>b</i>), while one condition (<i>b</i>) might itself depend on another (<i>a</i>). The graphical representation makes these relationships explicit, allowing us to visualize and reason about the flow of influence between variables. This is the essence of Bayesian networks: encoding probabilistic dependencies in a way that is both mathematically rigorous and intuitively accessible."
}
```

## [MISTRAL QA] Carte Corrigée

### Avant:
```json
{
  "front": "Generalize the decomposition of the joint probability distribution <i>p(x₁, ..., xₖ)</i> for <i>K</i> variables using the product rule, and describe the corresponding graphical representation.",
  "back": "For a joint probability distribution over <i>K</i> variables, <i>p(x₁, ..., xₖ)</i>, repeated application of the product rule yields the following decomposition:<br><br><br>\\[ p(x₁, \\dots, xₖ) = p(xₖ \\mid x₁, \\dots, x_{K-1}) \\dots p(x₂ \\mid x₁) p(x₁) \\]<br><br><br>This decomposition expresses the joint distribution as a product of conditional distributions, where each variable <i>xᵢ</i> (for <i>i > 1</i>) is conditioned on all preceding variables <i>x₁, ..., x_{i-1}</i>.<br><br><br>Graphical Representation:<br><br>- The graph consists of <i>K</i> nodes, one for each variable.<br><br>- For each conditional distribution <i>p(xᵢ | x₁, ..., x_{i-1})</i>, directed links are drawn from all nodes <i>x₁, ..., x_{i-1}</i> (parents) to the node <i>xᵢ</i> (child).<br><br>- The resulting graph is <b>fully connected</b>, meaning there is a directed link between every pair of nodes, with arrows pointing from lower-numbered nodes to higher-numbered nodes.<br><br><br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>This generalization highlights the flexibility of Bayesian networks in representing complex dependencies. However, a fully connected graph is often impractical for real-world problems because it implies that every variable depends on all preceding variables, leading to an explosion of parameters. In practice, Bayesian networks are used to encode <i>sparse</i> dependencies, where many conditional independencies are assumed (e.g., <i>xₖ</i> might depend only on <i>xₖ₋₁</i> and <i>xₖ₋₂</i>, not all preceding variables). This sparsity makes the models computationally tractable and easier to interpret."
}
```

{
  "front": "Consider a joint probability distribution <i>p(w, x, y, z)</i> over four variables. Using the product rule, decompose this distribution into a product of conditional distributions assuming the ordering <i>w, x, y, z</i>. Then, draw the corresponding directed graphical model and label all parent-child relationships.",
  "back": "Using the product rule, the joint distribution <i>p(w, x, y, z)</i> can be decomposed as follows:<br><br><br>1. First, apply the product rule to separate <i>z</i>:<br><br>\\[ p(w, x, y, z) = p(z \\mid w, x, y) p(w, x, y) \\]<br><br><br>2. Next, decompose <i>p(w, x, y)</i>:<br><br>\\[ p(w, x, y) = p(y \\mid w, x) p(w, x) \\]<br><br><br>3. Finally, decompose <i>p(w, x)</i>:<br><br>\\[ p(w, x) = p(x \\mid w) p(w) \\]<br><br><br>4. Combining these, the full decomposition is:<br><br>\\[ p(w, x, y, z) = p(z \\mid w, x, y) p(y \\mid w, x) p(x \\mid w) p(w) \\]<br><br><br>Graphical Representation:<br><br>- Nodes: <i>w</i>, <i>x</i>, <i>y</i>, <i>z</i>.<br><br>- Directed links:<br><br>  - From <i>w</i> to <i>x</i> (parent of <i>x</i>).<br><br>  - From <i>w</i> and <i>x</i> to <i>y</i> (parents of <i>y</i>).<br><br>  - From <i>w</i>, <i>x</i>, and <i>y</i> to <i>z</i> (parents of <i>z</i>).<br><br>- No incoming links to <i>w</i> (unconditional).<br><br><br>The graph would look like this:<br><br><pre><br>w → x → y → z<br>↗     ↗     ↗<br></pre><br>(Note: All arrows point toward <i>z</i> from <i>w</i>, <i>x</i>, and <i>y</i>.)<br><br><br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>This exercise illustrates how the product rule and variable ordering translate into a graphical model. The decomposition reveals the conditional dependencies explicitly, while the graph provides a visual summary of these relationships. In practice, such models are used to answer questions like 'What is the probability of <i>z</i> given evidence about <i>w</i> and <i>x</i>?' by leveraging the structure to perform efficient inference. This is particularly useful in scenarios where computing the full joint distribution is infeasible."
}

  "front": "How can the joint distribution <b>p(x<sub>1</sub>, x<sub>2</sub>)</b> for two discrete variables be factorized using the product rule, and how does this relate to the graphical model representation?",
  "back": "The joint distribution <b>p(x<sub>1</sub>, x<sub>2</sub>)</b> can be factorized using the product rule as:<br><br>\\[ p(\\mathbf{x}_{1}, \\mathbf{x}_{2}) = p(\\mathbf{x}_{2} | \\mathbf{x}_{1}) p(\\mathbf{x}_{1}) \\]<br><br>This factorization corresponds to a graphical model with two nodes:<br><ul><li>The node for <b>x<sub>1</sub></b> represents the marginal distribution <b>p(x<sub>1</sub>)</b>, requiring <b>K - 1</b> parameters.</li><li>The node for <b>x<sub>2</sub></b> represents the conditional distribution <b>p(x<sub>2</sub> | x<sub>1</sub>)</b>, requiring <b>K(K - 1)</b> parameters (since there are <b>K - 1</b> parameters for each of the <b>K</b> possible values of <b>x<sub>1</sub></b>).</li></ul><br>The total number of parameters is <b>(K - 1) + K(K - 1) = K<sup>2</sup> - 1</b>, matching the fully connected case.<br><br><hr><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br>This factorization is a cornerstone of graphical models, as it allows complex distributions to be broken down into simpler, conditional components. This approach is particularly powerful for extending models to larger networks of variables."
}

{
  "front": "For a chain of <b>M</b> discrete nodes (Figure 8.10), each with <b>K</b> states, how many parameters are required to define the joint distribution, and how does this scale with <b>M</b> and <b>K</b>?",
  "back": "For a chain of <b>M</b> discrete nodes (as shown in Figure 8.10), the joint distribution requires:<br><br>\\[ K - 1 + (M - 1)K(K - 1) \\]<br><br>parameters, where:<br><ul><li><b>K - 1</b> parameters define the marginal distribution of the first node <b>x<sub>1</sub></b>.</li><li><b>(M - 1)K(K - 1)</b> parameters define the conditional distributions <b>p(x<sub>i</sub> | x<sub>i-1</sub>)</b> for <b>i = 2, ..., M</b>.</li></ul><br>This scales <b>linearly</b> with the number of nodes <b>M</b> and <b>quadratically</b> with the number of states <b>K</b>.<br><br><hr><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br>The linear scaling with <b>M</b> is a major advantage of chain-structured graphical models, as it avoids the exponential growth seen in fully connected models. This makes chains practical for modeling sequences (e.g., time series or text), where <b>M</b> can be very large. The quadratic dependence on <b>K</b> is a trade-off for capturing dependencies between adjacent nodes."
}

## [MISTRAL QA] Carte Corrigée

### Avant:
```json
{
  "front": "What is parameter sharing (or tying) in the context of graphical models, and how does it reduce the number of parameters in a chain of <b>M</b> discrete nodes?",
  "back": "Parameter sharing (or tying) in graphical models refers to the practice of using the <b>same set of parameters</b> to govern multiple conditional distributions in the model.<br><br>In the context of a chain of <b>M</b> discrete nodes:<br><ul><li>Without parameter sharing, each conditional distribution <b>p(x<sub>i</sub> | x<sub>i-1</sub>)</b> for <b>i = 2, ..., M</b> requires <b>K(K - 1)</b> unique parameters, leading to a total of <b>K - 1 + (M - 1)K(K - 1)</b> parameters.</li><li>With parameter sharing, all conditional distributions <b>p(x<sub>i</sub> | x<sub>i-1</sub>)</b> are governed by the <b>same set of K(K - 1)</b> parameters.</li></ul><br>The total number of parameters is then reduced to <b>K<sup>2</sup> - 1</b>, regardless of the chain length <b>M</b>.<br><br><hr><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br>Parameter sharing is a key technique for reducing model complexity while preserving the ability to capture dependencies. It is particularly useful in structured models like chains, where the same type of relationship (e.g., transition probabilities) repeats across the graph. This approach is widely used in models like Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs)."
}
```

{
  "front": "What is the joint probability distribution for the observed target values <b>t</b>, the model parameters <b>w</b>, and the predicted target value <b>\\\\widehat{t}</b> in a Bayesian polynomial regression model, given the inputs <b>x</b>, <b>\\\\widehat{x}</b>, the precision parameter <b>\\\\alpha</b>, and the noise variance <b>\\\\sigma^2</b>?",
  "back": "<b>Joint Probability Distribution:</b><br><br>\\[ p (\\\\widehat{t}, \\\\mathbf{t}, \\\\mathbf{w} \\\\mid \\\\widehat{x}, \\\\mathbf{x}, \\\\alpha, \\\\sigma^{2}) = \\\\left[ \\\\prod_{n = 1}^{N} p \\\\left(t_{n} \\\\mid x_{n}, \\\\mathbf{w}, \\\\sigma^{2}\\\\\\right) \\\\right] p (\\\\mathbf{w} \\\\mid \\\\alpha) p (\\\\widehat{t} \\\\mid \\\\widehat{x}, \\\\mathbf{w}, \\\\sigma^{2}). \\]<br><br><br><br><b>Explanation:</b><br><ul><br><li>The term <i>\\\\prod_{n = 1}^{N} p (t_{n} \\\\mid x_{n}, \\\\mathbf{w}, \\\\sigma^{2})</i> represents the likelihood of the observed target values <b>t</b> given the inputs <b>x</b>, the model parameters <b>w</b>, and the noise variance <b>\\\\sigma^2</b>.</li><br><li>The term <i>p (\\\\mathbf{w} \\\\mid \\\\alpha)</i> is the prior distribution over the model parameters <b>w</b>, typically a Gaussian distribution with precision <b>\\\\alpha</b>.</li><br><li>The term <i>p (\\\\widehat{t} \\\\mid \\\\widehat{x}, \\\\mathbf{w}, \\\\sigma^{2})</i> represents the likelihood of the predicted target value <b>\\\\widehat{t}</b> for a new input <b>\\\\widehat{x}</b>.</li><br></ul><br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>This joint probability distribution is the foundation of Bayesian inference in regression models. It combines the likelihood of the observed data, the prior over the model parameters, and the likelihood of a new prediction. The graphical model in Figure 8.6 visually represents this structure, where shaded nodes indicate observed variables. This formulation allows us to incorporate uncertainty in both the data and the model parameters, leading to more robust predictions compared to maximum likelihood approaches."
}

## [MISTRAL QA] Carte Corrigée

### Avant:
```json
{
  "front": "How is the predictive distribution for a new target value <b>\\\\widehat{t}</b> derived in a Bayesian polynomial regression model, and what role does the sum rule of probability play in this derivation?",
  "back": "<b>Derivation of the Predictive Distribution:</b><br><br>The predictive distribution for <b>\\\\widehat{t}</b> is obtained by integrating out the model parameters <b>w</b> from the joint probability distribution:<br><br>\\[ p (\\\\widehat{t} \\\\mid \\\\widehat{x}, \\\\mathbf{x}, \\\\mathbf{t}, \\\\alpha, \\\\sigma^{2}) \\\\propto \\\\int p (\\\\widehat{t}, \\\\mathbf{t}, \\\\mathbf{w} \\\\mid \\\\widehat{x}, \\\\mathbf{x}, \\\\alpha, \\\\sigma^{2}) d \\\\mathbf{w}. \\]<br><br><br><br><b>Role of the Sum Rule:</b><br>The sum rule of probability (also known as the law of total probability) states that the probability of an event can be obtained by marginalizing over all possible values of another variable. Here, it is used to marginalize over the model parameters <b>w</b>, effectively averaging over all possible parameter values weighted by their posterior probability. This step accounts for the uncertainty in the model parameters when making predictions.<br><br><br><br><b>Details of the Calculation:</b><br>The integral is typically computed analytically for conjugate priors (e.g., Gaussian priors and likelihoods), leading to a closed-form expression for the predictive distribution. This was discussed in detail in Chapter 3, where the posterior distribution over <b>w</b> is combined with the likelihood of <b>\\\\widehat{t}</b> to yield the predictive distribution."
}
```

This distinction is essential for performing Bayesian inference, where the goal is to update beliefs about unobserved variables based on observed data.</li><br><li><b>Graphical Clarity:</b> The shading provides an intuitive way to understand the flow of information in the model, such as how the observed targets <b>t</b> influence the posterior distribution over the model parameters <b>w</b>.</li><br></ul><br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>In Bayesian networks, graphical conventions like shading are not just visual aids; they encode critical information about the status of variables in the model. Shaded nodes emphasize that the corresponding variables are fixed and used to condition the probability distributions of other variables. This is particularly important in regression tasks, where the observed targets drive the learning of model parameters and the prediction of new values."
}

Point estimates like maximum likelihood do not inherently include this regularization unless explicitly added (e.g., via ridge regression).</li><br><br><li><b>Generalization:</b><br>By accounting for parameter uncertainty, the Bayesian approach tends to generalize better to unseen data. The predictive distribution reflects a range of plausible outcomes rather than a single deterministic prediction, which is particularly valuable in scenarios with limited training data or high noise levels.</li><br></ol><br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>The process of integrating out parameters is a hallmark of Bayesian methods and directly addresses a key limitation of frequentist approaches: the inability to quantify uncertainty in model parameters. In polynomial regression, this is especially important because high-degree polynomials can easily overfit noisy data. The Bayesian predictive distribution provides a principled way to balance model complexity and data fit, leading to predictions that are both accurate and robust."

### Avant:
```json
{
  "front": "What is the role of the prior distribution <i>p(w | \\\\alpha)</i> in the joint probability distribution of a Bayesian polynomial regression model, and how does it influence the predictive distribution for <b>\\\\widehat{t}</b>?",
  "back": "<b>Role of the Prior Distribution <i>p(w | \\\\alpha)</i>:</b><br><br>The prior distribution <i>p(w | \\\\alpha)</i> represents the beliefs about the model parameters <b>w</b> before observing any data. In Bayesian polynomial regression, it serves several critical functions:<br><br><ul><br><li><b>Regularization:</b><br>The prior acts as a regularizer, penalizing extreme or implausible values of <b>w</b>. For example, a Gaussian prior with precision <b>\\\\alpha</b> (inverse variance) encourages smaller parameter values, which helps prevent overfitting, especially in high-degree polynomial models where the risk of fitting noise is high.</li><br><br><li><b>Incorporation of Domain Knowledge:</b><br>The prior allows the incorporation of domain knowledge or expert beliefs about the model parameters. For instance, if it is known that the true function is likely to be smooth, a prior favoring smaller parameter values can be chosen.</li><br><br><li><b>Mathematical Convenience:</b><br>Choosing a conjugate prior (e.g., Gaussian prior for Gaussian likelihood) simplifies the computation of the posterior distribution. This leads to closed-form solutions for the posterior and predictive distributions, making the Bayesian approach computationally tractable.</li><br></ul><br><br><b>Influence on the Predictive Distribution:</b><br><br>The prior distribution directly influences the predictive distribution for <b>\\\\widehat{t}</b> through the following mechanisms:<br><br><ol><br><li><b>Posterior Distribution:</b><br>The prior is combined with the likelihood of the observed data to form the posterior distribution <i>p(w | x, t, \\\\alpha, \\\\sigma^2)</i>. The posterior reflects the updated beliefs about <b>w</b> after observing the data. A stronger prior (higher precision <b>\\\\alpha</b>) will dominate the likelihood, pulling the posterior closer to the prior mean. Conversely, a weaker prior (lower precision) allows the data to dominate the posterior.</li><br><br><li><b>Predictive Uncertainty:</b><br>The prior contributes to the uncertainty in the predictive distribution. When integrating out <b>w</b>, the predictive distribution accounts for both the noise in the data (<b>\\\\sigma^2</b>) and the uncertainty in the model parameters (influenced by the prior). A stronger prior reduces the uncertainty in <b>w</b>, which in turn reduces the variance of the predictive distribution for <b>\\\\widehat{t}</b>.</li><br><br><li><b>Bias-Variance Trade-off:</b><br>The choice of prior influences the bias-variance trade-off in the model. A very strong prior (e.g., high <b>\\\\alpha</b>) may introduce bias by constraining the model parameters too tightly, leading to underfitting. A very weak prior may result in high variance, leading to overfitting. The optimal prior balances these two effects to achieve good generalization performance.</li><br></ol><br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>The prior distribution is a cornerstone of Bayesian inference, distinguishing it from frequentist methods. In polynomial regression, the prior plays a dual role: it encodes prior knowledge and acts as a regularizer. This duality is particularly valuable in scenarios with limited data, where the prior can compensate for the lack of information in the observed data. The influence of the prior on the predictive distribution ensures that predictions are not only data-driven but also consistent with prior beliefs, leading to more robust and interpretable models."
}
```

  "back": "<b>Completed Statement:</b><br><br>\\[ p (\\widehat{t}, \\mathbf{t}, \\mathbf{w} \\mid \\widehat{x}, \\mathbf{x}, \\alpha, \\sigma^{2}) = \\left[ \\prod_{n = 1}^{N} p \\left(t_{n} \\mid x_{n}, \\mathbf{w}, \\sigma^{2}\\right) \\right] p (\\mathbf{w} \\mid \\alpha) p (\\widehat{t} \\mid \\widehat{x}, \\mathbf{w}, \\sigma^{2}). \\]<br><br><br><b>Explanation:</b><br><ul><li><b>\\sigma^{2}:</b> This represents the noise variance in the observed target values <b>t</b>. It quantifies the uncertainty or variability in the data due to measurement noise or other random effects.</li><li><b>\\alpha:</b> This is the precision parameter (inverse variance) of the Gaussian prior distribution over the model parameters <b>w</b>. A higher value of <b>\\alpha</b> corresponds to a stronger belief that the parameters <b>w</b> are close to zero, acting as a regularizer.</li></ul><br><hr><b>Contexte Explicatif:</b><br><br>In Bayesian regression, the noise variance <b>\\sigma^2</b> and the prior precision <b>\\alpha</b> are hyperparameters that play a crucial role in shaping the model's behavior. The noise variance controls how much the observed data is trusted, while the prior precision controls the influence of the prior beliefs on the model parameters. Together, they determine the balance between fitting the data and regularizing the model."
}

{
  "front": "What is the graphical interpretation of a 'tail-to-tail' node in a directed graph, and how does it influence the dependence between two other nodes?",
  "back": "A 'tail-to-tail' node in a directed graph refers to a node that is connected to the tails of two arrows pointing toward it (e.g., <i>a</i> → <i>c</i> ← <i>b</i>). In this configuration, the node <i>c</i> acts as a common parent to both <i>a</i> and <i>b</i>.<br><br>The presence of a tail-to-tail node creates a path of dependence between <i>a</i> and <i>b</i>, meaning they are generally dependent when <i>c</i> is unobserved. However, conditioning on the tail-to-tail node <i>c</i> 'blocks' this path, rendering <i>a</i> and <i>b</i> conditionally independent given <i>c</i>.<br><br><img src='img-16.jpg'><hr><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>The tail-to-tail configuration is one of the three fundamental patterns (alongside head-to-tail and head-to-head) that determine conditional independence in directed graphical models. Recognizing these patterns is essential for understanding how dependencies propagate through a graph and for applying concepts like d-separation to simplify probabilistic models."
}
```

{
  "front": "Consider the graphical model in Figure 8.7, which extends the polynomial curve fitting model to include a new input <b>\\( \\widehat{x} \\)</b> and its corresponding output <b>\\( \\widehat{t} \\)</b>. <br><br>Given the observed data <b>\\( \\mathbf{T} = \\{t_n\\} \\)</b>, derive the joint distribution of all random variables in this model, conditioned on the deterministic parameters <b>\\( \\mathbf{x}, \\alpha, \\sigma^2 \\)</b>.",
  "back": "The joint distribution of all random variables in the extended model (Figure 8.7) is given by:<br>\\[ p(\\mathbf{t}, \\mathbf{w}, \\widehat{t} | \\mathbf{x}, \\widehat{x}, \\alpha, \\sigma^2) = p(\\mathbf{w} | \\alpha) \\prod_{n=1}^{N} p(t_n | \\mathbf{w}, x_n, \\sigma^2) \\cdot p(\\widehat{t} | \\mathbf{w}, \\widehat{x}, \\sigma^2). \\]<br><br>Step-by-step derivation:<br><ol><li><b>Prior for <b>\\( \\mathbf{w} \\)</b>:</b> <b>\\( p(\\mathbf{w} | \\alpha) \\)</b> (e.g., Gaussian prior).</li><li><b>Likelihood of observed data:</b> The product <b>\\( \\prod_{n=1}^{N} p(t_n | \\mathbf{w}, x_n, \\sigma^2) \\)</b> accounts for the <b>\\( N \\)</b> training points, assuming conditional independence given <b>\\( \\mathbf{w} \\)</b>.</li><li><b>Prediction for new input:</b> The term <b>\\( p(\\widehat{t} | \\mathbf{w}, \\widehat{x}, \\sigma^2) \\)</b> models the distribution of the new output <b>\\( \\widehat{t} \\)</b> given the input <b>\\( \\widehat{x} \\)</b> and the weights <b>\\( \\mathbf{w} \\)</b>.</li></ol><br>The graphical model enforces this structure via:<br><ul><li>Directed edges from <b>\\( \\mathbf{w} \\)</b> to <b>\\( t_n \\)</b> and <b>\\( \\widehat{t} \\)</b>, indicating dependence.</li><li>The plate notation for the <b>\\( N \\)</b> training points.</li></ul><hr><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br>This joint distribution is the foundation for making predictions in Bayesian models. The key insight is that the new output <b>\\( \\widehat{t} \\)</b> is conditionally independent of the training data <b>\\( \\mathbf{T} \\)</b> given <b>\\( \\mathbf{w} \\)</b>. This allows us to first infer <b>\\( \\mathbf{w} \\)</b> from the training data and then use it to predict <b>\\( \\widehat{t} \\)</b>. The model's structure ensures that the prediction step is a natural extension of the training process."
}
```

{
  "front": "What is the general formula for the joint distribution of a directed graphical model, and how is it applied to the 3-node graph shown in Figure 8.17?",
  "back": "The general formula for the joint distribution of a directed graphical model is given by the product of the conditional distributions of each node given its parents:<br><br>\\[ p(x) = \\prod_{k=1}^{K} p(x_k \\mid \\text{pa}_k) \\]<br><br>For the 3-node graph in Figure 8.17, where the edges are directed from <i>a</i> to <i>c</i> and from <i>c</i> to <i>b</i>, the joint distribution is:<br><br>\\[ p(a, b, c) = p(a) p(c \\mid a) p(b \\mid c) \\]<br><br><b>Proof/Derivation:</b><br>1. Identify the parents of each node: <i>a</i> has no parents, <i>c</i> has parent <i>a</i>, and <i>b</i> has parent <i>c</i>.<br>2. Apply the general formula by multiplying the conditional distributions of each node given its parents.<br><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br>This formula is the foundation of directed graphical models (Bayesian networks). It encodes the factorization of the joint distribution based on the graph's structure, allowing efficient computation and inference. The graph in Figure 8.17 illustrates how dependencies propagate through intermediate nodes (e.g., <i>c</i> mediates the relationship between <i>a</i> and <i>b</i>). This concept is critical for understanding how conditional independence arises in probabilistic models."
}
```

  "front": "In the 3-node graph of Figure 8.17, are variables <i>a</i> and <i>b</i> independent when no variables are observed? Justify your answer with a mathematical derivation.",
  "back": "No, variables <i>a</i> and <i>b</i> are <b>not</b> independent when no variables are observed. This is shown by marginalizing the joint distribution over <i>c</i>:<br><br>\\[ p(a, b) = p(a) \\sum_{c} p(c \\mid a) p(b \\mid c) = p(a) p(b \\mid a) \\]<br><br>Since <i>p(a, b)</i> does not factorize into <i>p(a)p(b)</i>, we conclude:<br><br>\\[ a \\not\\perp b \\mid \\emptyset \\]<br><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br>This result highlights how dependencies propagate through intermediate nodes in a directed graph. Even though <i>a</i> and <i>b</i> are not directly connected, their dependence is mediated by <i>c</i>. This is a key insight for understanding how graphical models encode conditional independence relationships, which is essential for tasks like inference and learning in Bayesian networks."
}

{
  "front": "What is the role of a 'descendant' in the context of head-to-head nodes in directed graphical models, and how does it affect conditional independence?",
  "back": "In directed graphical models, a node <i>y</i> is called a <b>descendant</b> of node <i>x</i> if there is a directed path from <i>x</i> to <i>y</i>. For a <i>head-to-head</i> node (e.g., <i>c</i> in Figure 8.19), the path between its parents (<i>a</i> and <i>b</i>) is blocked when <i>c</i> is unobserved. However, if <i>c</i> <b>or any of its descendants</b> is observed, the path becomes unblocked, and the parents <i>a</i> and <i>b</i> become dependent.<br><br><b>Example:</b><br>If <i>c</i> has a descendant <i>d</i>, observing <i>d</i> would also induce dependence between <i>a</i> and <i>b</i>, just as observing <i>c</i> would.<br><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br>This concept extends the idea of 'explaining away' to more complex graphs. It shows that dependencies can propagate not just through direct observations but also through descendants, which is critical for designing and interpreting large-scale Bayesian networks. Understanding this behavior is essential for tasks like diagnostic reasoning, where observing symptoms (descendants) can reveal dependencies between underlying causes."
}
```

{
  "front": "What is the graphical interpretation of a 'head-to-tail' node in a directed graphical model, and how does it affect the dependence between two variables?",
  "back": "A <b>head-to-tail</b> node is an intermediate node in a directed path where the arrow enters the node from one variable (tail) and exits toward another variable (head). For example, in Figure 8.17, node <i>c</i> is head-to-tail with respect to the path from <i>a</i> to <i>b</i>.<br><br><b>Effect on Dependence:</b><br>- When the head-to-tail node is <b>unobserved</b>, the path between <i>a</i> and <i>b</i> is <b>unblocked</b>, making them dependent.<br>- When the head-to-tail node is <b>observed</b>, the path is <b>blocked</b>, making <i>a</i> and <i>b</i> conditionally independent.<br><br><b>Example:</b><br>In Figure 8.17, observing <i>c</i> renders <i>a</i> and <i>b</i> independent because <i>c</i> mediates their relationship.<br><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br>This interpretation is crucial for understanding how evidence propagates in Bayesian networks. Head-to-tail nodes act as 'bottlenecks' that can either transmit or block information between variables, depending on whether they are observed. This concept is widely used in applications like medical diagnosis, where observing symptoms (intermediate nodes) can decouple underlying causes."
}
```

  "front": "What would happen to the conditional independence properties of the graph in Figure 8.19 if node <i>c</i> had a descendant <i>d</i>, and <i>d</i> was observed instead of <i>c</i>?",
  "back": "If node <i>c</i> in Figure 8.19 had a descendant <i>d</i>, and <i>d</i> was observed instead of <i>c</i>, the conditional independence properties would remain the same as if <i>c</i> itself were observed. Specifically:<br><br>- Variables <i>a</i> and <i>b</i> would become <b>dependent</b> because observing <i>d</i> (a descendant of <i>c</i>) unblocks the head-to-head path between <i>a</i> and <i>b</i>.<br><br><b>Reasoning:</b><br>The rule for head-to-head nodes states that a path is unblocked if the head-to-head node <b>or any of its descendants</b> is observed. Thus, observing <i>d</i> has the same effect as observing <i>c</i> in terms of inducing dependence between <i>a</i> and <i>b</i>.<br><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br>This result underscores the importance of descendants in graphical models. It shows that dependencies can propagate through chains of observations, not just direct ones. This concept is critical for designing inference algorithms in large-scale Bayesian networks, where observing a descendant can reveal hidden relationships between variables."
}

}

{
  "front": "Explain why the observations <i>x<sub>1</sub>, ..., x<sub>N</sub></i> in the directed graph of Figure 8.23 are no longer independent when the mean <i>μ</i> is marginalized out. Provide the mathematical expression for the marginal distribution <i>p(𝒟)</i>.",
  "back": "When the mean <i>μ</i> is marginalized out (i.e., integrated over), the observations <i>x<sub>1</sub>, ..., x<sub>N</sub></i> are no longer independent because the tail-to-tail path between any two observations <i>x<sub>i</sub></i> and <i>x<sub>j≠i</sub></i> is no longer blocked by the observed node <i>μ</i>. The marginal distribution <i>p(𝒟)</i> is obtained by integrating over <i>μ</i>:<br><br>\\[ p(\\mathcal{D}) = \\int_{0}^{\\infty} p(\\mathcal{D} | \\mu) p(\\mu) \\mathrm{d} \\mu. \\]<br><br>This distribution does not factorize into a product of individual marginals:<br><br>\\[ p(\\mathcal{D}) \\neq \\prod_{n=1}^{N} p(x_{n}). \\]<br><br>The variable <i>μ</i> is a latent variable in this context, as its value is not observed.<br><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>Marginalizing out <i>μ</i> introduces dependencies between the observations because they are now linked through their shared dependence on the unobserved <i>μ</i>. This is a critical insight in Bayesian inference, where integrating over latent variables often leads to more complex dependencies in the marginal distribution. Understanding this distinction is essential for grasping how graphical models represent conditional independence and how these relationships change when variables are observed or marginalized."
}
```

  "back": "In the directed graph of Figure 8.23, the latent variable <i>μ</i> represents the mean of the univariate Gaussian distribution. The joint distribution factorizes as <i>p(𝒟 | μ) = ∏ p(x<sub>n</sub> | μ)</i>.<br><br>- When <i>μ</i> is <b>unobserved</b> (i.e., marginalized out), the observations are no longer independent. The marginal distribution <i>p(𝒟)</i> does not factorize, as the observations become dependent through their shared reliance on <i>μ</i>.<br><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>Latent variables like <i>μ</i> are central to graphical models because they capture unobserved parameters that govern the relationships between observed variables. The status of <i>μ</i> (observed or unobserved) fundamentally alters the independence structure of the model, demonstrating how conditional independence is context-dependent in Bayesian networks. This concept is widely applicable, from simple Gaussian models to complex hierarchical models in machine learning."
}
```

## [MISTRAL QA] Carte Corrigée

### Avant:
```json
{
  "front": "In the context of Bayesian polynomial regression, what conditional independence property arises from the graphical model, and how does this property simplify the prediction process?",
  "back": "In the graphical model for Bayesian polynomial regression, the predictive distribution for a new target <i>\\widehat{t}</i> is conditionally independent of the training data <i>{t<sub>1</sub>, ..., t<sub>N</sub>}</i> given the polynomial coefficients <i>w</i>. This is expressed as:<br><br>\\[ \\widehat{t} \\perp t_{n} \\mid \\mathbf{w}. \\]<br><br><br>This property arises because the node for <i>w</i> is tail-to-tail with respect to the path from <i>\\widehat{t}</i> to any training node <i>t<sub>n</sub></i>, blocking the path and ensuring conditional independence.<br><br><br>This simplifies the prediction process in two steps:<br><br>1. Use the training data to determine the posterior distribution over the coefficients <i>w</i>.<br><br>2. Discard the training data and use the posterior distribution for <i>w</i> to make predictions for new input observations <i>\\widehat{x}</i>.<br><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>This conditional independence property is a powerful feature of graphical models, as it allows the model to 'forget' the training data once the posterior over the parameters is computed. This is particularly useful in online learning or streaming scenarios, where storing all historical data is impractical. The property also highlights the modularity of Bayesian inference, where parameters act as a bottleneck for information flow between past and future data."
}
```

  "back": "The <b>naive Bayes model</b> is a generative approach to classification that simplifies the model structure using conditional independence assumptions. It is designed to assign observed values of a <i>D</i>-dimensional input vector <i>x = (x<sub>1</sub>, ..., x<sub>D</sub>)<sup>T</sup></i> to one of <i>K</i> classes, represented by a <i>K</i>-dimensional binary vector <i>z</i> using the 1-of-<i>K</i> encoding scheme.<br><br><br>The key assumption of the naive Bayes model is that, <b>conditioned on the class <i>z</i></b>, the input variables <i>x<sub>1</sub>, ..., x<sub>D</sub></i> are <b>independent</b>. This means the joint conditional distribution factorizes as:<br><br>\\[ p(\\mathbf{x} | \\mathbf{z}) = \\prod_{i=1}^{D} p(x_{i} | \\mathbf{z}). \\]<br><br>The model is defined by a multinomial prior <i>p(z | μ)</i> over the class labels and a conditional distribution <i>p(x | z)</i> for the input vector.<br><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>The naive Bayes assumption drastically reduces the complexity of the model, especially in high-dimensional spaces, by assuming that features are independent given the class label. While this assumption is often violated in practice, the model remains effective for classification tasks because the decision boundaries can be robust to inaccuracies in the class-conditional densities. This model is widely used in applications like spam filtering, text classification, and medical diagnosis due to its simplicity and efficiency."
}
```

## [MISTRAL QA] Carte Corrigée

### Avant:
```json
{
  "front": "Using d-separation, explain why the input variables <i>x<sub>i</sub></i> and <i>x<sub>j≠i</sub></i> are conditionally independent given the class label <i>z</i> in the naive Bayes model. What happens to this independence when <i>z</i> is marginalized out?",
  "back": "In the naive Bayes model, the input variables <i>x<sub>i</sub></i> and <i>x<sub>j≠i</sub></i> are conditionally independent given the class label <i>z</i> because the path between them is tail-to-tail at the node <i>z</i>. This tail-to-tail configuration blocks the path, ensuring that <i>x<sub>i</sub></i> and <i>x<sub>j</sub></i> do not influence each other when <i>z</i> is observed.<br><br><br>When <i>z</i> is marginalized out (i.e., unobserved), the tail-to-tail path between <i>x<sub>i</sub></i> and <i>x<sub>j</sub></i> is no longer blocked. As a result, the marginal density <i>p(x)</i> does not factorize with respect to the components of <i>x</i>, meaning the input variables are no longer independent.<br><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>This behavior illustrates a core principle of graphical models: conditional independence is context-dependent. Observing a variable (like <i>z</i>) can 'block' dependencies between other variables, while marginalizing it out can 'unblock' these dependencies. This is why the naive Bayes model is computationally efficient for classification (where <i>z</i> is observed) but may not accurately model the joint distribution of the input variables (where <i>z</i> is unobserved)."
}
```

  "back": "In a naive Bayes model where the probability density within each class is Gaussian, the naive Bayes assumption implies that the covariance matrix for each Gaussian is <b>diagonal</b>. This means that the off-diagonal elements (covariances) of the matrix are zero, indicating that the input variables are uncorrelated within each class.<br><br><br>As a result, the contours of constant density within each class are <b>axis-aligned ellipsoids</b>. This is because a diagonal covariance matrix corresponds to an ellipsoid whose principal axes are aligned with the coordinate axes of the input space.<br><br><br>However, the marginal density <i>p(x)</i> (obtained by marginalizing out the class label <i>z</i>) is a superposition of these diagonal Gaussians, weighted by the class priors. While this assumption may not hold in practice (real-world data often exhibits correlations between features), the naive Bayes model can still perform well for classification tasks. The axis-aligned ellipsoids are a visual representation of how the model assumes independence between features, which is a key reason for its computational efficiency."
}

{
  "front": "How is the naive Bayes model fitted to a labelled training set using maximum likelihood, and why is the solution obtained by fitting the model for each class separately?",
  "back": "The naive Bayes model is fitted to a labelled training set using maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) under the assumption that the data are drawn independently from the model. The training set consists of inputs <i>{x<sub>1</sub>, ..., x<sub>N</sub>}</i> and their corresponding class labels.<br><br><br>The solution is obtained by fitting the model for each class separately because:<br><br>1. The naive Bayes assumption implies that the class-conditional distributions <i>p(x | z)</i> factorize into a product of univariate distributions. This allows the parameters of each class to be estimated independently.<br><br>2. The labelled data for each class can be treated as a separate dataset, enabling parallel estimation of the parameters for each class-conditional distribution.<br><br>3. The prior distribution <i>p(z | μ)</i> (e.g., multinomial) is estimated from the relative frequencies of the class labels in the training set.<br><br><br>For example, if the class-conditional densities are Gaussian, the mean and variance of each Gaussian are estimated separately for each class using the corresponding labelled data. The class priors are estimated as the proportion of training examples belonging to each class.<br><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>Fitting the model separately for each class leverages the conditional independence assumption to simplify the estimation process. This modularity is a key advantage of the naive Bayes model, as it allows the model to scale efficiently with the number of classes and input dimensions. The maximum likelihood approach ensures that the model parameters are optimized to maximize the likelihood of the observed data, providing a principled way to learn from labelled examples."
}
```

### Avant:
```json
{
  "front": "What is the conditional distribution of a node <b>x<sub>i</sub></b> given all other nodes <b>x<sub>{j≠i}</sub></b> in a directed graphical model, and how does it simplify in terms of the graph structure?",
  "back": "<b>Conditional Distribution Simplification:</b><br>\\[ p \\left(\\mathbf{x}_i \\mid \\mathbf{x}_{\\{j \\neq i\\}} \\right) = \\frac{p \\left(\\mathbf{x}_1, \\dots, \\mathbf{x}_D \\right)}{\\int p \\left(\\mathbf{x}_1, \\dots, \\mathbf{x}_D \\right) \\mathrm{d} \\mathbf{x}_i} = \\frac{\\prod_k p \\left(\\mathbf{x}_k \\mid \\mathrm{pa}_k \\right)}{\\int \\prod_k p \\left(\\mathbf{x}_k \\mid \\mathrm{pa}_k \\right) \\mathrm{d} \\mathbf{x}_i} \\]<br><br><br><b>Simplification Process:</b><br><br>- Any factor <i>p(x<sub>k</sub> | pa<sub>k</sub>)</i> that does not depend on <b>x<sub>i</sub></b> cancels out between numerator and denominator.<br><br>- The remaining factors are:<br><br>  1. <i>p(x<sub>i</sub> | pa<sub>i</sub>)</i>: The conditional distribution of node <b>x<sub>i</sub></b> given its parents.<br><br>  2. <i>p(x<sub>k</sub> | pa<sub>k</sub>)</i> for nodes <b>x<sub>k</sub></b> where <b>x<sub>i</sub></b> is a parent (i.e., children of <b>x<sub>i</sub></b>).<br><br>- These remaining factors depend on the parents, children, and co-parents of <b>x<sub>i</sub></b>.<br><br><br><b>Markov Blanket:</b><br><br>The conditional distribution <i>p(x<sub>i</sub> | x<sub>{j≠i}</sub>)</i> depends <b>only</b> on the <b>Markov blanket</b> of <b>x<sub>i</sub></b>, which consists of:<br><br>- Parents of <b>x<sub>i</sub></b>,<br><br>- Children of <b>x<sub>i</sub></b>,<br><br>- Co-parents of <b>x<sub>i</sub></b> (other parents of its children).<br><br><br><br><img src='img-30.jpg'><br><br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>This result shows that in a directed graphical model, the conditional distribution of a node given all other nodes simplifies to depend only on its Markov blanket. This is a foundational property for inference algorithms, as it reduces the computational complexity by limiting the scope of dependencies. The Markov blanket acts as a 'shield' isolating the node from the rest of the graph, which is critical for efficient probabilistic reasoning in complex models like Bayesian networks."
}
```

## [MISTRAL QA] Carte Corrigée

### Avant:
```json
{
  "front": "What is the <b>Markov blanket</b> of a node <b>x<sub>i</sub></b> in a directed graphical model, and why is it significant for conditional independence?",
  "back": "<b>Definition:</b><br><br>The <b>Markov blanket</b> of a node <b>x<sub>i</sub></b> is the minimal set of nodes that isolates <b>x<sub>i</sub></b> from the rest of the graph. It consists of:<br><br>- The <b>parents</b> of <b>x<sub>i</sub></b>,<br><br>- The <b>children</b> of <b>x<sub>i</sub></b>,<br><br>- The <b>co-parents</b> of <b>x<sub>i</sub></b> (other parents of its children).<br><br><br><br><b>Significance for Conditional Independence:</b><br><br>The conditional distribution of <b>x<sub>i</sub></b> given all other nodes in the graph depends <b>only</b> on its Markov blanket. This means that <b>x<sub>i</sub></b> is conditionally independent of all other nodes outside its Markov blanket, given its Markov blanket. This property is crucial for efficient inference, as it limits the dependencies that need to be considered.<br><br><br><br><img src='img-30.jpg'><br><br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>The Markov blanket is a key concept in graphical models because it defines the local neighborhood of a node that fully determines its behavior. Without observing the co-parents, the 'explaining away' effect (where observing a child node can make co-parents dependent) would violate conditional independence. This concept is widely used in machine learning for feature selection, as the Markov blanket of a target variable contains all the information needed to predict it."
}
```

## [MISTRAL QA] Carte Corrigée

### Avant:
```json
{
  "front": "Why is it <b>not sufficient</b> to include only the parents and children of a node <b>x<sub>i</sub></b> in its Markov blanket, and what additional nodes must be included?",
  "back": "<b>Explanation:</b><br><br>Including only the parents and children of <b>x<sub>i</sub></b> is insufficient due to the <b>'explaining away'</b> phenomenon. When a child node is observed, the co-parents of <b>x<sub>i</sub></b> (other parents of that child) can become dependent on <b>x<sub>i</sub></b>. This means that observing the child node does not block the path to the co-parents, so the co-parents must also be included in the Markov blanket to ensure conditional independence.<br><br><br><b>Additional Nodes Required:</b><br><br>- The <b>co-parents</b> of <b>x<sub>i</sub></b> (other parents of its children).<br><br><br><b>Example:</b><br><br>Consider a graph where <b>x<sub>i</sub></b> and <b>x<sub>j</sub></b> are co-parents of <b>x<sub>k</sub></b>. If <b>x<sub>k</sub></b> is observed, <b>x<sub>i</sub></b> and <b>x<sub>j</sub></b> may become dependent, so <b>x<sub>j</sub></b> must be included in the Markov blanket of <b>x<sub>i</sub></b>.<br><br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>This question targets the subtle but critical role of co-parents in graphical models. The 'explaining away' effect is a counterintuitive property where observing a common child can make its parents dependent, even if they were independent before. This is why the Markov blanket must include co-parents to fully isolate a node. Understanding this is essential for designing correct inference algorithms and interpreting dependencies in real-world models."
}
```

  "front": "How does the conditional distribution <i>p(x<sub>i</sub> | x<sub>{j≠i}</sub>)</i> simplify when the joint distribution <i>p(x<sub>1</sub>, ..., x<sub>D</sub>)</i> is expressed as a product of conditionals in a directed graphical model?",
  "back": "<b>Simplification Process:</b><br><br>1. Start with the joint distribution expressed as a product of conditionals:<br><br>   \\[ p \\left(\\mathbf{x}_1, \\dots, \\mathbf{x}_D \\right) = \\prod_k p \\left(\\mathbf{x}_k \\mid \\mathrm{pa}_k \\right) \\]<br><br>2. Substitute into the conditional distribution formula:<br><br>   \\[ p \\left(\\mathbf{x}_i \\mid \\mathbf{x}_{\\{j \\neq i\\}} \\right) = \\frac{\\prod_k p \\left(\\mathbf{x}_k \\mid \\mathrm{pa}_k \\right)}{\\int \\prod_k p \\left(\\mathbf{x}_k \\mid \\mathrm{pa}_k \\right) \\mathrm{d} \\mathbf{x}_i} \\]<br><br>3. Cancel out factors that do not depend on <b>x<sub>i</sub></b> (they appear in both numerator and denominator).<br><br>4. The remaining factors are:<br><br>   - <i>p(x<sub>i</sub> | pa<sub>i</sub>)</i>: The conditional distribution of <b>x<sub>i</sub></b> given its parents.<br><br>   - <i>p(x<sub>k</sub> | pa<sub>k</sub>)</i> for nodes <b>x<sub>k</sub></b> where <b>x<sub>i</sub></b> is a parent (i.e., children of <b>x<sub>i</sub></b>).<br><br>5. The final simplified form depends only on the Markov blanket of <b>x<sub>i</sub></b>.<br><br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>This simplification is a cornerstone of efficient inference in graphical models. By leveraging the factorization of the joint distribution, we reduce the problem of computing a high-dimensional conditional distribution to a local computation involving only the Markov blanket. This is why graphical models are so powerful: they enable scalable algorithms for complex probabilistic systems by exploiting local structure."
}

{
  "front": "Compare the roles of <b>parents</b>, <b>children</b>, and <b>co-parents</b> in determining the conditional distribution of a node <b>x<sub>i</sub></b> in a directed graphical model. How do they contribute to the Markov blanket?",
  "back": "<b>Roles in the Markov Blanket:</b><br><br>- <b>Parents of x<sub>i</sub>:</b><br><br>  Directly influence <b>x<sub>i</sub></b> through the conditional distribution <i>p(x<sub>i</sub> | pa<sub>i</sub>)</i>. They are part of the Markov blanket because <b>x<sub>i</sub></b> depends on them.<br><br><br>- <b>Children of x<sub>i</sub>:</b><br><br>  Depend on <b>x<sub>i</sub></b> through their conditional distributions <i>p(x<sub>k</sub> | pa<sub>k</sub>)</i>. Observing a child provides information about <b>x<sub>i</sub></b>, so they are included in the Markov blanket.<br><br><br>- <b>Co-parents of x<sub>i</sub>:</b><br><br>  Other parents of the children of <b>x<sub>i</sub></b>. They are included because of the 'explaining away' effect: observing a child can make <b>x<sub>i</sub></b> and its co-parents dependent, so they must be observed to ensure conditional independence.<br><br><br><b>Contribution to the Markov Blanket:</b><br><br>The Markov blanket is the union of these three sets. It ensures that <b>x<sub>i</sub></b> is conditionally independent of all other nodes in the graph, given its Markov blanket. This localizes the dependencies and enables efficient inference.<br><br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>This comparison highlights the distinct but complementary roles of parents, children, and co-parents in graphical models. Parents represent 'causes' of <b>x<sub>i</sub></b>, children represent 'effects', and co-parents represent 'alternative causes' of the same effects. Understanding these roles is essential for interpreting dependencies and designing inference algorithms in Bayesian networks."
}
```

  "front": "What is the 'explaining away' phenomenon in directed graphical models, and how does it affect the Markov blanket of a node?",
  "back": "<b>Definition:</b><br><br>The 'explaining away' phenomenon occurs when observing a common child node makes its parents dependent, even if they were independent before the observation. This is a form of conditional dependence.<br><br><br><b>Effect on the Markov Blanket:</b><br><br>- The Markov blanket of a node <b>x<sub>i</sub></b> must include its co-parents (other parents of its children) to account for this phenomenon.<br><br>- Without including co-parents, observing a child node would not block the path to the co-parents, violating conditional independence.<br><br><br><b>Example:</b><br><br>Consider nodes <b>A</b>, <b>B</b>, and <b>C</b>, where <b>A</b> and <b>B</b> are parents of <b>C</b>. If <b>C</b> is observed, <b>A</b> and <b>B</b> may become dependent, so <b>B</b> must be included in the Markov blanket of <b>A</b>.<br><br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>Explaining away is a counterintuitive but critical concept in probabilistic reasoning. It shows that dependencies can emerge dynamically based on observations, which is why the Markov blanket must be carefully constructed. This phenomenon is common in real-world scenarios, such as medical diagnosis (where observing a symptom can make two potential causes dependent)."
}
```

  "front": "What fundamental equivalence does the d-separation theorem establish in the context of directed graphical models, and how does this equivalence manifest in terms of filtering probability distributions?",
  "back": "The d-separation theorem establishes the equivalence between two key properties of a directed graph:<br><br><br>1. The ability of the graph to factorize a joint probability distribution <i>p</i>(<b>x</b>) into a product of conditional probabilities as implied by the graph's structure (Equation 8.5).<br><br>2. The set of conditional independence statements derived from the graph using the d-separation criterion.<br><br><br>This equivalence manifests as follows:<br><br>- When a graph is used as a <i>factorization filter</i>, it allows a distribution <i>p</i>(<b>x</b>) to pass if and only if it can be expressed as the product of conditional probabilities specified by the graph. The set of such distributions is denoted <i>&#x1D4B7;&#x1D4B9;</i>.<br><br>- When the same graph is used as a <i>conditional independence filter</i>, it allows a distribution to pass only if it satisfies all the conditional independence properties derived from d-separation. The d-separation theorem guarantees that the set of distributions passing this second filter is exactly the same set <i>&#x1D4B7;&#x1D4B9;</i>.<br><br><br><b>Proof/Illustration:</b><br><br>Consider a directed graph and a joint probability distribution <i>p</i>(<b>x</b>) over its nodes. The graph implies a factorization:<br><br>\\[ p(\\mathbf{x}) = \\prod_{i=1}^{D} p(x_i | \\text{pa}_i) \\]<br>where <i>pa<sub>i</sub></i> denotes the parents of node <i>i</i>.<br><br>The d-separation criterion identifies all conditional independencies implied by the graph (e.g., <i>X &#x2AEB; Y | Z</i> if <i>X</i> and <i>Y</i> are d-separated by <i>Z</i>). The d-separation theorem states that a distribution <i>p</i>(<b>x</b>) satisfies the factorization if and only if it satisfies all the conditional independencies implied by d-separation.<br><br><br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>This theorem is the cornerstone of graphical models because it bridges the intuitive visual representation of dependencies (the graph) with the formal mathematical properties of probability distributions. The 'filter' analogy helps conceptualize how a graph restricts the space of possible distributions to those compatible with its structure. This equivalence is what allows us to use graphs as a powerful tool for modeling complex systems: the graph's structure directly encodes the dependencies and independencies we assume about the world, and the theorem ensures these assumptions are mathematically consistent. In practice, this means we can design models by drawing graphs (intuitive) and then rely on the theorem to guarantee that the implied probabilistic properties hold (rigorous)."
}
```

### Avant:

{
  "front": "What is the set <i>&#x1D4B7;&#x1D4B9;</i> in the context of directed graphical models, and how does its size vary with the connectivity of the graph?",
  "back": "The set <i>&#x1D4B7;&#x1D4B9;</i> (denoted <i>DF</i> for 'directed factorization') represents the set of all joint probability distributions <i>p</i>(<b>x</b>) over the variables <b>x</b> that can be expressed as the factorization implied by a given directed graph. Specifically, a distribution <i>p</i>(<b>x</b>) belongs to <i>&#x1D4B7;&#x1D4B9;</i> if and only if it can be written as:<br><br>\\[ p(\\mathbf{x}) = \\prod_{i=1}^{D} p(x_i | \\text{pa}_i) \\]<br>where <i>pa<sub>i</sub></i> are the parents of node <i>i</i> in the graph.<br><br><br>The size of <i>&#x1D4B7;&#x1D4B9;</i> varies with the graph's connectivity as follows:<br><br>- <b>Fully connected graph:</b> No conditional independencies exist, so <i>&#x1D4B7;&#x1D4B9;</i> includes <i>all possible</i> joint distributions over the variables. The set is maximally large.<br><br>- <b>Fully disconnected graph (no edges):</b> The joint distribution factorizes into the product of marginals, i.e., <i>p</i>(<b>x</b>) = <i>&#x220F;<sub>i</sub></i> <i>p</i>(<i>x<sub>i</sub></i>). Here, <i>&#x1D4B7;&#x1D4B9;</i> is highly restricted and contains only fully factorized distributions.<br><br>- <b>Intermediate connectivity:</b> The set <i>&#x1D4B7;&#x1D4B9;</i> includes distributions that respect the conditional independencies implied by the graph, as well as any distributions with <i>additional</i> independencies (e.g., a fully factorized distribution will always pass through any graph's filter).<br><br><br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>The set <i>&#x1D4B7;&#x1D4B9;</i> formalizes the idea that a graph acts as a 'model class' for probability distributions. A more connected graph imposes fewer restrictions, allowing a broader range of distributions to be represented. Conversely, a sparser graph enforces more independencies, narrowing the set of compatible distributions. This trade-off between expressivity and simplicity is central to model design: a fully connected graph can represent any distribution but may overfit, while a sparser graph may underfit by missing true dependencies. Understanding <i>&#x1D4B7;&#x1D4B9;</i> helps in selecting graphs that balance these trade-offs for specific applications."
}
```

{
  "front": "Why can a fully factorized distribution always pass through the filter implied by <i>any</i> directed graph over the same set of variables?",
  "back": "A fully factorized distribution is one that can be written as the product of its marginals:<br><br>\\[ p(\\mathbf{x}) = \\prod_{i=1}^{D} p(x_i) \\]<br><br><br>This distribution inherently satisfies <i>all possible</i> conditional independence statements, because every variable is independent of all others (no dependencies exist).<br><br><br>When a directed graph is used as a filter, it only requires that a distribution <i>p</i>(<b>x</b>) respects the conditional independencies implied by its d-separation properties. Since a fully factorized distribution satisfies <i>more</i> independencies than any graph could imply (it satisfies <i>all</i> independencies), it will always trivially satisfy the graph's specific independencies. Thus, it will always pass through the filter, regardless of the graph's structure.<br><br><br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>This property highlights that the set <i>&#x1D4B7;&#x1D4B9;</i> for any graph is a <i>superset</i> of the set of fully factorized distributions. The fully factorized case represents the 'most independent' scenario, where no edges (dependencies) exist in the graph. Even if a graph has edges, the fully factorized distribution is still compatible because it doesn't violate any of the graph's implied independencies—it simply has <i>extra</i> independencies. This is why sparse graphs (with many independencies) can still represent distributions with even more independencies, but not vice versa."
}

Even if a graph has edges, the fully factorized distribution is still compatible because it doesn't violate any of the graph's implied independencies—it simply has <i>extra</i> independencies. This is why sparse graphs (with many independencies) can still represent distributions with even more independencies, but not vice versa."

In other words, the conditional distribution of <i>x<sub>i</sub></i> given its Markov blanket is independent of the remaining variables:<br><br>\\[ p(x_i | \\text{Markov blanket of } x_i, \\mathbf{x}_{\\text{rest}}) = p(x_i | \\text{Markov blanket of } x_i) \\]<br><br><br>For a directed graph, the Markov blanket of node <i>x<sub>i</sub></i> consists of:<br><br>1. The <b>parents</b> of <i>x<sub>i</sub></i> (nodes with edges pointing to <i>x<sub>i</sub></i>).<br><br>2. The <b>children</b> of <i>x<sub>i</sub></i> (nodes that <i>x<sub>i</sub></i> points to).<br><br>3. The <b>co-parents</b> of <i>x<sub>i</sub></i>'s children (other parents of <i>x<sub>i</sub></i>'s children, excluding <i>x<sub>i</sub></i> itself).<br><br><br><b>Derivation from Factorization:</b><br><br>The joint distribution factorizes as:<br><br>\\[ p(\\mathbf{x}) = \\prod_{j=1}^{D} p(x_j | \\text{pa}_j) \\]<br><br><br>The conditional distribution of <i>x<sub>i</sub></i> given all other variables is:<br><br>\\[ p(x_i | \\mathbf{x}_{j \\neq i}) = \\frac{p(\\mathbf{x})}{\\int p(\\mathbf{x}) \\, dx_i} \\propto p(x_i | \\text{pa}_i) \\prod_{k \\in \\text{children of } i} p(x_k | \\text{pa}_k) \\]<br><br><br>The terms in the product depend on <i>x<sub>i</sub></i> only through:<br><br>- <i>p</i>(<i>x<sub>i</sub></i> | <i>pa<sub>i</sub></i>): Depends on <i>x<sub>i</sub></i> and its parents.<br><br>- <i>p</i>(<i>x<sub>k</sub></i> | <i>pa<sub>k</sub></i>) for each child <i>x<sub>k</sub></i>: Depends on <i>x<sub>i</sub></i> (a parent of <i>x<sub>k</sub></i>) and the other parents of <i>x<sub>k</sub></i> (co-parents of <i>x<sub>i</sub></i>).<br><br>Thus, conditioning on the parents, children, and co-parents of <i>x<sub>i</sub></i> captures all dependencies, rendering <i>x<sub>i</sub></i> independent of the rest.<br><br><br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>The Markov blanket is a critical concept because it defines the 'local neighborhood' of a variable in the graph. In practical terms, it tells us which variables we need to observe to predict <i>x<sub>i</sub></i> without needing to consider the entire system. This is invaluable for feature selection in machine learning (e.g., identifying which variables to include in a model) and for efficient inference algorithms (e.g., Gibbs sampling, where we only need to sample from the conditional distribution given the Markov blanket). The derivation from the factorization shows how the graph's structure directly informs this local dependency."
}

## [MISTRAL QA] Carte Corrigée

### Avant:
```json
{
  "front": "How does the concept of a directed graph as a 'filter' for probability distributions illustrate the relationship between graphical models and machine learning?",
  "back": "The 'filter' analogy for directed graphs illustrates the relationship between graphical models and machine learning in two key ways:<br><br><br>1. <b>Model Specification:</b> In machine learning, we often seek to specify a model that captures the dependencies in our data without overfitting. A directed graph acts as a <i>filter</i> by defining a class of probability distributions (<i>&#x1D4B7;&#x1D4B9;</i>) that are compatible with its structure. This allows us to encode domain knowledge (e.g., 'variable A influences variable B') directly into the model's architecture, restricting the hypothesis space to distributions that respect these assumptions. For example, a sparse graph (with few edges) filters out distributions with many dependencies, reducing the risk of overfitting.<br><br><br>2. <b>Inductive Bias:</b> The filter analogy highlights the <i>inductive bias</i> imposed by the graph. The graph's structure (e.g., edges, d-separation properties) determines which distributions are 'allowed' through the filter, effectively biasing the model toward certain types of dependencies. This bias is crucial for generalization: by restricting the model to distributions that align with our prior beliefs (e.g., 'smoking causes cancer'), we improve its ability to generalize from limited data. The d-separation theorem ensures that this bias is mathematically consistent, as the filter's output (<i>&#x1D4B7;&#x1D4B9;</i>) is the same whether we use factorization or conditional independence as the criterion.<br><br><br>3. <b>Efficiency and Interpretability:</b> The filter perspective also explains why graphical models are efficient and interpretable. By decomposing a joint distribution into conditional probabilities (factorization), we reduce the number of parameters needed to describe the distribution (e.g., modeling <i>p</i>(<i>x<sub>i</sub></i> | <i>pa<sub>i</sub></i>) instead of <i>p</i>(<b>x</b>)). This makes learning and inference tractable. Additionally, the graph's visual nature provides an intuitive way to communicate the model's assumptions and dependencies to stakeholders.<br><br><br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>The filter analogy bridges the gap between the abstract mathematics of probability theory and the practical needs of machine learning. It shows how graphical models transform the problem of modeling complex distributions into a problem of designing a 'filter' (the graph) that captures the right balance between flexibility and constraint. This perspective is foundational for understanding more advanced topics like Bayesian networks, hidden Markov models, and variational inference, where the graph's structure plays a central role in defining the model's behavior."
}
```

## [MISTRAL QA] Carte Corrigée

### Avant:
```json
{
  "front": "Compare and contrast the roles of a fully connected directed graph and a fully disconnected directed graph in representing joint probability distributions. What are the implications of choosing one over the other in a modeling context?",
  "back": "<b>Fully Connected Directed Graph:</b><br><br>- <b>Structure:</b> Every node has edges pointing to every other node (no missing edges).<br><br>- <b>Conditional Independencies:</b> None. The graph implies no conditional independencies between variables.<br><br>- <b>Set <i>&#x1D4B7;&#x1D4B9;</i>:</b> Contains <i>all possible</i> joint probability distributions over the variables. No restrictions are imposed.<br><br>- <b>Factorization:</b> The joint distribution cannot be simplified; it must be written as a single term:<br><br>  \\[ p(\\mathbf{x}) = p(x_1, x_2, \\ldots, x_D) \\]<br>- <b>Implications for Modeling:</b><br><br>  - <b>Expressivity:</b> Maximally expressive; can represent any distribution, including those with complex dependencies.<br><br>  - <b>Overfitting Risk:</b> High. The model has no built-in assumptions about independencies, so it may fit noise in the data.<br><br>  - <b>Parameter Count:</b> Requires estimating a large number of parameters (e.g., for <i>D</i> binary variables, <i>2<sup>D</sup> - 1</i> parameters are needed).<br><br>  - <b>Inference:</b> Computationally expensive, as no factorization is available to simplify calculations.<br><br><br><b>Fully Disconnected Directed Graph:</b><br><br>- <b>Structure:</b> No edges between any nodes.<br><br>- <b>Conditional Independencies:</b> All variables are marginally independent. The graph implies that <i>x<sub>i</sub> &#x2AEB; x<sub>j</sub></i> for all <i>i &#x2260; j</i>.<br><br>- <b>Set <i>&#x1D4B7;&#x1D4B9;</i>:</b> Contains only fully factorized distributions, i.e., those that can be written as the product of marginals:<br><br>  \\[ p(\\mathbf{x}) = \\prod_{i=1}^{D} p(x_i) \\]<br>- <b>Implications for Modeling:</b><br><br>  - <b>Expressivity:</b> Minimally expressive; can only represent distributions where all variables are independent. Fails to capture any dependencies.<br><br>  - <b>Overfitting Risk:</b> Low. The model assumes complete independence, which may underfit if true dependencies exist.<br><br>  - <b>Parameter Count:</b> Requires estimating only <i>D</i> marginal distributions (e.g., for <i>D</i> binary variables, only <i>D</i> parameters are needed).<br><br>  - <b>Inference:</b> Computationally trivial, as the joint distribution is the product of marginals.<br><br><br><b>Comparison and Trade-offs:</b><br><br>- <b>Expressivity vs. Simplicity:</b> The fully connected graph prioritizes expressivity (can model any distribution) at the cost of simplicity (many parameters, high overfitting risk). The fully disconnected graph prioritizes simplicity (few parameters, low overfitting risk) at the cost of expressivity (cannot model dependencies).<br><br>- <b>Modeling Context:</b><br><br>  - Use a fully connected graph when you have strong evidence that all variables are interdependent and sufficient data to estimate the parameters without overfitting.<br><br>  - Use a fully disconnected graph when you have strong evidence that all variables are independent or when computational resources are extremely limited.<br><br>  - In practice, most models use graphs with <i>intermediate connectivity</i>, balancing expressivity and simplicity by including edges only where dependencies are hypothesized or observed.<br><br>- <b>Inductive Bias:</b> The choice of graph reflects the modeler's inductive bias. A fully connected graph assumes 'everything depends on everything,' while a fully disconnected graph assumes 'nothing depends on anything.' Neither extreme is realistic for most real-world problems, but they serve as useful theoretical boundaries.<br><br><br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>This comparison highlights the fundamental trade-off in graphical modeling: the tension between a model's ability to capture complex dependencies (expressivity) and its ability to generalize from limited data (simplicity). The fully connected and fully disconnected graphs represent the two extremes of this spectrum. In practice, the art of graphical modeling lies in designing a graph that strikes the right balance—retaining enough edges to capture meaningful dependencies while omitting enough to avoid overfitting. This trade-off is analogous to the bias-variance trade-off in machine learning, where the graph's structure acts as a form of regularization."
}
```

Write the factorization of the joint distribution <i>p</i>(<i>X</i>, <i>Y</i>, <i>Z</i>) implied by this graph.<br><br>2. Use the d-separation criterion to identify all conditional independence statements implied by the graph.<br><br>3.   "back": "<b>1. Factorization of the Joint Distribution:</b><br><br>The graph <i>X &#x2192; Y &#x2192; Z</i> implies the following factorization:<br><br>\\[ p(X, Y, Z) = p(X) \\cdot p(Y | X) \\cdot p(Z | Y) \\]<br><br><br>This is because:<br><br>- <i>X</i> has no parents, so its term is <i>p</i>(<i>X</i>).<br><br>- <i>Y</i> has parent <i>X</i>, so its term is <i>p</i>(<i>Y</i> | <i>X</i>).<br><br>- <i>Z</i> has parent <i>Y</i>, so its term is <i>p</i>(<i>Z</i> | <i>Y</i>).<br><br><br><b>2. Conditional Independence Statements:</b><br><br>Using the d-separation criterion, we identify the following conditional independencies:<br><br>- <i>X &#x2AEB; Z | Y</i>: <i>X</i> and <i>Z</i> are d-separated given <i>Y</i> because the path <i>X &#x2192; Y &#x2192; Z</i> is blocked by <i>Y</i> (a <i>head-to-tail</i> node).<br><br>- No other conditional independencies exist in this graph. For example:<br><br>  - <i>X</i> and <i>Y</i> are <i>not</i> independent (no d-separation).<br><br>  - <i>Y</i> and <i>Z</i> are <i>not</i> independent (no d-separation).<br><br>  - <i>X</i> and <i>Z</i> are <i>not</i> marginally independent (the path <i>X &#x2192; Y &#x2192; Z</i> is unblocked when <i>Y</i> is not observed).<br><br><br><b>3. Verification of Consistency with the d-Separation Theorem:</b><br><br>The d-separation theorem states that a distribution <i>p</i>(<i>X</i>, <i>Y</i>, <i>Z</i>) satisfies the factorization if and only if it satisfies all the conditional independencies implied by d-separation. We verify this as follows:<br><br>- <b>Factorization &#x2192; Conditional Independence:</b><br><br>  From the factorization:<br><br>  \\[ p(X, Y, Z) = p(X) \\cdot p(Y | X) \\cdot p(Z | Y) \\]<br>  The conditional distribution of <i>Z</i> given <i>X</i> and <i>Y</i> is:<br><br>  \\[ p(Z | X, Y) = \\frac{p(X, Y, Z)}{p(X, Y)} = \\frac{p(X) \\cdot p(Y | X) \\cdot p(Z | Y)}{p(X) \\cdot p(Y | X)} = p(Z | Y) \\]<br>  This shows that <i>Z</i> is independent of <i>X</i> given <i>Y</i>, i.e., <i>X &#x2AEB; Z | Y</i>, which matches the d-separation result.<br><br>- <b>Conditional Independence &#x2192; Factorization:</b><br><br>  Assume <i>p</i>(<i>X</i>, <i>Y</i>, <i>Z</i>) satisfies <i>X &#x2AEB; Z | Y</i>. Then:<br><br>  \\[ p(Z | X, Y) = p(Z | Y) \\]<br>  The joint distribution can be written as:<br><br>  \\[ p(X, Y, Z) = p(X, Y) \\cdot p(Z | X, Y) = p(X, Y) \\cdot p(Z | Y) \\]<br>  Expanding <i>p</i>(<i>X</i>, <i>Y</i>):<br><br>  \\[ p(X, Y, Z) = p(X) \\cdot p(Y | X) \\cdot p(Z | Y) \\]<br>  This matches the factorization implied by the graph, confirming consistency.<br><br><br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>This example illustrates how the d-separation theorem provides a bridge between the visual structure of a graph and the mathematical properties of probability distributions. The factorization and conditional independencies are two sides of the same coin: the graph's edges determine both. In practice, this means we can use the graph to reason about dependencies (e.g., 'Does observing <i>Y</i> make <i>X</i> and <i>Z</i> independent?') without delving into the algebra of the joint distribution. This is particularly useful for designing models, as it allows us to encode our assumptions about dependencies directly into the graph's structure."

Verification of Consistency with the d-Separation Theorem:</b><br><br>The d-separation theorem states that a distribution \\( p(X, Y, Z) \\) satisfies the factorization if and only if it satisfies all the conditional independencies implied by d-separation. We verify this as follows:<br><br>- <b>Factorization &#x2192; Conditional Independence:</b><br><br>  From the factorization:<br><br>  \\[ p(X, Y, Z) = p(X) \\cdot p(Y | X) \\cdot p(Z | Y) \\]<br>  The conditional distribution of <i>Z</i> given <i>X</i> and <i>Y</i> is:<br><br>  \\[ p(Z | X, Y) = \\frac{p(X, Y, Z)}{p(X, Y)} = \\frac{p(X) \\cdot p(Y | X) \\cdot p(Z | Y)}{p(X) \\cdot p(Y | X)} = p(Z | Y) \\]<br>  This shows that <i>Z</i> is independent of <i>X</i> given <i>Y</i>, i.e., <i>X &#x2AEB; Z | Y</i>, which matches the d-separation result.<br><br>- <b>Conditional Independence &#x2192; Factorization:</b><br><br>  Assume \\( p(X, Y, Z) \\) satisfies <i>X &#x2AEB; Z | Y</i>. Then:<br><br>  \\[ p(Z | X, Y) = p(Z | Y) \\]<br>  The joint distribution can be written as:<br><br>  \\[ p(X, Y, Z) = p(X, Y) \\cdot p(Z | X, Y) = p(X, Y) \\cdot p(Z | Y) \\]<br>  Expanding \\( p(X, Y) \\):<br><br>  \\[ p(X, Y, Z) = p(X) \\cdot p(Y | X) \\cdot p(Z | Y) \\]<br>  This matches the factorization implied by the graph, confirming consistency.<br><br><br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>This example illustrates how the d-separation theorem provides a bridge between the visual structure of a graph and the mathematical properties of probability distributions. The factorization and conditional independencies are two sides of the same coin: the graph's edges determine both. In practice, this means we can use the graph to reason about dependencies (e.g., 'Does observing <i>Y</i> make <i>X</i> and <i>Z</i> independent?') without delving into the algebra of the joint distribution. This is particularly useful for designing models, as it allows us to encode our assumptions about dependencies directly into the graph's structure."
}

{
  "front": "What is the primary purpose of using a directed graph to represent a joint probability distribution?",
  "back": "The primary purpose of using a directed graph to represent a joint probability distribution is to decompose the distribution into a product of conditional probabilities, thereby:<br><br>1. <b>Encoding Dependencies:</b> The graph's edges explicitly represent direct dependencies between variables (e.g., an edge from <i>X</i> to <i>Y</i> indicates that <i>Y</i> depends on <i>X</i>).<br><br>2. <b>Revealing Independencies:</b> The graph's structure (via d-separation) identifies conditional independencies, which simplify the model and reduce the number of parameters needed to describe the distribution.<br><br>3. <b>Enabling Efficient Computation:</b> The factorization allows for efficient inference and learning algorithms (e.g., belief propagation, Gibbs sampling) by breaking down the joint distribution into local, tractable components.<br><br>4. <b>Providing Interpretability:</b> The visual nature of the graph makes it easier to communicate and reason about the model's assumptions, facilitating collaboration between domain experts and modelers.<br><br><br><hr><br><b>Contexte Explicatif :</b><br><br>Directed graphical models transform the abstract problem of modeling a joint distribution into a concrete, visual task of designing a graph. This shift is powerful because it allows us to leverage our intuition about causality and dependence while ensuring mathematical rigor through the d-separation theorem. The graph's structure acts as a 'blueprint' for the model, guiding both the specification of the distribution and the design of algorithms for inference and learning."
}
